items.title: Pre-launch number audit: two wrong numbers, one restored section
items.body:
## What this PR does

A full pre-launch pass: every quantitative claim in the README and docs re-measured against a fresh run of the actual benchmark scripts, rather than trusted from memory.

**Two numbers were wrong:**

- *"Our benchmark shows graph memory preserves +5% more information than a summary baseline"* — the real, currently-measured delta is **+10 points** (89% vs 79%), matching every other mention of this same benchmark. The +5% was never updated after the underlying number moved.
- A resume block averaging **"249 tokens"**, cited in two places as *"measured, n=3"* — re-running `benchmarks/checkpoint_accuracy/runner_v2.py` today gives **178 tokens** (197 / 193 / 144 across the three sessions). A third, unrelated "247 tokens" attached to a *fictional* worked example in `docs/architecture.md` was measured against nothing — removed rather than replaced with another fake-precise number.

**Also fixed:**
- `docs/api.md` carried the MCP registry's `mcp-name:` ownership marker as bare visible text instead of an HTML comment — rendered as a stray, out-of-place line in the middle of the MCP setup instructions. New guard test.
- `TESTING.md` described a "no network access" audit environment from an early debugging session that no longer exists, and claimed 23 stdlib tests where the script now runs 25. Rewritten to describe the current suite (600 tests) instead of a frozen historical snapshot.
- `CONTRIBUTING.md`'s project-structure tree said "42 files" for `tests/`; actual count is 44.
- Persist-latency and label-quality numbers in `docs/benchmarks.md` refreshed against a clean run on this machine.

**Restored "Why TokenMizer and not X?" to the README.** It answers Git history, RAG, plain summaries, Mem0/Zep, and a longer context window — and had been moved into `docs/comparisons.md` during the documentation split, one click away from the page most likely to be the first thing a new reader scrolls past. It's the README's canonical copy now; the comparisons page links back rather than holding a second copy that can drift the way the two token-count numbers just did.

**All six contributor PR credits** (#21, #22, #25, #26, #31, #35) verified against the live GitHub API — correct author, correct description, genuinely merged.

## Type
- [x] Documentation
- [x] Bug fix — two incorrect benchmark numbers

## Tests
- [x] `pytest tests/ -v` passes — 601 tests, up from 600
- [x] `ruff check tokenmizer/` clean
- [x] Memory accuracy test added/updated (if extraction change) — n/a, no extraction change

## Checklist
- [x] No raw dicts crossing layer boundaries (use DTOs)
- [x] No `os.getenv()` outside `config/settings.py`
- [x] External imports are lazy (inside functions, with try/except ImportError)

items.title: docs: add the benchmark harness used to produce the readme numbers
items.body:
The numbers in the README should be reproducible by someone who does not trust them.

This is the script that produced them, with the three ways this benchmark lies written into it as comments and guards: a `crictl rmi` that does not make a pull cold, a localhost registry that is invisible to the NIC byte counter, and an exit code that must be captured immediately or every failed pull reads as a fast one. Each of those produced convincing wrong numbers before being caught.

items.title: feat(benchmarks): standalone checkpoint benchmark suite + speed benchmarks
items.body:
## Summary

New top-level `benchmarks/` suite: evaluate any checkpoint — pretrained HF, or UniRL-saved (a raw checkpoint dir is auto-exported to a PEFT adapter via `unirl.tools.export_adapter`) — across standard benchmarks under fixed, paper-comparable protocols. Zero changes to the `unirl/` package; this is the direction settled when closing #199 (the trainer's in-loop `eval/*` is a training-time signal and cannot reproduce official benchmark numbers — the 8.68-vs-12.4 confusion in #182).

- **One ckpt × N benchmarks**: `python -m benchmarks.run -b image/geneval2,image/preference --ckpt <base> [--lora <ckpt>]`; `generate` / `score` stages can run on different machines; `--report` merges all results into markdown tables.
- **Anti-bloat layout**: all code in `benchmarks/core/` (5 small modules) + `run.py`; benchmark folders hold README + data only. Adding a benchmark = data (or fetch script) + one `BenchmarkSpec` in the registry.
- **Benchmarks**: image — GenEval2 (in-repo test split), official GenEval, DPG-Bench, preference (PartiPrompts × HPSv3/PickScore/ImageReward); text — AIME24/25, MATH-500, GPQA-Diamond; video — VBench (vendored prompt suites + official-toolkit guide).
- **Scoring** reuses the `unirl-reward-service` `/score` API where its scorer *is* the benchmark metric — the geneval/geneval2 specs ship each record's `vqa_list` / `tag`+`include` as `RewardRequest.metadata`, so no service-side `dataset_path` is needed. The geneval2 scorer must honor request metadata (RewardService-side patch prepared during GPU verification, landing there separately); since a pre-metadata scorer silently degrades to a single-question template, **the runner canary-checks the service first and refuses to score non-Soft-TIFA** (verified against both scorer generations, see Test Plan). Text grading is local (math-verify, the same grader as the trainer's `mathverify` scorer, including the `\boxed{}`-wrapped gold).
- **LoRA loading is PEFT-native** (`PeftModel.from_pretrained` + `merge_and_unload`, with an all-zero-`lora_B` loud guard): `pipe.load_lora_weights()` silently drops the exported `base_model.model.` keys on SD3-family and ignores `adapter_config.json`'s `lora_alpha` (rank=32/alpha=64 recipes would be halved).
- **Data policy**: vendored when small + redistributable (licenses verified: GenEval MIT; PartiPrompts, VBench Apache-2.0; AIME24, MATH-500 MIT), fetch scripts otherwise (DPG-Bench 7.4 MB with md5 check; AIME25 card has no license; GPQA gated + canary — all three git-ignored).
- **`speed_benchmarks/`**: a general framework-speed measurement guide (wandb `perf/*` keys + `parse_perf.py`, which turns a raw training log into median s/step and samples/GPU-hour) and `verl_omni/` with the upstream **pinned as a git submodule** (exact measured commit, no code copied), a **runnable aligned SD3.5+FlowGRPO pair** (same workload/reward/hardware on both sides), and the **first measured rows**: UniRL 45.0 s/step / 7680 samples/GPU-h vs verl-omni 111.4 / 3102.8 (SDPA-aligned) and 113.6 / 3042.2 (its FA3 default) on 1×8 H20 — with work-parity reward cross-check and full disclosures in the README.

## Related Issue

Closes #182.

## Test Plan

CPU-verifiable paths first, then the GPU pass.

- `python -m benchmarks.run --list` and `--dry-run` across all specs; prompt counts match upstream exactly (553 / 800 / 1065 / 1632 / 30 / 30 / 500 / 198-gated).
- Text score stage end-to-end on synthetic completions: hand-computed acc 0.3000 reproduced; `--report` renders the table.
- `RewardServiceClient` exercised against a schema-faithful local HTTP stub (chunk boundaries, partial per-reward errors, unserved-reward rejection) mirroring `unirl-reward-service/reward_service/schemas.py`.
- Graders unit-checked: math-verify (incl. `\left(3, \frac{\pi}{2}\right)`-style golds that mis-parse unless boxed) and MC letter extraction (`\boxed{X}` + "the correct answer is (X)").
- Fetch scripts executed for real: `dpg_bench/fetch.sh` (md5 OK, 1065 unique prompts load) and `fetch_aime2025.py` (30 deduped problems; upstream ships the same set three times).
- `parse_perf.py` on a synthetic log: median/mean/p90/samples-per-GPU-hour verified by hand.
- `SKIP=no-commit-to-branch pre-commit run` on all changed files: all hooks pass.
- An adversarial multi-agent review (5 dimensions, every finding independently verified) ran over the diff; all 16 confirmed findings are fixed and regression-tested, notably: results-tag collisions across `checkpoint-<step>` dirs (now two-component tags + a `.source` marker that fails loudly), `--shard` partitioning that could overlap/leave holes under staggered launches (now partitions the full grid before the exists-filter), text scoring silently folding missing completions in as `acc=0` (now a hard error mirroring the t2i path), the SD3 LoRA-loading no-op above, `trust_env=False` on all internal HTTP calls (repo convention), and atomic PNG/torn-jsonl handling for killed runs.

**GPU verification (1×8 H20, 2026-07-14; subsets via `--num-prompts` — protocol constants untouched):**

- **t2i generate**: SD3.5-medium × {geneval2 12·k4, geneval 12·k4 **sharded `--shard 0/2`+`1/2`** (disk shows a disjoint, complete 48-image grid), preference 24·k1, dpg_bench 6·k4}; plus **FLUX.2-klein-4B** and **Z-Image-Turbo** × geneval2 (AutoPipeline coverage beyond the SD3 family). 7.1–7.2 s/img @1024²; resume short-circuit and atomic PNG publish exercised.
- **Reward-service scoring e2e** (self-deployed: geneval2 TP1 Qwen3-VL-8B + hpsv3 + pickscore + imagereward on 4 GPUs): `geneval2/vqascore` = 0.9359 (SD3.5) / 0.9066 (SD3.5 + 3-rollout LoRA) / 0.9210 (FLUX.2-klein) / 0.9162 (Z-Image-Turbo); preference = hpsv3 5.326 / pickscore 0.7901 / imagereward 0.0856; `n_errors=0` everywhere; `--report` renders the merged tables.
- **Soft-TIFA-via-metadata proven by control probe**: a deliberately false vqa question injected via request metadata scores 0.500 (mean of true+false) vs 1.0 without metadata — the scorer consumed the per-request vqa_list. The new canary guard was exercised on both paths e2e: against the **unpatched** scorer the false canary question scored 1.0000 and the runner refused with the actionable message (exit 1, nothing overwritten); against the **patched** scorer it proceeds and scores normally.
- **UniRL-ckpt → LoRA path**: 3-rollout FlowDPPO smoke (`+save_interval=3` → `checkpoint-3/checkpoint.pt`, 113 MB) → `--lora <raw-ckpt-dir>` auto-export (382 LoRA tensors + `.source` marker) → PEFT load + merge. All 48 same-seed images differ pixel-wise from base (adapter provably applied — the silent-drop failure mode excluded); merged throughput identical to base (7.1 s/img).
- **text**: vLLM-served Qwen3-8B (native 40960 ctx); math500 8×2 + aime24/25 4×2 — generate on the GPU box, **score on a different machine** (math-verify over the shared FS): acc 1.0 subsets. A first aime attempt behind `--max-model-len 32768` 400'd every request (prompt + 32768 > ctx): surfaced as per-request FAILED + hard error at score (no silent acc deflation); the aime README now documents the serving-context requirement.
- **speed_benchmarks**: pinned SD3.5+FlowGRPO pair, `sd3_vllmomni.yaml` all-default hyperparams (48 prompts × 16 samples/prompt, 10 denoise steps @512², PickScore, 2 updates/rollout), 25 rollouts on 1×8 H20. `parse_perf.py` on the real console log (`--skip 2`): **22 steady-state steps, median 94.0 s/step (mean 93.8, p90 95.0), 8.17 samples/s → 3676.6 samples/GPU-h**; engine cold-start→first rollout ≈ 6.9 min. Regex additionally validated on a trainside FlowDPPO log (11.5 s/step; samples/GPU-h hand-checked). **verl-omni side subsequently run for real** (source bring-up at its `01c87ee`, now the submodule pin): at the aligned 48×16@384² 10-step PickScore workload, UniRL 45.0 s/step / 7680.0 samples/GPU-h vs verl-omni 111.4 / 3102.8 (SDPA-aligned) and 113.6 / 3042.2 (FA3 default) — 2.48× e2e; all three runs reach the same PickScore after 25 steps (work parity). Full fairness sheet, per-phase breakdown, and engine-pin disclosures in `speed_benchmarks/verl_omni/README.md`.
- **Found + fixed during the GPU pass** (in this PR): the geneval2 canary guard above; aime serving-context README; DPG 2×2 tiling snippet (p → `item_id` mapping verified against the CSV); distilled/turbo pipeline-defaults note (Z-Image-Turbo measured 49 s/img on base-schedule defaults). Upstream **RewardService** patches prepared separately: geneval2 request-metadata support; `envs/hpsv3.txt` missing `tensorboard` + `trl==0.8.6` pins.
- **Not run**: GPQA end-to-end (gated dataset; no HF token on the boxes — fetch script + grader remain unit-tested), official-GenEval mmdet scoring and DPG mPLUG scoring (external scorers per their READMEs; generation + layout mapping verified), video/vbench generation (official-toolkit protocol; the runner does not drive video models).

## Compatibility / Risk

- Purely additive; no `unirl/` code changes. `benchmarks/` is not packaged (setuptools include stays `unirl*`).
- `.pre-commit-config.yaml`: `benchmarks/*/*/data/` joins the byte-pristine exclusions so vendored prompt sets keep verifiable upstream checksums.
- `.gitignore`: fetched/gated data and `benchmarks_results/` can never be committed.
- `image/geneval2` scoring requires a reward service whose geneval2 scorer reads `metadata["vqa_list"]`; the runner fails fast (canary) against older deployments instead of returning wrong numbers.

## Reviewer Notes

- AI-assisted; the submitter reviewed the full diff. Duplicate-work check: supersedes the closed #199 (per its closing comment) and complements #202 (in-loop periodic eval — training-time signal vs. this suite's official protocols).
- Deferred by design (tracked in `benchmarks/README.md` roadmap): VL understanding (Geo3K test / MathVista), unified-model und-side, UniGenBench++, image-editing benchmarks. The SD3.5+FlowGRPO verl-omni pair is measured and recorded in `speed_benchmarks/verl_omni/` (upstream pinned as a submodule); the Qwen-Image and Wan2.2 pairs remain to be run under the same protocol. The extension contract (new modalities = one driver; bespoke benchmarks = per-benchmark dotpath hooks when first needed; agent-style suites = wrap the official harness) is recorded at the bottom of `benchmarks/README.md`.
- Suggested review order: `core/registry.py` → `run.py` → `core/score.py` (wire format) → READMEs.

## Checklist

- [x] I reviewed the changed code and removed unrelated/generated artifacts.
- [x] I updated tests, docs, and configs where needed, or explained why not.

items.title: LOCO end-to-end, first C++ vs R wall-clock benchmark, and repo hygiene
items.body:
## LOCO (leave-one-chromosome-out)

Implemented end to end. Step 1 estimates `tau` once on the full-genome GRM,
then holds it fixed and re-solves only the fixed effects per chromosome,
writing a `chr<N>/` subdirectory per autosome. Exclusion is subtractive, not a
GRM rebuild. Chromosomes run serially because each warm-starts from the
previous one's coefficients, as in R.

Step 2 gains `LOCO` and `chrom` config keys and restricts tested markers to
that chromosome, for both single-variant and region tests, across plink, pgen,
bgen and vcf.

On-disk contract: `SAIGE_cpp_260716/LOCO_FORMAT.md`. `X` and `y` are never
duplicated per chromosome; at UKB scale that alone would add ~570 MB.

**Not supported:** survival traits. Step 1 logs and skips rather than emitting
a wrong per-chromosome model.

## Silent-failure bugs fixed

None of these raised an error. They just produced wrong numbers.

- `loco` defaulted to true and printed "LOCO: on" while doing nothing at all.
- `getPCG1ofSigmaAndVector_LOCO` called the **non**-LOCO `getDiagOfSigma` and
  `getCrossprod`, making LOCO a numerical no-op.
- Chromosome ranges used raw BIM indices instead of post-QC compacted ones, so
  the wrong markers were excluded.
- (Pre-existing) VCF region tests found **zero** markers, because
  `getMarkerIDToIndex` was built from metadata only populated during streaming,
  while region lookups happen before streaming. The prescan now records it,
  with a run-time check that the prescan and stream index spaces agree - a
  shifted index would attribute one variant's genotypes to another.
- (Pre-existing) `nullmodel.json` reported a length-1 `alpha` next to `p: 3`.

## Agreement with R

Step 2 single-variant is bit-exact. Region burden/SKAT agree to ~1e-12; SKAT-O
differs on 4 of 2,853 genes, none near significance. Step 1 `mu` agrees to
~9e-3 and `tau` to ~11% - **not a porting bug**: the same binary yields `tau`
0.2796 at one thread and 0.2336 at four, so the gap sits inside the stochastic
trace estimator's own noise.

## Repo hygiene

- Removed the stale duplicate `step1_saige-null/` and `step2_saige-step2/`
  trees at the repo root (a 2026-05-24 snapshot superseded by
  `SAIGE_cpp_260716/`).
- Stopped tracking the built binaries. A committed binary is older than its
  sources, so `make` sees it as up to date and a regression run silently
  compares against the wrong build - this already produced one false
  regression report.
- README rewritten. The old one described the region-test memory peak as
  "~N x N scale; ~240 GB at ~165k samples ... not yet optimized", which was
  both already fixed and wrong (the peak is linear in N). As written it told a
  reader the feature was unusable at UKB scale. The build section also
  hardcoded one developer's mamba prefix and omitted `R_HOME`, which Step 1
  requires because it embeds R.

## Tests

73 assertions across three suites, all passing:

    bash SAIGE_cpp_260716/tests/run_loco_e2e.sh                             # 30
    bash step2_saige-step2/tests/run_loco_tests.sh          ./saige-step2   # 21
    bash step2_saige-step2/tests/run_loco_bgen_vcf_tests.sh ./saige-step2   # 22

Pin `nthreads: 1` when comparing numbers; at 4 threads the float32 reduction
order makes `tau` nondeterministic.

## Note

This branch also added wall-clock benchmark tooling. The resulting numbers are
still under investigation and have deliberately been left out of the README and
of this description; they will be reported once they are understood.

items.title: fix: the gap between the two recalls was wrong in both places that stated it
items.body:
The README said turn recall is **15 points** lower than session recall; `docs/api-reference.md` said **18**. The table directly above each of them gives 0.970 and 0.830, so the answer is **14**, and neither figure is a typo of the other.

Found by auditing every number in a document written for somebody outside the project. That is the reading that catches this class: the two wrong numbers sit in different files, each next to a table that is itself correct, so nothing looks wrong from either side.

### The gate now holds it

`scripts/readme-numbers.sh` already recomputes the recall table from `benchmarks/results/*.jsonl`, so the difference costs one subtraction and a scan over both files. This is the first **derived** number it holds, and the reason is in the comment: a number computed from two published numbers is exactly as unowned as they are, and cheaper to check than either.

### Proven by breaking

Restoring 15 in the README and 18 in the API reference makes the gate report both, independently, and exit 1:

```
FAIL: README.md says turn recall is 15 points lower; 0.970 minus 0.830 is 14
FAIL: docs/api-reference.md says turn recall is 18 points lower; 0.970 minus 0.830 is 14
```

On the fixed tree it exits 0.

labels.name: agent:reviewed-clean
labels.description: Reviewer found no Blocking issues this round

items.body:
Refreshing every published surface against what the code now does, rather than
what it did this morning.

## Throughput — six figures, all stale

#81 added the KV-cache term to the decode denominator. Every published
transcript kept its old number:

| surface | invocation | was | now |
|---|---|---|---|
| README | `run llama-3.1-8b --quant q4` | 87 | **45** |
| site/docs | `run qwen3-30b-a3b --dry-run` | 119 | **60** |
| site hero | `fit --context 32k --concurrency 8` | 119 / 27 | **60 / 18** |
| site/docs | `box qwen3-30b-a3b` | 731 / 1156 / 119 | **370 / 585 / 60** |

Roughly **2×, in the flattering direction**, on the pages a reader uses to decide
whether their hardware is enough. The site/docs `explain()` block was also still
the pre-#81 single-line form, showing a format the tool no longer emits.

## Counts

**992 tests — 765 Python, 227 Rust** — across the badge, the prose, both gate
comments and the site stat.

## Left alone, deliberately

- mlx-lm's own published benchmarks in `00-verdict.md`
- vLLM's throughput in `10-landscape.md`
- the memory-bandwidth teaching table in the docs site
- `docs/40-ux.md`, a UX sketch whose models are not in the catalogue

Those are third-party figures, a pedagogical illustration, and mock output.
Rewriting them to match our solver would be fabricating agreement.

## The guard, which is the actual fix

`test_the_lab_totals_match_a_real_solve` already ties published **memory**
figures to `solve()`. Nothing tied the **throughput** ones — which is exactly why
six of them rotted silently through a model change. Hand-correcting them is a
fix; the guard is the solution.

The new test pins each published transcript to a real solve at the invocation it
shows, so a figure and the solver cannot drift apart again in silence.

**Negative control:** restoring the README's 87 fails with

```
README.md should quote 45 tok/s for llama-3.1-8b q4 @32768 x1;
the solver moved and the page did not
```

## Verified

755 passed, 10 skipped, ruff clean.

items.body:
**Closes #316.** Ships both halves of the same job:

1. `docs/benchmarking.md` — methodology for external evaluators (measurement side).
2. `README.md` `## Limitations` extended with a **"When NOT to run this"** subsection (adoption-decision side, per AITL's 2026-08-06 addendum).

## Why this scope, not more

Per the issue: an evaluator with a real audience is mid-measurement, and the two natural ways to A/B this proxy (cold sessions, uncontrolled TTL tier) both produce wrong-and-unflattering numbers that read as "this tool does nothing." That's guidance-shaped, not code-shaped. A bench harness in `bin/` produces a number *we* control — exactly what an outside evaluator should distrust. Prose that lets them build their own harness is worth more here.

## What the doc covers

- **Cost per turn, not hit rate, as the outcome.** Explicit table of the 0.1× / 1.25× / 2.0× billing weights so a hit-rate delta translates to a real cost delta. Cited to `tools/quota-analysis.mjs:57` (`W_CACHE_CREATION = 2.0`) and `:241` (`H_billed = 0.1x`).
- **The two dominating preconditions**, stated as invalidation rules not footnotes:
  1. **Warm turn** — operational definition: ≥ 1 prior request completed in the same session, transcript written, base URL unchanged.
  2. **TTL tier match** — both variants must land on the same tier or the pair is discarded.
- **Where the numbers already live**: per-session JSON at `~/.claude/quota-status/sessions/`, written by `cache-telemetry.mjs:230`, with the real file shape inline so the evaluator knows what fields to expect. Also `prefix-diff.mjs` for cache-key attribution (diagnosis, not measurement).
- **A concrete A/B protocol**: workload definition, alternating pairing (not all-A-then-all-B — server-side state drifts), turn-2-onward recording, tier confirmation per pair, minimum runs discussion, what to report.
- **"What the proxy does NOT improve"** — explicit section listing cold single-turn, short-fresh-session patterns, small system prompts, tool-latency-bound workloads, 5m-throughout sessions. On those workloads the honest answer is "no significant difference" and this proxy is the wrong tool.

## The 95.5%/82.3% provenance

The current README callout says: *A/B baseline (v3.0.0 on v2.1.117): **95.5% cache hit rate through proxy vs 82.3% direct** on first warm turn.*

Traced through git history and release notes:
- Number originates in the v3.0.0 release (`2026-04-22`, [release notes](https://github.com/cnighswonger/claude-code-cache-fix/releases/tag/v3.0.0)) and `docs/extension-impact-guide.md:80` (added `2026-04-23`, commit `573fd42`).
- What we **can** reproduce: the shape — first warm turn, hit-rate reported, CC v2.1.117, all-extensions-on proxy vs direct.
- What we **cannot** fully reproduce from the record on disk: exact workload, number of paired runs, tier per variant.
- **Not re-measured on v4.x** — the pipeline has changed materially since v3.0.0.

The doc treats the headline as *directional guidance* for the current release, not a claim of current-release provenance. It also commits: the next headline in `README.md` will follow this doc's protocol and carry a companion note in `docs/` pinning the inputs.

## Verified before pushing

- Every file:line citation resolves on current `main`:
  - `proxy/extensions/cache-telemetry.mjs:230` (file: 458 lines)
  - `proxy/extensions/prefix-diff.mjs` (277 lines)
  - `docs/extension-impact-guide.md:80` (quoted text verified byte-for-byte)
  - `tools/quota-analysis.mjs:57` and `:241` (weight constants + hypothesis labels verified)
  - `tools/cost-report.mjs`, `tools/cache-test.sh` — present
- v3.0.0 release URL resolves.
- IPv4 scan: only `127.0.0.1` appears in doc text as an example of what an evaluator sees, not a real host.
- Commit `573fd42` still on `main`.

## Non-Functional Requirements

- **Size/complexity budget** — one file, 145 lines. Docs-only.
- **Threat model** — n/a. Docs.
- **Maintainability constraints** — no new abstractions. Points at existing instrumentation (`cache-telemetry.mjs`, `prefix-diff.mjs`) and existing tools rather than duplicating. If the pointed-at code moves, the file:line citations rot — the doc says "as of writing" style throughout and the linked file itself carries the authority.
- **Performance/reliability** — n/a.
- **Load-bearing?** — **No.** Docs-only, no wire behavior, no schema change.

## Deferred to a follow-up (not this PR)

A re-measurement on current v4.x that would let us replace the v3.0.0 headline in `README.md` with a provenance-clean current-release number. The doc names that as a commitment — "when we ship a new headline number, it will follow this document's protocol" — but the measurement itself is separate work.

— Proxy Builder

items.title: 📊 Speedometer 3.1 cross-browser benchmark + reproducible harness
items.body:
Runs [Speedometer 3.1](https://browserbench.org/Speedometer3.1/) against the live browserbench.org site across every measurable browser installed on one machine — including BOSS's Fluck browser — and adds the harness so the result is reproducible rather than a one-off screenshot.

The README now surfaces the benchmark with its limitations and adds the Docker and Kubernetes plugins as first-class infrastructure tools, including their `docker_*` and `k8s_*` MCP capabilities.

## Results

Observed median of **3 runs**, `iterationCount=10`. Score is iterations/minute; higher is better. The five external browsers were interleaved round-robin. Fluck runs separately inside BOSS, so the top comparison was also repeated as a paired back-to-back experiment.

| Browser | Version | Median | Spread | Method |
|---|---|---:|---:|---|
| **BOSS Fluck browser** | BOSS 9.2.63 | **47.9** | 1.9% | MCP `browser_run_js` |
| Comet | 150.0.7871.228 | 46.2 | 1.3% | CDP |
| Google Chrome | 151.0.7922.71 | 35.5 | 2.5% | CDP |
| ChatGPT Atlas | 1.2026.189.1 | 34.6 | 1.2% | screenshot |
| Safari | 26.5.2 | 29.9 ⚠️ | 3.7% | screenshot |
| Firefox | 153.0.1 | 22.5 | 40% | WebDriver |

**Treat Fluck and Comet as tied within measurement precision.** In the paired experiment Fluck led all three pairs, but its 3.4% median margin was within each browser's run-to-run spread and 3/3 gives p = 0.125 under a sign test. The durable signal is that Fluck and Comet both scored roughly 30% above Chrome and Atlas in these conditions.

## Main finding: the engine version does not explain the spread

Comet (150.0.7871.228) and ChatGPT Atlas (150.0.7871.115) ship the same Chromium build family yet differ by **34%**, with Chrome 151 landing between them. A Speedometer score here is therefore a property of the whole browser product, not just its engine version.

Chrome's deficit against Comet is concentrated in DOM-mutation/style-recalculation workloads (WebComponents 1.89×, jQuery 1.83×, Preact 1.83×) and nearly absent in canvas (Charts-chartjs 1.04×), SVG (1.06×), and navigation (NewsSite-Next 1.07×). Chrome's field-trial configuration was tested and refuted as the cause.

## Limitations

- **Ambient CPU was 800–1300%** (8–13 of 16 cores), including roughly four cores from Docker Desktop's VM. Absolute scores are depressed and should not be compared with published browserbench figures from quiet machines.
- **Safari is not comparable.** Chrome and Comet used throwaway profiles; Safari ran on a live profile with roughly 14 background tabs and extensions. Its 29.9 is likely an underestimate.
- **Firefox spread 40%** (22.0–30.9). Three runs are insufficient to characterize it reliably.
- **Safari and Atlas are screenshot-derived.** Their committed evidence shows the score, not Speedometer's validity banner, so their `valid` field is `null` rather than an unsupported `true`.
- **Fluck could not join the automated round-robin sweep** and used a different viewport. That is why its small numerical lead over Comet is not presented as a win.

Also not benchmarked, with reasons in the report: Dia (blocked on one-time account sign-in), Antigravity (an IDE whose browser feature drives an external browser), and Codex (a CLI, not a browser).

## Harness

macOS-only and dependency-free apart from Node ≥21 and geckodriver for Firefox:

```bash
cd benchmarks/speedometer
RESULTS=results-final REPEATS=3 ITERATIONS=10 \
  BROWSERS="chrome comet firefox safari atlas" ./run-all.sh
```

| Script | Role |
|---|---|
| `run-all.sh` | Round-robin orchestrator with repeat, iteration, browser, and failure tracking |
| `run-chromium.mjs` | CDP runner for Chrome and Comet; fresh profiles, ambient-CPU samples, verified teardown, and occlusion guards |
| `run-webdriver.mjs` | Firefox via geckodriver/WebDriver |
| `run-screenshot.mjs` | Safari, Atlas, and Dia; CPU-baseline completion detection plus screenshots |
| `crop-score.sh` | Crops a full-display capture to a safe score-card artifact |

The report documents the harness failures found during measurement because each silently produced plausible wrong numbers: leaked browser processes, load drift from grouped ordering, swallowed startup URLs, WebKit-wide CPU matching, occluded-window rAF throttling, and `sips` reporting success for missing input.

## README and infrastructure plugins

- Adds a concise browser-performance section linked to `benchmark.md` and the committed scripts/results.
- Adds the **Docker** plugin: Dockerfiles/Compose, containers, images, volumes, networks, logs, inspect, inline previews, and `docker_*` MCP tools.
- Adds the **Kubernetes** plugin: contexts/namespaces, workloads, pods, services, Helm, logs, supervised port-forwards, inline previews, and `k8s_*` MCP tools; kubeconfig context remains untouched and Secret values stay redacted.
- Adds both plugins to the MCP examples and open-source ecosystem index.

## Privacy note

Raw full-display captures are gitignored; only cropped score cards are tracked and each was inspected before commit. Endpoint-security vendor names observed during the run were generalized rather than published.

## Validation

- Result medians recomputed from the committed JSON.
- New README local links, anchors, and Docker/Kubernetes repository links verified.
- `git diff --check`, `bash -n`, and `node --check` pass for the harness.
- CI runs again for the README commit.

items.title: feat: Bring the benchmark suite to a production-ready state
items.body:
Brings the v2 rework to a production-ready state: completes it, fixes the bugs found along the way, and adds the tests, linting, CI and documentation the project had none of.

> **Base branch note:** this targets `main` because it contains all of `feat/classes` plus the work that finishes it — `feat/classes` on its own is missing 15 of the 17 trials and its source-display feature, so it was never mergeable alone. Merging this supersedes `feat/classes`, which can then be deleted. Happy to retarget to `feat/classes` if you'd rather review the 8 new commits in isolation.

## Why

`main` (v1, dormant since Sept 2022) produced statistically wrong numbers and froze the game for minutes. `feat/classes` (dormant since June 2023) had the right architecture — a coroutine runner and IQR statistics — but the rewrite left 15 trials behind and commented out the report's source display. Neither branch could publish a report worth trusting, and neither shipped a README, licence, tests or CI.

## What changed

### The v1 tree is gone

Deleted rather than patched — its statistics were superseded. This also surfaced a latent bug: the v2 reporter was still reading `style.css`/`script.js` out of the **v1** directory, so it would have broken the moment v1 was removed.

### Correctness

- **`draw_rect` didn't measure what it claimed.** The function labelled "RoundedBox" actually called `surface.DrawRect` with a wrong signature — the published comparison was meaningless. It now calls `draw.RoundedBox`.
- **Per-call average was `mean / runs`**, not `mean / iterations`.
- **`Statistic` rewritten over an explicitly sorted array.** The old index-replacement scheme could double-replace a rank when a run time collided with an index; bounds are now inclusive, so identical run times and single-run trials are no longer rejected as their own outliers.
- **Introspection serialised the wrong variable** (an undefined global instead of the parameter), mangling every captured string, number and Color. It now also snapshots upvalues *before* the runs mutate them, and iterates `1..nups`.
- **Report sources weren't HTML-escaped** — v1 emitted raw `<` from code like `if b < 0`.
- **`coroutine.isyieldable` doesn't exist in Garry's Mod.** It's Lua 5.2; the public branch ships LuaJIT 2.0 (5.1), so `BENCH:Yield()` errored on *every* call. Since `Benchmark` yields between runs, this broke the entire measuring path in-game — a full `internet_benchmark_run` would have failed immediately on a real server. Now uses `coroutine.running()`, which is correct on 5.1 and later.
- **`WriteAsset` didn't create its output directory**, relying on a side effect of `HTMLReport` having run first. GMod's `file.Write` fails *silently* when the directory is missing, so calling it standalone quietly wrote nothing. All writes now go through a shared `BENCH:WriteOutput`.
- **`ReadSource` left a carriage return on every line** of a CRLF-saved file, corrupting sources in reports generated on Windows servers.
- Zero-valued results crashed the formatter on a nil prefix concat; percentages produced `nan%` against a zero minimum mean.
- `Title()` left the extension's dot behind; the standard prefix list was missing `10^24`.
- `Force*` log variants double-printed with a stray `true`; `Parse()` couldn't clamp to `NONE`.

### Architecture

Five nested per-layer coroutine pumps collapsed into a single yield-through design driven by one tick-budgeted `Async` pump. Resume errors now propagate with a traceback instead of being silently swallowed as results, and a faulted job clears its state so a crash can't wedge the suite until a map change.

### All 17 trials

The 15 missing trials are ported to the `TRIAL` builder. Render trials are gated `:If(CLIENT)` (v1 errored on include serverside, where `surface`/`draw`/`cam` don't exist); `ns_accessors` now probes for its gamemode's globals instead of erroring everywhere; helper functions that leaked as globals are local; colliding tab orders are unique.

### Entry points

`internet_benchmark_run`, `internet_benchmark_trial <name>` (with autocomplete) and `internet_benchmark_environment`, superadmin/console-gated serverside. Previously the only way in was `lua_run INTERNET_BENCHMARK:HTMLReport()`, documented nowhere.

### Methodology and environment statement

Every report now ships an `environment.txt` recording everything plain GLua exposes (realm, hosting mode, OS family, branch, game version, LuaJIT version/arch, JIT state, map, tickrate, players). The README states plainly what **cannot** come from plain GLua and needs a binary module or manual recording.

When the optional [gm_sysinfo](https://github.com/JoshPiper/gm_sysinfo) 3.x module is installed, the suite detects it and extends the statement with the precise OS version, kernel, distribution, CPU architecture, physical cores, memory/swap totals, 1/5/15-minute load averages and uptime — the load averages answering the "concurrent load" caveat the statement previously could only disclaim. Every getter is `pcall`-guarded (they raise rather than return nil, and future versions may change the surface), absence changes nothing, and the host name is deliberately never collected since these statements are meant to be published. CPU model/clock (not yet exposed by the module) and GPU remain manual.

CI installs the released **v3.0.1** binaries (checksum-pinned against the release's `SHA256SUMS`) into the test server, so the integration is verified against the real module in a live server, not just injected fakes — the real-binary case asserts the actual rows it produces.

### Tests, linting, CI, packaging

Two tiers, both in CI:

| Tier | Location | Covers |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Unit | `tests/` | Statistics and formatting maths under stock LuaJIT via a GMod shim. No game needed. |
| Integration | `lua/tests/internet_benchmark/` | 56 [GLuaTest](https://github.com/CFC-Servers/GLuaTest) cases in a real GMod server: trial discovery and realm gating, introspection, the timing loop, the background pump, report rendering, file output, console commands, and the gm_sysinfo integration (via an injected fake module). |

Plus glualint, a README documenting methodology and its microbenchmark caveats, MIT `LICENSE`, and an `addon.json` that keeps repo-only files out of the packed addon.

## Verification

All three CI jobs green:

- **GLua Lint** — glualint 1.29.0, clean
- **Unit Tests** — 63 assertions under LuaJIT
- **In-Game Tests** — 56/56 GLuaTest cases passing in a real Garry's Mod server, including the environment integration exercised against the released gm_sysinfo v3.0.1 binary

Locally in addition: 42 files parse under LuaJIT, and full report generation driven end-to-end through the real `Async` pump (17 trials discovered, 13 run, 4 correctly gated, 12/12 structural checks).

### The first CI run failed, and that was the point

Running GLuaTest in a real server immediately caught the two bugs listed above — `coroutine.isyieldable` and the missing `file.CreateDir` — with 8 failing cases. Both were invisible locally because the shims were *more forgiving than the game*: the local interpreter is LuaJIT 2.1 (which has `isyieldable`), and the simulation created parent directories on write. Both shims were tightened to model the game's actual behaviour, and both bugs have regression coverage in the fast tier.

Two further CI bugs were caught before that, by running the tools by hand rather than trusting the workflow: the lint job downloaded the **aarch64** glualint asset (wrong architecture for the runner), and glualint exited 123 on `string_templating.lua`'s mixed quote styles. The quote change leaves the string literals byte-identical, so the benchmark measures exactly what it did before.

## Still worth doing before release

A manual `internet_benchmark_run` on a live server: CI proves the code paths work, but not that the *numbers* are sane. The client-only render trials (`draw_rect`, `set_draw_color`) can't be integration-tested headlessly at all — GLuaTest runs serverside, so they're only covered as correctly skipped.

## Follow-ups

- The report pulls Bootstrap, highlight.js, jQuery 2.1.3 (2014) and CanvasJS from CDNs. **CanvasJS is commercially licensed** — worth confirming that's acceptable, or swapping for a self-contained alternative.
- ~~Wire up `gm_sysinfo`~~ — done; the environment statement now uses it when installed. When gm_sysinfo grows CPU model/clock getters, two more rows in `sh_environment.lua` finish the hardware picture.

items.title: fix(bench): never benchmark three.js, never publish another repo's data
items.body:
## Summary

The first live benchmark run measured **nestjs** and **shadcn-ui**, but the published badges said **`corpus: three.js`** with parity over 751 files. The numbers were real measurements — of the wrong repository.

## Two causes

**1. three.js was still a target.** It remained the default in `run.ts`, the default dispatch input, and was still being cloned. It's a graphics library with almost no security-relevant surface, so our security rules find nothing there and the run measures parse cost. Removed — nestjs (Node) and shadcn-ui (frontend) are the corpus.

**2. The badge step silently fell back.** When no snapshot matched the requested repo, it took "whatever sorted last". Runners cache the results directory, so a stale three.js snapshot survived and was rendered as this week's numbers.

The fallback is gone — it now exits 1 and names what it found. Wrong-but-plausible numbers are worse than no numbers, and a silent fallback is exactly the failure mode that let the old README publish a 51% figure its own source contradicted.

## Also

- `BENCH_HEADLINE_REPO` set explicitly in the workflow instead of relying on a default.
- `benchmarks/results/ilb-headline` cleared before each run, so a leftover snapshot from a previous corpus can't be mistaken for a fresh measurement.

## Test plan

- [x] Requesting a repo with no snapshot → **exit 1** with a readable message, no badges written
- [x] Requesting nestjs → renders `corpus: nestjs` correctly
- [x] Full local run: nestjs, 751-file parity verified, snapshot written as `2026-08-09-nestjs.json`
- [x] Workflow YAML validated

## Follow-up (not in this PR)

ILB-Flagship is **1,762s of the ~2,220s run (79%)**. Cause is corpus choice, not rule cost: next.js (20,859 files) and supabase (6,912) are 88% of it, and both supabase rules find **zero** issues. Right-sizing that corpus plus `--repeat=3` should take flagship from ~29 min to ~3–4 min without dropping a rule.

items.title: chore(npm): drop hardcoded rule count and stale benchmark from the package description
items.body:
The published npm description reads:

> "Open detection standard -- like Sigma, but for AI agents. **751 rules** for prompt injection, tool poisoning, context exfiltration, and MCP attacks. Shipped in Cisco AI Defense. **97.2% recall on NVIDIA garak**."

Both numbers are wrong on the registry right now. The corpus is at 780 on `main` (770 effective), and garak was re-measured to 91.5% on 2026-07-28.

Neither can be kept correct by updating it. The rule count moves most days via auto-crystallize and ecosystem PRs, while the registry description only refreshes on publish — so any number written here is stale between releases by construction. The benchmark has the same problem plus a worse failure mode: a recall figure that drifts upward in a reader's memory while the measured value goes down.

This removes both rather than refreshing them. `data/stats.json` and the README badges stay the place where a current number lives, and they move with the corpus.

Note: the registry listing only changes on the next publish, so this PR fixes the source, not the live description.

items.title: bench: first real benchmark numbers from summitt-cloud, plus five defects that blocked them
items.body:
## What this is

The benchmark harness added under P2-8 / O7 was validated **offline only** — its README said *"no numbers are committed until a real run produces them"*, and none had been. `benchmarks/results/` was empty and `benchmark_results` held one 2026-07-12 run covering q01–q07, so every query shape added since (q12, q13, q15) and every BI Engine column had **no data at all**.

This is that run, against `summitt-cloud.repath_bench` (1 732 954 step rows / 60 000 trajectories): **210 jobs, zero errors**, promoted to `benchmarks/baselines/`. Full report: [`docs/review/2026-07-25-query-benchmark-run.md`](docs/review/2026-07-25-query-benchmark-run.md).

## The result: the snapshot works, the live TVF is plan-bound

The same detail document, two ways:

| | q04 (live TVF) | q07 (snapshot) |
| --- | --- | --- |
| p95, 1–10 steps | 4209 ms | **357 ms** |
| p95, 200+ steps | 8185 ms | **865 ms** |
| stages | 54–58 | **1–2** |
| avg slot-ms | ~220 000 | **~80** |

~2900× the slot cost for the same answer on similar bytes (~110 MiB both). The cost is assembly, not I/O — so **q04 is the suite's only budget breach**, and it breaches in all four size buckets against the §2.6 sub-second claim. q07 stays under 1 s everywhere.

Also: clustering is worth **29.6–36.4×** in bytes, and the designed `q05`/`q13` pair confirms predicates **prune the scan** rather than being applied after assembly.

**The 20 % regression gate fires twice; neither is a regression.** q04's slot-ms went *down* (244 555 → 218 422) and bytes down while wall-clock rose, and per-iteration slot-ms swings 116 748–337 100 for identical work (same 57–58 stages, same bytes). On-demand slot contention. Read work metrics before latency when the gate fires.

## Five defects fixed — each would have produced *wrong* numbers, not no numbers

1. **`.env` silently overrode explicit environment** in all three scripts. `set -a; source` assigns unconditionally, so `DATASET_ID=repath_bench bash …` ran against the **production** dataset named in `.env`. Worst in `generate_volume.sh`, which *writes* synthetic rows into the primary table and whose own header says "never production", and in `bi_engine_ab.sh`, where it would size **paid capacity** against an unintended dataset.
2. **`BENCH_PROFILE` was dead code** — defaults ran before the preset `case`, so `quick`/`deep` both silently ran the `full` shape.
3. **q12 errored on every iteration** — references `model_pricing_effective`, never deployed to the bench dataset. Deployed there.
4. **The engine-side cross-check was skipped entirely** on a missing permission. `JOBS_BY_PROJECT` needs project-level `bigquery.jobs.listAll`; now falls back to `JOBS_BY_USER`, which needs no grant and returns the same rows since the harness runs every job as the caller. It independently confirms the client-side numbers (q04 200+: 8877 ms engine-side vs 8185 ms client-side).
5. **Failure logs pointed at an always-empty file** — `bq --format=json` prints query errors on *stdout*, redirected to `/dev/null`, so `<job>.stderr` was empty for exactly the failures worth reading.

## Honest limits (recorded, not glossed)

- **BI Engine is NOT measured.** No reservation was created, `bi_engine_mode` is NULL on all 210 jobs, and the `studio.md` ruling is neither confirmed nor revised. Verified afterwards that `BI_CAPACITIES` is empty and no reservation exists — nothing is billing.
- **q06 is the brute-force path.** The index exists but is `TEMPORARILY DISABLED` at 0 % coverage: BigQuery declines to index a base table under 10 GiB and this one is 3.3 GiB. Deploying the index cannot fix it; it needs volume.
- **q14 skips** for want of a content plane (`gcs_payloads`), which the README treats as a valid deployment.
- **The default `WINDOWS=7` would have measured an empty window** — the synthetic volume ends 2026-07-11, so q05/q06/q12/q13/q15 would have reported the latency of aggregating zero rows. This run used `WINDOWS="30 90 365"`; the README now warns about the trap.
- **n=5 per cell**, so a single p95 is one sample. Treat single-cell deltas as noise unless slot-ms and bytes move with them.

`benchmarks/results/<run_id>/` stays gitignored (9.8 MB of raw Jobs API documents); the promoted `summary.json` and the report carry the numbers.

## Follow-ups

- **q04 is the actionable finding** — 54–58 stages for a 7-step trajectory is a plan problem the snapshot path already avoids.
- **BI Engine remains unsettled**; the prerequisite argument stands (over `trajectory_steps_compacted` the R15 dedup is a provable no-op, and its window function is what blocks acceleration).
- Raise volume past 10 GiB for an index-backed q06.
- `smoke_164444` / `pre_171706` are throwaway runs from this session that reached the append-only table; `smoke_164444` carries 3 q12 error rows and empty-window timings. Filter by `run_id`, or purge those two ids.

items.title: Restructure the README to the portfolio standard
items.body:
Brings `README.md` into the shared portfolio structure: hero, badge row, fenced disclosure block, then overview / what it does / get it / docs / contributing / licence.

## Wrong facts removed

- **Mangled one-liner.** The description read "Self-hostable **mantis** key service" — apparently a find/replace that ate the word "canary". Restored to "Self-hostable canary key service", which is what the docs source calls it.
- **Stale version numbers in prose.** The beta warning claimed "CLI `v0.1.6`, full server `v0.1.1`, edge `v0.1.3` at time of writing". Actual versions on `main` are CLI 0.2.0 and edge 0.1.4 — two of the three were wrong. Prose version numbers are now gone entirely; the release badge carries the version so it cannot drift again.
- **The "80+ notification channel" claim** on the Uptime Kuma bullet was an assertion about Kuma, not about this repo, and is not verifiable here. Rewritten to say only what Mantis does (a per-key status URL that flips on hit).
- **The "9-file honey-directory `.zip`"** count could not be confirmed from the source, so the count was dropped. The `.zip` artefact itself is real and stays.

## Links

- **Eight links to `privacykey/mantis-docs`** — that repo has been renamed to `privacykey/docs-mantis`. They resolved only through GitHub's rename redirect, which is not a guarantee. All eight repointed at the real name.
- **No live docs site.** `docs.json` in the docs repo defines no domain, and neither `docs.privacykey.org` nor `mantis.privacykey.org` resolves. The README now says plainly that the rendered site is not live yet and links the Markdown on GitHub, rather than implying a docs host exists.
- Every remaining relative path and URL across all four files was checked: all resolve, nothing 404s.

## Badges

Replaced the ad-hoc row with the four standard badges. Each was verified to render a real value rather than "no status" / "not found":

| Badge | Renders |
| --- | --- |
| status | `status: Active` |
| release | `release: cli-v0.2.0` |
| licence | `licence: MIT` |
| ci | `ci: passing` |

`ci.yml` does run on `main` (`on: push: branches: [main]`) and has green runs there, so the CI badge is genuine. The decorative Homebrew and Cloudflare Workers badges were dropped — the `brew install` line is in "Get it" and the edge worker has its own paragraph.

The status badge currently resolves, but note it reads from the `privacykey/.github` hub; if the status-hub PR is still in flight it may briefly render "resource not found". The path is correct.

## Kept deliberately

The **HTTPS-only** warning is preserved as its own block immediately below the disclosure. It makes a different claim to the pre-1.0 notice and is deliberately not merged into it.

## Size

`README.md` 9702 → 6625 bytes. Nothing was deleted; the long-form material moved:

- `CONTRIBUTING.md` (new) — run from source, the full CI job matrix, the three test tiers, benchmarks, versioning. Records that pnpm is the only supported package manager and that CI reads the pinned version from `packageManager`.
- `docs/GETTING-STARTED.md` (new) — both quickstarts, bootstrap admin key, the one-command Fly.io launch, edge caveats, component index.
- `docs/FLEET-PROVISIONING.md` (new) — idempotent `external_id` minting and enrollment-scoped API keys.

items.title: [stale-price-tag] Correct the price tag to what the bench prints
items.body:
## Motivation

`make bench` prints `33 / 35 (94%)` incidents stopped at a cost of `2 / 30 (7%)`
of ordinary work. Two documents still described that as 8%, and the English
README also called the catch rate 93%.

`README.md:205` contradicted its own table two lines above, which already read
`33 / 35` and `2 / 30`. `docs/agent-layer.md` is the repository's source of truth
for these numbers, so it was the wrong one to leave stale.

Codex raised the `agent-layer.md` half on #49. The Korean README was corrected to
7% at that time; the English side was not, which left the mirror pair disagreeing
as well.

## Changes

- `README.md:205` — `8% is the price of the 93%` → `7% is the price of the 94%`
- `docs/agent-layer.md:220` — `the 8% price tag` → `the 7% price tag`

## Verification

`make verify` and `make verify-all` exit 0; the published check total still
reconciles at 738.

The figures come from running the benchmark, not from arithmetic on the table:

    harness    33 / 35  (94%)      2 / 30  (7%)

Grepping for the old strings across every tracked `.md` returns nothing, so these
were the last two.

## Notes

`README.ko.md` is deliberately untouched. Its line already reads `7% 가 가격표다`
and states the catch rate as the fraction `33/35` rather than a percentage, so it
was already correct — this PR brings the English side into agreement with it
rather than the other way round. Flagging it because a one-sided README change is
normally a defect here.

Nothing measured changed; only the prose describing the measurement. The
benchmark fixture fix in #56 is the other unapplied review finding and is
independent of this one — it moves no published number.

items.title: docs: refresh the counts the README states about itself
items.body:
The README claimed `6,500 lines of runtime, 3,200 lines of tests` and `# 132 tests`. Both predate this round of work — the repo is now **7,089** and **4,070** lines with **226** tests.

Small numbers, but they are the first thing a reader checks against `wc -l` and `pytest`, and being wrong about your own repository reads worse than the numbers read well.

**The rest of the README was verified rather than assumed**, since a stale claim is exactly what I had just missed:

- every path it names exists (`ledger/evaluation/`, `examples/mini-ledger/`, `tests/test_safety_invariants.py`, the provenance directory)
- every symbol it names exists (`ToolExecutor.execute`, `Ledger.path`, `reject_durable_reason`, `write_json_atomic`, `legal_tool_names`)
- the benchmark is still 12 tasks across those five named categories
- `docs/architecture/` states no numbers and its eight-step flow still matches `agent_loop`
- the archive's figures still match the JSON they describe (6994.33 / 5575.67 / 16.36% / 0.00% / 90% / 0%), and the tests pinning its published import paths pass

226 tests pass.

items.title: feat(corpus): generate the README accuracy table from a real run + CI-gate it
items.body:
**accuracy-40.** The per-category Accuracy column was hand-typed with no reproducible source — the newest committed benchmark (`.benchmarks/latest.json`) is a 3-document run, and a spot-recompute (#58) found `medical_records` at 65.8% against a claimed 97.7%. This replaces it with a **generated, provenance-stamped table and a CI gate**, so those numbers can never silently drift again.

## Architecture — expensive half vs cheap half

Split so CI keeps the README honest **without ever running extraction**:

```
run-accuracy.ts   → predictions   (production intelligentExtract engine)
accuracy_score.py → fieldbench    → .benchmarks/accuracy-*.json  (committed, provenanced)
accuracy_table.py → render/write/check  (stdlib only, between README markers)
ci.yml            → accuracy_table.py check   → fails on drift
```

CI runs only the last line — stdlib, no model, no fieldbench, no API key — mirroring the composition-report gate from #55.

## The numbers (first real run)

`gpt-4o-mini`, koji `df31155`, `fieldbench 0.1.0`, N=40/category capped, **380 docs, 0 missing → overall 91.3%**:

| Category | N | Accuracy | | Category | N | Accuracy |
|---|--:|--:|---|---|--:|--:|
| irs_forms | 20 | 100.0% | | insurance_certificates | 40 | 85.4% |
| sec_filings | 40 | 100.0% | | medical_records | 40 | 85.4% |
| insurance_policies | 40 | 99.6% | | contracts | 40 | 80.5% |
| insurance_claims | 40 | 94.4% | | receipts | 40 | 79.8% |
| legal_filings | 40 | 91.4% | | | | |
| invoices | 40 | 88.6% | | | | |

`receipts` (all-OCR) lowest, consistent with the render/degrade ladder (#57). `medical_records` **85.4% — up ~20pp from the pre-fix 65.8%**, reflecting the oss-471 scalar-array fix now live on main.

## Two real findings, caught by looking at numbers that didn't make sense

Both would have shipped as wrong published numbers if I'd trusted the first run:

1. **irs_forms mixes 10× W-2 + 10× 1099-NEC under two schemas.** My runner applied the first `.yaml` to all 20 → the W-2 docs scored ~0 on their own fields → a fake **44.4%**. The runner now uses each doc's **manifest-declared `schema`** (correct, general — matches how koji actually routes). → real **100%**. README corrected to describe the mix.
2. **fieldbench's real/synth classifier mislabelled every synthetic as real** — it keys on `"synth" in original_format`, but this corpus records synthetic-ness in `source_name` while the format stays `markdown`. The scorer now classifies the same way `composition_report.py` does.

- **Coverage table** keeps doc counts + notes, **drops the fake Accuracy column**; accuracy moves to its own generated section.
- New: `scripts/{run-accuracy.ts, accuracy_score.py, accuracy_table.py}`, `docs/accuracy-methodology.md`, `.benchmarks/accuracy-2026-07-23.json` (+ `accuracy-latest.json` pointer).
- CI gate added; composition gate still green.

## Honest scope

- **N is a capped sample (40/category)**, stated in the table's own header and the N column. Not the full corpus — the provenance line says so.
- These are **extraction-from-text** numbers; ~91% of the corpus is clean text (see `docs/composition.md`). The ladder (#57) quantifies the parse-quality gap separately.
- `adversarial` and `multi_format` aren't scored (they use the newer bundle layout, not `documents/expected/schemas/`) — absent rather than guessed.

- [x] `docs/accuracy-methodology.md` added; README regenerated + gated

items.title: docs(readme): make the benchmark-image note merge-order-independent (follow-up to #2654)
items.body:
## Why this is a separate PR

**#2654 was merged at `c3dfd2b5` while this commit was still being written**, so `3fc0747c` never landed. This is that one commit, rebased on nothing — its parent `c3dfd2b5` is already an ancestor of `release/v1.0.0`, so the diff here is exactly two lines.

## What

The note #2654 shipped at `README.md:826` flatly asserted **"The image above is stale."** That is true today and becomes **false** the moment the `docs/benchmark.svg` correction lands (#2652, branch `lane-e/claims-gate-2`, commit `1a170806`) — and false in the *worse* direction: a reader who checks the image against the note finds the note wrong, and then discounts the corrected numbers sitting right next to it.

Verified the peer branch's SVG **without merging it**, so the lanes stay independent and the orchestrator can land them in any order:

```
$ git show origin/lane-e/claims-gate-2:docs/benchmark.svg
  >96.4%<   R@5 (482/500)   >1.2 q/s<   harness.py
$ git show origin/release/v1.0.0:docs/benchmark.svg
  >97.0%<   R@5 (485/500)   >232 q/s<
```

`482/500 = 96.4%` and `485/500 = 97.0%`, both exact — the substitution resolves rather than approximates.

## The fix

I deliberately did **not** write "the image now renders 96.4%". That assertion is false until #2652 merges, and this branch cannot know the merge order; asserting another branch's file contents from here would move the staleness rather than remove it. The note is now a conditional that is true under **every** merge order:

```diff
-> **The image above is stale.** `docs/benchmark.svg` is regenerated separately and still
-> renders the retired shadow-harness figures (97.0% R@5 / 232 q/s) …
+> **The table and prose in this section are the published numbers.** If the image above
+> shows **97.0% R@5** or **232 q/s**, you are looking at a stale render of
+> `docs/benchmark.svg` — neither figure was produced by the shipped binary; both came
+> from Python shadow harnesses. The binary-faithful keyword row is **96.4% R@5**
+> (482/500) at **1.2 q/s** (`harness.py`).
```

- **SVG still stale** → the conditional fires, the reader is warned, and the correct values are right there.
- **SVG already fixed** → the conditional does not fire, and every remaining sentence is still true.

Deleting the note was the other option on the table and was rejected: an absent note cannot go stale, but it also cannot stop a reader from trusting a headline overclaim rendered **as pixels** — which is the exact failure this note exists to prevent. A conditional gets the safety without the blind spot.

The matching `CHANGELOG.md` `[Unreleased]` sentence is updated to describe the note as merge-order-independent and to say why.

## Scope

`docs/benchmark.svg` is **not** touched here — it is #2652's surface. Two files, two lines.

## CI

Docs-only; `paths-ignore` will skip most of the matrix. Gates run locally: `cargo fmt --all --check`, `bash scripts/check-docs-vs-ssot.sh` (**PASS** — schema=88, full_tools=103, routes=94, paths=80, cli 89/91, mem_fields=30, release=1.0.0), `bash scripts/check-hardcoded-literals.sh` (**PASS**).

## AI involvement

Authored by Claude Opus 5 under operator direction (CERT GATE 2 follow-up). The peer branch's SVG values were re-derived from the file itself rather than taken on report.

items.title: Fix three benchmark defects, one of which invalidates every published number
items.body:
Three benchmark defects, one of which invalidates every number the project has published. No library behaviour changes — `rowform/engine.py` is a docstring edit only.

## 1. Contenders were not running the same race

SQLAlchemy's `connect()` and `AsyncSession` autobegin on first statement and roll back on release. rowform's engine-level `fetch_all()` opens no transaction at all. So Core and the ORM paid for a transaction on every read, rowform did not, and the difference went into the published ratio as though it were row-layer speed.

Every contender now reads inside `BEGIN`…`COMMIT`. The one-shot path is still registered as `rowform (no transaction)` and priced separately — it is a real and cheaper way to read (0.83x on `flat`), it just buys part of its margin with a weaker isolation guarantee.

One subtlety worth knowing if you touch the floors: they spell it with the DBAPI's `commit()`, never literal `BEGIN`/`COMMIT` SQL. pysqlite only implicitly begins before DML, so SQLAlchemy's `begin()` around a `SELECT` emits nothing and never enters a transaction — a floor issuing the SQL by hand *does*, and would do strictly more work than the contenders it bounds.

## 2. Pools were three different configurations

rowform ran `1+3`, the SQLAlchemy contenders ran the engine default `5+10`, and the asyncpg floor ran `min1/max4`. Now uniformly `pool_size=4, max_overflow=0`.

`1+3` and `4+0` have the same ceiling and behave differently: SQLAlchemy *closes* overflow connections on return, asyncpg retains them. Measured with four concurrent checkouts over two rounds — `1+3` reused **1** connection and opened three fresh; `4+0` reused **4**. So the asyncpg floor was holding four alive while every SQLAlchemy contender re-established three per request, which on postgres is a TCP connect plus auth on three quarters of the traffic.

The sqlite floors also had no pool at all — one hoisted `aiosqlite.Connection`, which meant no checkout *and* a concurrency ceiling of one, since aiosqlite gives each connection a single worker thread. Two errors pushing in opposite directions. They now use a minimal pool (`benchmarks/harness/aiosqlite_pool.py`).

## 3. The harness was monkey-patching itself

`python -m benchmarks` mounted every subcommand eagerly. `benchmarks.cli.load` imports `benchmarks.load.locust`, and importing locust runs `gevent.monkey.patch_all()`, which replaces `threading.Thread` process-wide. aiosqlite runs every statement on a per-connection worker thread — so the driver under test was not using real threads.

Measured A/B, one process per arm, three reps:

| | gevent off | gevent on | |
|---|---|---|---|
| hand-rolled floor, sqlite flat | 1.2940 ms | 1.6451 ms | +27% |
| rowform, sqlite flat | 1.3580 ms | 1.8076 ms | +33% |
| ratio | 1.05x | 1.10x | |

Absolutes ~30% slow; the ratio skewed ~5% because it does not hit both arms equally. **Every entry in `RUNS.md` before today, and every table published from one, was taken this way.** Nothing looked wrong — runs completed, the equivalence gate passed, trial spread stayed tight.

`load`/`profile` are now mounted lazily, and `timing.assert_unpatched_threading()` fails the run rather than quietly inflating it.

It surfaced sideways: a new import deadlocked the suite, and I fixed the deadlock by deferring that import without asking why a benchmark process had a patched `threading` at all. That hour is corrections #13's actual lesson.

## A third floor

"Floor" was answering two questions and the reader could not tell which:

- `floor: hand-rolled` — no SQLAlchemy anywhere. *What would this cost written from scratch?*
- `floor: on SQLAlchemy` — its pool, its transaction, hand-written dicts where rowform hydrates. *I am already on SQLAlchemy; what does rowform cost me?*

The gap between them is the plumbing (~0.21 ms on `flat`), and it used to be published as row-layer cost. Also added `hand-written dict (mock)` as the parsing floor, and the two `raw aiosqlite`/`raw asyncpg` floors were renamed so the two questions can't be conflated again.

## What the numbers now say

```
flat/sqlite                                    ms      vs rowform
  raw driver -> dicts (no SQLAlchemy)        0.9129      0.64x
  + the same hydrator (no SQLAlchemy)        1.0044      0.70x
  same pool + transaction -> dicts           1.1272      0.79x
  rowform fetch_all()                        1.4251      1.00x
  rowform, off the engine (no transaction)   1.1802      0.83x
  SQLAlchemy Core (positional)               1.5388     ~1.08x
  SQLAlchemy ORM                             6.2281      4.37x
```

The headline moves from *"1.2–1.3x Core's result layer"* to **a tie with Core, and 2.4–4.4x the ORM**. The row-layer comparison survives intact and is where it always was — with the driver, pool and transaction removed, it is 0.17 / 0.30 / 0.43 / 3.55 ms for hand dicts / rowform / Core / ORM. End-to-end ratios compress that because a read is mostly not the row layer.

The claim I would actually defend: **the compiled hydrator costs +5.7–12.6% over hand-written dict-building, and that overhead does not grow as the conversions get expensive** — the widest shape, eight of nine columns needing `DateTime`/`Numeric`/`Enum`/`Uuid` parsing, is the *cheapest* of the three at +5.7%, against +10.0% for the one column needing a `bool()`. That is what inlining the processors buys.

## Please read these caveats before quoting anything

- **The numbers are provisional.** First sweep of the right *kind*, but taken on a workstation with a browser and a music player scheduled onto the pinned cores: 15.2% worst spread against 8.1% for a quiet run. Anything within ±10% is not ordered, which includes rowform vs Core on `flat` and `join`. Both README and METHODOLOGY carry a "do not quote" block. A clean run replaces them; `scripts/publish_tables.py` regenerates both tables from the recorded `run.json`.
- **Postgres is withdrawn, not updated.** All three changes above move it and none of them were measured there. I removed the table rather than leave known-wrong numbers — in particular `~0.96x`, "as fast as hand-rolling the driver", which does not survive the transaction change on its own (there the transaction is two real round trips).
- **`--pin` is advisory in one direction.** It pins the benchmark *onto* cores; it cannot keep anything else *off* them, and the gate has no way to see that. Now documented.

## Docs

Full sweep, per the write-once-at-PR-time rule. README example switched to `async with db.begin() as conn:` so the docs and the benchmarked call agree; GUIDE gained an explicit statement that `db.*` off the engine opens no transaction (the ORM equivalence table is where that omission actually misled); `PLAN_SQLA_API.md` §2's ablation withdrawn; `FINDINGS.md`'s `AUTOCOMMIT` entry annotated. Two new corrections in `METHODOLOGY.md` — #12 scoring an isolation guarantee as row-layer speed, #13 the harness monkey-patching itself. `RUNS.md` has a new entry; the previous one is marked superseded rather than edited.

## Also

`.github/workflows/benchmarks.yml`: the checkout was pinned to `ref: main`, so dispatching against a branch silently benchmarked main. Removed, and posting to the tracking issue is now gated on `github.ref == refs/heads/main` — branch runs keep their results in the step summary and an artifact, since the issue's comments are also the change-detection state. Concurrency is per-ref, and `wide` was added to the sweep.

---

781 tests, lint and typecheck green. Equivalence gates pass byte-identical on all three shapes (same sha256 as before the change — the transaction did not alter output).

items.title: Document Arm server CPU setup for LM7
items.body:
Three PRs ([#134](https://github.com/lmontigny/lm7/pull/134), [#135](https://github.com/lmontigny/lm7/pull/135), [#136](https://github.com/lmontigny/lm7/pull/136)) have now used a Neoverse Linux server, and everything learned about *getting one working* lived in commit messages rather than anywhere a reader would look. `docs/` has [amd-cpu.md](docs/amd-cpu.md) for the AMD-CPU-specific half of CPU inference and had nothing equivalent for Arm. This is that file.

Your item 5 — the setup traps turned out to be the interesting part, so it is not a thin doc.

## The traps, in the order they bite

- **`python3-dev` is not optional if you intend to use Inductor.** It compiles C++ at run time and needs `Python.h`. A cloud image ships the interpreter without the headers, and the failure arrives on the first `lm7.compile(..., backend="inductor")` rather than at install time.
- **The boot disk is too small.** Arm cloud images default to ~10 GiB; `torch` plus one checkpoint fills it. `HF_HOME` targets it by default, so the venv *and* the cache want moving to a data disk.
- **`numpy` is not a `torch` dependency.** Its absence prints `Failed to initialize NumPy` and continues — easy to carry a long way.
- **The CPU wheel index is the one that was tested.** Whether plain `pip install torch` resolves to a CPU build on aarch64 was *not* checked, and CUDA-on-Arm wheels now exist for server parts, so the historical "aarch64 means CPU-only" assumption is called out rather than repeated.

## What the toolchain says about itself

Three layers, three different questions, and only the last is about matrix hardware:

| | on the N3 |
| --- | --- |
| `torch.backends.cpu.get_cpu_capability()` | `SVE128` — the *vector length*, not a matrix-unit answer |
| `torch.__config__.show()` | `USE_MKLDNN=1`, `USE_OPENMP=ON`, `BLAS_INFO=open` |
| oneDNN | `v3.12.0`, `isa:AArch64 SVE (128 bits)` |

Vector width decides which oneDNN kernels are eligible at all — `matmul:brg:sve_512` is rejected for `unsupported isa` on a 128-bit core — so a Neoverse N-series result should not be carried onto a V-series part.

## The extras table is deliberately weak

It is `pip install --dry-run` output, so it records **that a wheel exists and nothing else**. Nothing was installed, imported, or run. `torch-tensorrt` resolves too, and is for NVIDIA GPUs. The doc says this in an `[!IMPORTANT]` callout rather than letting the table read as validation.

`zentorch` is the one certainty — no aarch64 wheel, x86-64 Linux only by construction.

## Also

Ends with the two mistakes made on this host that produced plausible, wrong numbers, so the next person does not repeat them: a benchmark process outliving the `ssh --command` that started it and contending with the next run (10x inflated medians, silently), and `ONEDNN_VERBOSE=all` exhausting 31 GiB when something buffers it.

Indexed in [docs/README.md](docs/README.md) under Hardware setup, and cross-linked from `cpu.md` and `tested-hardware.md`. All anchors and link targets verified to resolve.

items.title: fix: correct tier-2/3 CER (<DR> editor-token contamination) + v0.1.1 corrections
items.body:
## The public benchmark ships wrong numbers

`benchmark-v0.1.0` reports tier-2 CER **0.0172** and tier-3 **0.0234**. Both are wrong.

| figure | v0.1.0 (withdrawn) | corrected |
|---|---|---|
| tier-2 CER, B vs consensus | 0.0172 [0.0105, 0.0248] | **0.0031 [0.0006, 0.0062]** |
| tier-3 CER, B vs consensus | 0.0234 [0.0166, 0.0309] | **0.0119 [0.0085, 0.0156]** |
| adjudication, tier-2 edits | 165 | **33** |
| adjudication, tier-3 edits | 280 | **148** |

## Cause

`<DR>`, the annotator-tool token for a double *rafe*, was scored as four literal ASCII characters in the tier-2/3 CER path. `iaa/cer.py` asserted editor tokens were "already stripped during `split_chunks`" — they were not. `split_chunks` strips only `PASSTHRU_TAGS`, and `<DR>` is deliberately excluded so tier-4 extraction can emit a `double_rafe` record from it. Nothing removed it afterwards.

The three sides carry unequal counts (A 25, B 56, consensus 27), so every excess token scored as four spurious edits.

Self-contradictory as well as wrong: `strip.py` already excludes U+05BF (*rafe*) from tier 2 precisely "so it is not double-counted across tiers". The single *rafe* was stripped; the double *rafe*, in ASCII, was not.

## Direction

**Conservative.** The bug made the two annotators look *less* consistent than they are. No conclusion reverses.

## Not affected

Verified field-by-field over regenerated result JSONs — **262 tier-4 and stratification fields compared, zero changed**: tier-1 CER 0.0029; tier-4 F1 exact 0.9187; Krippendorff α 0.7470; BL-05 *rafe* baseline F1 0.6210; every corpus count. Tier 1 is immune because its projection keeps only Hebrew consonants, space and *maqaf*.

## Also in this PR

- **`personnel_note` removed** from four public fixtures — it named a collaborator in full alongside an internal personnel correction and referenced a private-repo file. It remains in the immutable `v0.1.0` tag.
- **David Zev Moster added** to `CITATION.cff`, README citation, `LICENSE.md` attribution and `ACKNOWLEDGMENTS.md`. He produced half the reported agreement and was named only in the changelog and data files, while his projection ships under attribution-required terms.
- **Two false statements removed from this repo's own documentation.** `generate_iaa_report.py` claimed in two places that the headline CER was "NOT recomputable without the gitignored UXLC 2.5 cache." Tiers 1–3 recompute from the three committed projections alone. **Two independent external reviewers repeated that claim in their audits, having taken it from this docstring rather than testing it.**
- The shipped `_note` described the metric as code-point Levenshtein on NFC; it is cluster-aligned code-point CER on NFD, macro-averaged over verses.

## Structural fix

`masoretic_eval.iaa.cer.tier_view()` is now the single definition of a chunk's scoring view. The same sequence had been inlined in **three** places — `cer.py`, `scripts/generate_iaa_report.py`, and the release test meant to guard reproducibility — and the latter two would have silently missed the new strip.

Regression test `tests/iaa/test_editor_token_cer_isolation.py` asserts tier CER is invariant to editor tokens at every tier, and that tier-4 extraction still consumes `<DR>`.

## Gates

- `pytest` — 360 passed, 8 skipped
- `generate_iaa_report.py --check` — ok
- `verify_gt_hash.py --check` — ok
- `audit_release.py --all --release-tier` — **PASS**

## Provenance

Found while verifying three independent external reviews of `benchmark-v0.1.0`. The tier-3 half was flagged by the Codex reviewer; the larger tier-2 half and the adjudication-count contamination were found during verification of that finding.
