items.title: chore(docs): remove the internal benchmarks and manuals, and correct the offload figures
items.body:
## Description

Most of what is removed here already has a counterpart upstream in the backend repo and will
arrive through the backend sync. What lives in this repo today is a second, hand-maintained
copy, so the two drift apart. Dropping them leaves a single source.

| This repo (removed) | backend counterpart |
|---|---|
| `backend/tests/benchmark_llama_server_prefill.py` | `tests/e2e/benchmark_llama_server_prefill.py` |
| `backend/tests/benchmark_offload_vram.py` | `tests/e2e/benchmark_offload_vram.py` |
| `docs/benchmarks.md` (zh) · `docs/benchmarks.en.md` | `docs/benchmarks.md` (en) |
| `docs/inference_manual.html` (zh) · `.en.html` | `docs/inference_manual.zh-TW.html` · `inference_manual.html` |
| `docs/finetune_manual.html` (zh) · `.en.html` | `docs/finetune_manual.zh-TW.html` · `finetune_manual.html` |
| `docs/site-map.html` | `docs/site-map.html` |

Note the language-suffix convention is **inverted** between the two repos: here the bare
`.html` / `.md` is the Traditional Chinese file and `.en` marks English, while upstream the
bare name is English and `.zh-TW` marks Chinese. The names collide but the languages do not
line up, so the sync needs to account for it rather than assume a same-name overwrite.

Three things have no upstream counterpart and are simply dropped:

- The two raw result files, `benchmark_llama_server_prefill_results.json` and
  `benchmark_offload_vram_results.json`. Upstream deliberately keeps benchmark output out of
  git (`chore(tests): keep the llama-server benchmark results out of git`) and writes it to a
  gitignored `tests/results/` instead. This repo now matches that.
- The three example configs: `examples/fine-tune_configs/Llama3.3-70B-finetune.json`,
  `examples/fine-tune_configs/qwen3.5-122b-lora-finetune.json`, and
  `examples/inference_configs/GPT-OSS-120B-demo-inference.json`. These were written here and
  exist nowhere else, so they go away rather than moving. The `examples/` directory is emptied
  and disappears.

**References updated:**

- `README.md` / `README.zh-TW.md` — drop the links and directory entries pointing at
  benchmarks, the site map, both HTML manuals, and `examples/`.
- `wiki/{en,zh}/comparisons/trusta-ast-vs-market-solutions.md`,
  `concepts/offload-mechanism.md`, `summary/trusta-ast-core-differentiation.md` — replace
  "see `benchmark_*.py` / reproduce it with that script / raw data in `*_results.json`" with
  "measured in-house". Those paths were already stale once upstream moved `tests/` to
  `tests/e2e/`; naming no path means a future upstream reorganisation cannot rot these pages
  again.

## Corrected figure

The published VRAM reduction was wrong and is corrected here, in
`wiki/{en,zh}/concepts/offload-mechanism.md` and
`wiki/{en,zh}/summary/trusta-ast-core-differentiation.md`.

The old figure compared whole-device VRAM against model weights. The device peak includes
whatever other processes were already holding, and the benchmark recorded that baseline
without ever subtracting it, so the reduction was understated. The backend PR fixes the
benchmark; this applies the same correction to what is already published:

    model peak = 13.39 - 1.65 = 11.74 GB
    reduction  = 1 - 11.74 / 27.508 = 57.3%        (was published as 51.3%)

This is **recomputed from the raw fields the original run recorded, not a new run**. The
full-GPU requirement, the pre-load baseline and the device peak were all captured correctly;
only the final arithmetic was wrong. The pages now state both numbers — the ~11.7 GB
attributable to the model and the ~13.4 GB the device actually peaked at — so the two are no
longer conflated.

**The tok/s figure is deliberately left at ~0.5 and flagged as pending.** The original run
stored a count of SSE chunks in the `completion_tokens` field, so the real token count was
never recorded and cannot be recovered. Confirming it needs the benchmark re-run against a GPU
with the weights available.

## Related Issues

<!-- e.g. Closes #123, Relates to #456 -->

## Checklist

- [x] The PR title follows [Conventional Commits](https://www.conventionalcommits.org/en/v1.0.0/)
- [x] Commits follow Conventional Commits (see [CONTRIBUTING.md](CONTRIBUTING.md))
- [ ] `pytest` passes locally — not run; no collected test was touched (`backend/pytest.ini`
      sets no `python_files`, so `benchmark_*.py` was never collected)
- [x] Tests were added or updated where relevant — n/a, deletions and documentation only
- [x] Documentation was updated where relevant (English and 繁體中文 where applicable)
- [x] I have read the [Code of Conduct](CODE_OF_CONDUCT.md)

## Notes for Reviewers

- **Merge order matters.** `benchmark_offload_vram.py` only exists upstream once the
  corresponding backend PR lands — it is added there in the same change that fixes the
  hard-coded paths. Merge that one first, or this table describes a file that is not there yet.
- The corrected reduction is arithmetic on already-recorded measurements, so it needs no GPU to
  verify: the three inputs are in the deleted `benchmark_offload_vram_results.json`, visible in
  this PR's diff.
- Every deleted filename was grepped across the repo; nothing links to them any more. The only
  remaining mentions are provenance notes in `wiki/{en,zh}/log.md` and
  `wiki/{en,zh}/sources/finetune_manual.md` ("Ingested `inference_manual.html`"), which record
  where the wiki content came from rather than linking to the file, so they were left as they
  are.
- The HTML manuals' content was already absorbed into `wiki/{en,zh}/sources/`; the wiki itself
  is untouched.

items.title: Make the benchmark harness fail loudly instead of silently dropping data (#425)
items.body:
Addresses the data-integrity subset of #425 (items 5, 1, 4, 2). Item 3 (CI wiring) and the k6 digest pin are deliberately out of scope — see below.

## Why this comes before any further published numbers
The #424 OKE validation run **silently dropped `tuned burst rep 2`'s k6 metrics and exited 0**. A human reviewing the docs caught it, not the tool — and it nearly produced a published "0 errors across all four reps / ~145k requests" claim the data didn't support. A benchmark that omits a rep while reporting success is worse than one that crashes: the partial dataset *looks complete*.

## What the harness now guarantees — and what it doesn't

**Guarantee (capture integrity):** a run cannot report `dataset is complete` when any of these occurred:
- a rep captured **zero** metrics,
- a rep captured a **partial** metric set (completeness is a required-key check — `http_req_duration`, `http_req_failed`, `http_reqs`, `checks` — not a line count; the warning names the missing keys),
- a rep's Job **failed or timed out**, even if its summary looks whole,
- **zero reps ran** (prints `no reps ran; no data collected — this file is NOT a dataset`).

All exit non-zero except the zero-rep dry run, which exits 0 while explicitly stating it is not a dataset.

**Explicit non-guarantee (experimental validity):** completeness is verified at the level of *which metric keys are present and whether the Job finished cleanly* — **not** the semantic validity of the values. A rep that ran cleanly and emitted all four keys from a *misconfigured* load (wrong VU count, unintended think-time) still reads as complete. That is the "false-result traps" class documented in the README, not something this check can catch. **The claim is about capture integrity, not experimental validity.**

## Changes
- **Item 5 (HIGH).** Root cause: both `kubectl wait` calls discarded their exit code, so a not-yet-finished Job fell through to `kubectl logs | grep`; k6 prints its summary only at end of run, so the grep matched nothing and appended nothing — then the Job was deleted, destroying the evidence. Now: waits are exit-code-checked and reported per rep as **completed/failed/timed-out**; completeness is the required-key check above; incomplete reps are recorded with a **reason**; the **raw k6 log tail is captured into the results file** (bounded, default 200 lines) so the evidence survives the end-of-run label sweep; every run prints an integrity verdict.
- **Item 1.** Empty sampler data reports `peak pods = <no sampler data>`, never a fabricated `0`.
- **Item 4.** The `did NOT fan out` warning is scoped to the **burst** phase; cold/soak state the expected peak. It was firing on every cold sample, where 1 pod for 1 request is the only correct outcome — crying wolf on the one signal designed to prevent published-but-wrong numbers.
- **Item 2.** The dry-run banner no longer claims "no kubectl mutation" while the `DRY_RUN_EXERCISE_KC` seam is mutating.

**Design decision — a failed/timed-out Job is flagged even when its summary looks complete.** k6 prints a summary on abort too, so a whole-looking summary from a Job that never reached `condition=complete` describes a *truncated* test, not the configured one. For publication-bound output, under-reporting confidence is the safe direction: a false "incomplete" costs a re-run; a false "complete" costs a retracted claim.

## Testability was the root cause
`run_k6`/`wait_zero` early-returned on dry-run, so **the entire path was uncoverable** — which is why the bug survived review. Both now sit on the existing `kc_live()` seam.

## Tests (TDD)
- `k6-metrics-integrity.test.sh` — **37 assertions**, written red-first (including the truncated-summary and zero-rep cases raised in review).
- `capture-restore.test.sh` — **17/17**, no regression to the #424 fail-closed capture path.
- **54/54 total**; `bash -n` + `shellcheck -S warning` clean; `--dry-run --phases all` unchanged.

## Not verified without a cluster (stated honestly)
The original drop was a real Knative/k6 timing event. The tests reproduce its **shape** via a stub, not live timing. The OKE validation stage on this PR exercises the real path. No rerun has been performed; the benchmark numbers in `docs/` are unchanged and no new measurements are claimed.

## Out of scope (tracked in #425)
- CI wiring of the harness tests — needs a decision on adding a `jq` dependency to a job.
- k6 digest pinning — registry unreachable; the digest was deliberately not invented.

items.title: Fix metric correctness, harden the CLI, and drop redundant files
items.body:
Two independent reviews of the package — one on metric correctness, one on code quality and packaging — turned up defects that produce wrong headline numbers on ordinary input. Every claim was reproduced numerically before being acted on.

## Critical: wrong numbers on ordinary input

**24/7 tapes were annualized at 252.** Median bar spacing cannot distinguish an exchange tape from a crypto one — both sit at one day. `BTC-USD` is a normal yfinance ticker, and a coin that exactly doubled over a calendar year reported **61.37% CAGR instead of 100%**, with vol understated ~17%. Sharpe, Calmar and alpha all inherited it. Weekend bars discriminate cleanly (0.00 of an equity index vs 0.28 of a crypto one).

**A single zero tick made the report confidently wrong.** Filtering interior non-positive prices spliced the peak straight onto the recovery, so `[100, 50, 0, 80]` reported a **50% drawdown instead of 100%**. The zero also made the next bar an infinite return, which turned `(1+r).prod()` into `NaN` and slipped past the `gross <= 0` guard — return, vol, Sharpe and skew all rendered as `—`. Non-positive prices are now dropped once in `_prices`, and `max_drawdown` does the honest peak-to-trough arithmetic.

**Every non-US ticker silently lost beta, alpha and R².** yfinance stamps a daily bar at midnight in the *exchange's* timezone, so `tz_convert(None)` put Frankfurt at 23:00 the previous day and New York at 05:00. The regression aligns on the index, so the two overlapped on **zero bars** — three blank rows against the default `^GSPC`, with no message. Overlap goes from 0 to 249.

**`--rf` was discontinuous.** `1` meant 100% while `1.0000001` meant 1%; `-3` meant −300%; `nan`/`inf`/`abc` passed through or silently became zero, poisoning Sharpe, Sortino and alpha — the tool's headline numbers.

**JSON export was not valid JSON.** Bare `NaN` is a normal result below 100 observations and strict parsers reject the file outright. A mistyped `--export` path dumped a traceback instead of `error:` + exit 2.

## Important

- Jensen's alpha was **compounded** while Sharpe was **scaled** — the same file using two conventions for the same operation. Compounding overstated alpha by 1pp on daily bars and 67pp on hourly. Now scaled.
- The regression accepted **n=2**, where a line fits perfectly and prints **R² = 100%** — reachable via `--period 3mo --interval 1mo`. Floor is now 30.
- `avg_daily_dollar_vol` was per *bar*, not per day: 5× off on weekly data, 21× on monthly. Renamed to `avg_value_traded_per_bar`.
- The retry slept after the *final* failed attempt — over half the total backoff, bought nothing, and paid twice because the benchmark fetch uses the same path.
- `tail_ratio` could return a negative "ratio" on a losing series.

## Simplification

Removed `_with_spark` and the spark values smuggled through the metadata dict, the unused `ticker` parameter, the no-op `SPARK_POINTS`, the `"Adj Close" if ... else "Close"` triplicated across three modules, and the second source of truth for terminal width. Errors now go to stderr. The interactive menu's namespace is layered over the parsed args, so a flag absent from `MENU` still reaches `main()`.

Deleted `requirements.txt` (duplicated pyproject, listed pytest as a runtime dep, referenced nowhere) and `docs/screenshot.svg` (byte-identical to the PNG, wrong extension, referenced nowhere). Fixed the two setuptools license deprecations.

## Documentation accuracy

The README claimed *"every number is unit-tested against a hand-derived expected value"* — Sharpe, tail ratio, skew and kurtosis had **no value assertion at all**. They do now. `__init__.py` claimed submodules were imported lazily; there is no `__getattr__`.

## Reviewer notes

- **The metric field rename and the `--rf` contract are breaking changes** for anyone parsing exports or scripting the CLI. Version is still 0.1.0.
- **Deliberately not changed:** `--compare --export` still exports only the primary period (documented in help + README rather than changed, since exporting both would break the flat `{metric: value}` CSV). Annualized figures still have no minimum sample while VaR gates at 100 — the asymmetry is real but adding gates everywhere costs more simplicity than it buys; it is now in the README's known limits next to the bar count the panel already shows. Returns are still differenced before alignment (≈0.02 beta bias), also documented.
- **One honest caveat:** the zero-tick fix makes the numbers coherent and finite, but a series that is flat at 100 then flat at 80 still grades "Low" — after dropping the bad tick it genuinely is low-variance. The fix is correctness of the arithmetic, not a smarter grade.

## Verification

**106 tests pass, up from 66**, with coverage added for each defect above. pyflakes clean; the wheel builds with no deprecation warnings; the report renders end to end. The timezone test is a real regression test — `beta=None` under the old code, `1.0` under the new. The compare test previously asserted only that the ticker appeared, which the first panel satisfies, so it passed with compare mode disabled entirely.

items.title: feat: experiment 005 — stdout/stderr capture under load
items.body:
## Summary

Closes #27. Extends experiment 004's static-page architecture: instead of one line, `line_flood.wasm` prints N interleaved, per-stream-sequenced lines to stdout/stderr (10 / 1,000 / 100,000), to find where the Worker → shim → postMessage → main-thread pipeline costs something, and whether it's ever wrong.

## Two timing numbers per run, not one

- `workerElapsedMs` — wraps only `wasi.start()`: WASM execution + N synchronous `postMessage` dispatch calls
- `mainThreadElapsedMs` — full wall time from run-sent to last-message-received, including fetch/instantiate/DOM

Two DOM variants (`?dom=1` naive per-line append, `?dom=0` array-only) to separate pipeline cost from rendering cost.

## One hypothesis refuted, reported as such

Per-line worker-side overhead does **not** stay roughly constant as N grows — it drops from 0.0425ms/line at N=10 to 0.0016ms/line at N=100,000, a ~26x decrease. A fixed per-run cost (browser/JIT warmup, the same effect experiment 004 found) dominates small N and amortizes away at scale.

## DOM rendering, not the pipeline, is the real cost at scale

At N=100,000, naive per-line append adds **~780ms** on top of the array-only baseline (352ms → 1,135ms), while worker-side WASM execution barely moves (316ms → 338ms). It does not hang or time out even at 200,000 DOM nodes in headless Chromium — slower, not broken.

## Correctness

Zero drops, duplicates, or reordering at any tested N, up to 200,000 total captured lines — verified via exact per-stream monotonic sequence checks (`seq[k] === k`), not just line counts.

## Changes

### Added
- `experiments/005_stdout_capture_load/` — Rust line-flood binary, N×dom benchmark matrix, Playwright measurement harness

### Fixed
- Top-level `README.md` experiment table to include #005

## Testing

- [x] `./benchmark.sh` runs the full N×dom matrix (6 runs), all pass correctness
- [x] Clean-room rebuild reproduces the same qualitative findings (100% correctness both runs; DOM-dominance and per-line-cost-decreases-with-scale both hold), with the exact run-to-run variance the README's own Limitations section anticipates

## Related Issues

Closes #27.

items.title: fix: template the CI runner description from the run that produced the numbers
items.body:
## What this changes

The runner hardware in both READMEs was static prose reading "2-core AMD EPYC 7763, 8GB RAM". It hasn't matched a run since March: the vCPU allocation moved to 4 cores and 16GB in April, and GitHub's hosted pool has since served 7763, 9V45 and 9V74 parts. `benchmarks/README.md` asks the reader to weigh which runner produced the numbers, so naming the wrong one undercuts the page.

This templates it from the run's own `system_info.json` behind a new `prose:ci_runner_hardware` marker, so it tracks whatever machine the refresh actually landed on.

Verified against all thirteen runs stored on `benchmark-data`. The March entries reproduce the original wording exactly, which checks the formatter against the convention it replaces rather than inventing a new one:

```
runs/2026-03-24-17db926  -> 2-core AMD EPYC 7763, 8GB RAM
runs/2026-04-02-ec7253a  -> 4-core AMD EPYC 7763, 16GB RAM
runs/2026-04-24-aefc68a  -> 4-core AMD EPYC 9V74, 16GB RAM
runs/2026-07-24-f7e7d96  -> 4-core AMD EPYC 9V45, 16GB RAM
runs/2026-07-30-bc2a16c  -> 4-core AMD EPYC 9V74, 16GB RAM
```

Re-running the updater over the committed result reports `Updated 0 values`, so what's in the tree is what the script generates. A missing `cpu_model` leaves the marker unpopulated rather than writing a half-formed string, and a malformed `total_ram_gb` drops the RAM clause instead of throwing.

`benchmarks/README.md` also had "the 2-core EPYC VM" in the local-vs-CI explanation; that now refers to the shared CI runner without asserting a core count.

## Checklist

- ~~Tests added or updated~~ - nothing covers `benchmarks/scripts/` today. Verified by running the formatter across all thirteen stored runs, including the malformed-input cases, and by a full round-trip of the updater.
- ~~`cargo fmt --check` and `cargo clippy -- -D warnings` pass locally~~ - no Rust changed.

items.title: study2: correct the public record, freeze the eval inputs, preregister study 2
items.body:
Brings `main` up to date with the study-2 branch. The immediate reason is that the public README currently contradicts the project's own evidence.

## What `main` says today, and why it is wrong

> BFCL benchmark numbers are not yet available. Formal evaluation ... is scheduled for Week 7

> **DPO v2: designed, optional scope.**

Both are stale. BFCL v4 `simple_python` was run and committed; DPO v2 was run and closed as a documented negative result. A reader checking the repo against the shipped claims would conclude the 92.25% headline is unsupported.

## What this changes

**The public record.** SFT scored **369/400 = 92.25%** on the 400-item pinned set. DPO v2 is closed as a second negative result — held-out tool-use came in below SFT at every evaluated checkpoint (364/363/359 against 369), with no contrast significant after Holm correction. The earlier `n=399` text was a newline-counting error; the score itself was always 92.25%.

**Eval inputs are frozen and verifiable.** `eval/manifests/bfcl_v4_study2.json` pins every scored file by sha256, git blob id, row count, and sorted-id digest. `eval/fetch_pinned_bfcl.py --verify-only` re-checks them, and now also runs an answer-name preflight over every pinned category: an answer key may not expect a function name the item never presented to the model.

**A benchmark defect, found and reported.** BFCL v4's release-commit key for `simple_python_363` expects `find_closest`, but that item only ever offers `restaurant_search.find_closest` — unpassable by construction. Filed upstream as [ShishirPatil/gorilla#1354](https://github.com/ShishirPatil/gorilla/issues/1354). The canonical key was selected by a rule fixed in advance of the outcome (`canonical = pinned AND valid; the preflight decides`), and `eval/results/answer_key_comparison.json` fails to build if the recorded choice is not the one that rule produces.

**Study 2 is preregistered.** `docs/prereg-study2.md` carries Amendments 1 and 2. §2 (mining) is explicitly `[DRAFT]` — it does not govern anything until frozen.

## Scope note

29 commits. §2 of the preregistration and the mining rewrite are in progress and labelled as such; nothing here reports an unmeasured number as measured.

items.title: release/v0.3.0
items.body:
Minor rather than patch: the shipped rule text changed, the metric the project publishes changed, and the competitive figures changed with it.

## The rule

**The shipped rule is now 305 words, down from 666** (~426 tokens against ~956, paid on every session). `variants/magpie-tight.md` keeps the longer, more explicit version as a documented opt-in; it is still a benchmark arm so it cannot rot.

One rule text now generates **all seven** host files including the Claude Code skill. Previously `skills/magpie/SKILL.md` was hand-maintained at 102 lines while the bench measured a 35-line `AGENTS.md`, so the artifact users installed had never been benchmarked. Drift is now impossible rather than merely tested.

## The published numbers were wrong, and are replaced

`lines` counted the runnable check the floor mandates, so it charged the ladder for the floor and flattered whichever arm tested least. Retained diffs settled it: on one task two arms wrote the **byte-identical** implementation and the entire 15-line gap was a test.

| | published before | measured now (impl) | checks left |
|---|--:|--:|--:|
| magpie | −55% | **−22%** | 11/12 |
| ponytail | −45% | −15% | 10/12 |
| **caveman** | **−33%** | **−2%** | **7/12** |
| baseline | | | 8/12 |

**Caveman never reduced implementation code.** Its advantage was tests it does not write, and it leaves a check on fewer tasks than using no rule at all. Confirmed on two independent runs.

**Magpie and ponytail are not separable** at 12 tasks. Three runs failed to put the gap outside the noise, so the README says that instead of ranking them.

**Pass rate does not separate the arms either.** Four arms running byte-identical text scored 46, 47, 48 and 48 out of 48. Floor probes do separate them, and every arm kept 12/12.

## Harness

- **impl / test split**, tokens (`usage` was returned by the CLI all along and discarded), and cost reporting
- **control arm**: injects the shipped rule under a second name, so every run measures its own error bar. Four identical arms landed 4 points apart; two rules swapped places by 29 lines between runs
- **preflight**: the check command runs against the untouched fixture before the first paid session. A missing container image once cost $15.69 for 27 uniformly failed checks
- **all-fail banner**, **check-coverage reporting**, fixture collision fix that penalised only arms writing checks
- `median()` returned the upper middle on even counts: −16% where the true median was −28%

## Verification

`go test ./...`, gofmt, vet clean; 7 adapters match `AGENTS.md`; fixture suite passes. Five benchmark runs committed under `benchmarks/results/`, ~$470 of agent time, every number reproducible from the raw `.jsonl` via `-resummarize`.

## Known limits, stated in the README

One fixture, one language, 12 tasks. Between-run variance exceeds within-run variance, so single-run rankings of close arms are unreliable regardless of repetitions. The shipped short rule and the tight variant are **not separable** on code output; the short one is default because its token cost is lower and that part is arithmetic, not a measurement.

items.title: NewSingleCore: an unsharded cache for GOMAXPROCS=1, measured against the whole field
items.body:
Adds a second, independent cache implementation for processes pinned to one core, establishes what it is actually worth by measurement, and corrects the record where earlier measurement was wrong.

## Why

A Kubernetes pod with `limits.cpu: 1000m` or less runs at `GOMAXPROCS=1` under Go 1.25+. At one core, goache's sharding buys nothing — there are no concurrent writers to spread across shard mutexes — and [ADR 0025](docs/adr/0025-cpu-constrained-benchmarks.md) had measured goache losing to patrickmn/go-cache there.

`NewSingleCore` returns `*SingleCoreCache[K, V]`: one map behind one `sync.RWMutex`, no routing hash, no shard-slice indirection, no `limit > 0` checks on the unbounded path. Same API and same options as `Cache`, so `WithShardCount` is accepted and ignored and one shared `[]Option` works for either constructor.

`cache.go` is deliberately untouched. No branch, no flag, no shared storage type — the sharded path cannot regress. Two alternatives were built, measured and rejected before landing on a second type: a `len(c.shards) == 1` branch in `shardFor` (reached parity with go-cache, not victory) and having `New` return an interface (+7.8% on single-core `Get` and +2-5% on 24-core `ParallelGet`, paid by every user). Both are recorded in [ADR 0026](docs/adr/0026-single-core-cache.md).

## What it measures

At `-cpu=1`, n=100000, `-count=10`, benchstat medians: fastest of the seven caches `bench/` compares, in all eight categories. The margins vary far too much to quote as one number, so all of them are in the README and [ADR 0027](docs/adr/0027-single-core-field-claim.md):

| | goache | best competitor | |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Bounded | 54.84 | ristretto 105.6 | -48% |
| Set | 23.90 | go-cache 38.20 | -37% |
| SetWithTTL | 33.27 | go-cache 52.56 | -37% |
| ParallelGetSet | 17.14 | go-cache 19.37 | -11.5% |
| Get | 16.17 | go-cache 17.29 | -6.5% |
| GetWithTTL | 21.03 | go-cache 22.41 | -6.2% |
| ParallelGet | 16.11 | go-cache 16.94 | -4.9% |
| Delete | 75.11 | go-cache 75.39 | tie |

Two caveats stated up front rather than buried:

**One category does not hold across sizes.** With `WithMaxSize` below roughly 10k entries the sharded `Cache` evicts faster even at one core (50.60 vs 47.77 ns/op at n=1k). Sharding is useless for locking at one core but still *partitions* — 256 shards means CLOCK rings one or two nodes long. Reproduced three times, crossover between 5k and 50k, map pre-sizing tested as the cause and refuted. Documented, not fixed; the README says to use `New` there.

**Above one core `SingleCoreCache` loses to `Cache` and is the wrong choice.** Said in the doc comment, the README and the ADR.

## Two numbers ADR 0026 got wrong

Both from `-count=3`, both corrected here against `-count=10`:

- the read lead over go-cache was reported as 20-25%; it is 4.9-6.5%
- `Delete` was reported as a win; it is a tie, and that tie is the pointer-storage trade being paid — one lookup costing ~9.6 ns on churn to save ~2.9 ns on every `Get`

ADR 0026 keeps its decision and loses its numbers. README, the plan document and the `SingleCoreCache` doc comment now point at ADR 0027.

## No implementation change came out of the analysis, and that is the finding

`Get` costs 16.35 ns: 11.4 the Go map, 3.55 the lock, 0.64 ours. `sync.Mutex` is not cheaper than `sync.RWMutex` here (15.74 vs 15.71). A hand-rolled `atomic.Int32` reader scheme buys 0.35 ns. Keying the freelist to skip the pre-write lookup would speed up the benchmark pattern and tax every other `Set`. All recorded in ADR 0027 so the same ground is not re-covered.

## Measurement discipline

Two comparisons in this work came out backwards before being caught. A 29-minute full-suite sweep reported `SingleCoreCache` losing `Set` by 18-48% at ±1-3% variance; a focused run of the same benchmarks showed it winning at every size. Our benchmarks sit at the end of `bench/compare_test.go` and ran after twenty minutes of load. Tight variance proves nothing about cross-benchmark comparability — every sample of a late benchmark is taken under the same degraded conditions.

Now a standing section in CLAUDE.md and the last part of ADR 0027: `-count=10` and benchstat for any comparative claim, comparisons only from short runs containing just the benchmarks compared, never two measurements at once.

## Also in here

- `bench/` gains the four missing `SingleCore` categories and `ParallelGetSet` for freecache, ristretto, theine and otter — the comparison matrix was four of eight categories and three of seven libraries
- `example_test.go`: ten runnable `Example*` functions verified against `// Output:` under `make test`. This caught a README snippet calling `SetWithTTL("session-token", "abc123", ...)` on a `Cache[string, int]`, which does not compile. [ADR 0028](docs/adr/0028-runnable-examples-as-api-tests.md)
- charts follow the numbers: `singlecore-vs-gocache.svg` replaced by `singlecore-vs-field.svg`, plus `singlecore-field`, `singlecore-get-budget` and `singlecore-bounded-crossover`
- `make bench-compare-singlecore` and `bench-compare-singlecore-sizes`

## Verification

`make ci` green locally: vet, lint (0 issues, both modules), test, test -race.

items.title: docs: make the benchmark citable as a baseline and lead with the bug it measures
items.body:
## Summary

Four things stood between this repository and being something a stranger clones, runs, and reports a number against. None of them are new features; three are defects in what was already claimed.

**1. Published numbers recorded the wrong code version.** `_version()` looked up the distribution `"eads"`, which is not this project's distribution name, so every `results.json` recorded `eads_version: "unknown"` — and under an editable install that metadata is stale regardless. It now reads `eads.__version__`, the value `tests/test_release.py` already holds consistent with `pyproject.toml` and `CITATION.cff`, and each benchmark on the results page states the EADS and Python version it came from. Two numbers that cannot be attributed to code versions cannot be compared, which is the only reason to publish them.

**2. A manifest written elsewhere had no guarantee of meaning the same thing.** Unknown fields were dropped in silence:

```diff
- "repeat": 5               # ignored; the run used repeats=3 and published the number anyway
- "injected_signal": [...]  # ignored; the scenario claimed to be adversarial and injected nothing
```

Manifests now declare `schema_version`, a newer format is refused rather than guessed at, unknown top-level and scenario fields are errors, and required scenario fields are checked at load instead of surfacing as a `KeyError` mid-run. `benchmarks/manifest_template.json` sits *outside* `manifests/` so its placeholder scenario is never published, and a test loads it — a template that does not parse is a trap for the first person who copies it.

**3. Both notebooks had been broken since typed actions landed.** They printed `record.verdict.approved`, a field that no longer exists, and the quickstart omitted the region governance requires — so a reader following the Colab badge in the README watched it fail. Nothing was checking them. `tests/test_notebooks.py` now executes every code cell in order in one namespace, without nbclient or a kernel, so the check costs nothing and runs in the default suite. It also asserts each notebook keeps its install cell and ships no stored output.

**4. `docs/wow_demo.md` showed output the code stopped producing.** A trust score of `0.9` where the code produces `0.392`, three evidence items where it produces two, and a benchmark block from a removed API. Nobody had lied; the page was not re-run. `tests/test_docs.py` now compares any block fenced between `<!-- BEGIN <script> -->` and `<!-- END <script> -->` against a live run of that script, so adding a checked block to a page is two comments.

### The argument is now executable

`examples/injection_demo.py` runs the injected supplier email past two guards on the same compromised model:

```text
Naive guard, quantity in a form it matches: rejected (quantity exceeds limit)
Naive guard, same action phrased in prose:  approved (no violation found)  <-- the bug

EADS governance:            rejected
Reason:                     order_quantity_exceeds_policy_max; quantity_hard_limit
```

The naive guard is not a straw man: it catches the quantity when the model phrases it the way the pattern expects, and approves the same action phrased as prose. The injection never has to defeat the check.

The README and `notebooks/eads_killer_demo.ipynb` are rebuilt around that, and `docs/benchmarks/about.md` gains the citable form for quoting a number (manifest digest + code version + label) and how to contribute a scenario. `injection_resistance` carries the clause it should always carry: it is measured against a backend that *always* obeys the injection, so it bounds what the governance layer blocks when the model is maximally compromised, and says nothing about how often a real model complies. Quoting it as a model's resistance is the misreading most likely to happen.

No metric definition, scenario, or published value changes.

## Type of change

- [x] Bug fix
- [x] New capability
- [x] Breaking change to a public type or signature
- [x] Documentation only
- [ ] Build, CI, or tooling

Breaking only for third-party manifests, of which there are none yet: a manifest with an unrecognised field now fails to load instead of loading with the field ignored. That is the point.

## Verification

```
ruff check eads tests examples   All checks passed!
mypy eads                       Success: no issues found in 39 source files
pytest -q                       206 passed, 8 skipped   (was 189)
mkdocs build --strict           Documentation built in 0.35 seconds
scripts/run_benchmarks.py --check  docs/benchmarks/index.md is up to date
```

17 new tests: manifest schema and unknown-field refusal, the template loads and is not published, results record a real code version, every notebook cell executes, notebooks keep their install cell and ship no output, and pasted doc output matches a live run.

- [x] Lint, typecheck, and tests pass locally
- [x] `mkdocs build --strict` passes (if docs changed)

## Claims check

- [x] Every capability this PR documents is implemented, or is explicitly labelled as a stub
- [x] No DOI, metric, or numerical result is stated without a verifiable source
- [x] Governance changes cannot approve an action that could not be checked (fail closed)

Every number and reason string quoted in the README and demo page is copied from a run, and two of them are now asserted by tests rather than trusted.

items.title: Report a vanished vendored path, name a build failure, and benchmark python
items.body:
Three findings of a second audit, over the files the first one did not
reach: the CI script, the build hook, and the benchmark. Everything here
is outside `btclib_libsecp256k1/` — the boundary itself came out of the
first audit and this one found nothing new in it.

## 1. The vendored-vector re-checker crashed on the drift it exists to catch

`repos/{repo}/commits?path=` answers `[]` with a **200** when no commit
touches that path any more — renamed, moved or deleted upstream — and
`(commit,) = json.loads(...)` unpacked one commit out of it:

```text
a path that still exists:
  ('200f9b26fe0a2f235a2af8b30c4be9f12f6bc9cb', '2023-04-20')
a path upstream has renamed or deleted:
  !! ValueError: not enough values to unpack (expected 1, got 0)
```

The `ValueError` took `find_drift` down and `report` was never reached:
**red monthly run, no issue opened.** The workflow's own comment is the
argument for why that matters — *"a vendored vector is trusted without
anybody looking at it again, and that is exactly what a monthly issue is
for"* — and a pin standing on a file that is gone is exactly the thing
nobody would notice.

`_latest_commit` answers `None` there now, `Drift` carries a
`path_is_gone` that reads the encoding in one place, and the report says
`GONE` with the reason instead of naming a tip that does not exist.
Called with no README, or two, it prints its usage and exits 2 rather
than `IndexError: list index out of range` about a list nobody saw.

btclib's copy of this script is the same code and carries the same fix
with the tests (btclib-org/btclib#471 and #472). `.github/scripts` is
outside the coverage source here, so what holds this is that suite plus
the hand check above — worth knowing, and arguably worth a test module of
its own here one day.

## 2. Both failures of the build hook were mute

`get_ext_object` raised a **bare** `RuntimeError` — no message at all —
for a `cffi_modules` entry naming an object its script does not define.
The line is excluded from the coverage measure, so the message was the
whole of what a maintainer would have had to go on, and there wasn't one.

`dynamic_platform_tag` subscripted a dict of three Windows architectures
where `scripts/cffi_build.py` aims CMake at four:

```text
win32        machine=win32   cffi_build=Win32  hatch_build=win32
win-amd64    machine=amd64   cffi_build=x64    hatch_build=win_amd64
win-arm32    machine=arm32   cffi_build=ARM    hatch_build=** KeyError **
win-arm64    machine=arm64   cffi_build=ARM64  hatch_build=win_arm64
```

Both name what went wrong now, the second matching the `RuntimeError`
policy `shared_library_extension` beside it already had.

## 3. The benchmark stopped measuring python

Two of the eight rows are labelled *"through btclib's pure python
arithmetic"*. `dsa.verify_` and `ssa.verify_` delegate to **these
bindings** for secp256k1 with sha256 — which is exactly the fixture the
script sets up. Traced:

```text
dsa_btclib() reaches: ['dsa.verify']      ← the bindings
ssa_btclib() reaches: ['ssa.verify']      ← the bindings
```

| row | µs/call |
| --- | --- |
| `dsa_btclib` | 22.5 |
| `dsa_libsecp256k1` | 13.9 |
| `ssa_btclib` | 24.9 |
| `ssa_libsecp256k1` | 13.8 |
| *the python path* | *1214 / 1270* |

So `benchmark()`'s *"two orders of magnitude slower"* is true **of the
python path** and was not what those rows ran.

`python_arithmetic_only` turns the dispatch off before they do, in
**three** namespaces: `_libsecp256k1_applicable` is imported *by name*
into `ecc.dsa`, `ecc.ssa` and `curves.curve`, so patching one leaves the
other two delegating — a partial patch that still measures C and still
looks like python. The first measurement I took for this was wrong that
way, which is why the numbers above are the second set.

The two rows drop to `mult=1` (a thousand calls of a millisecond is a
second of clock, where they had been sized for twenty microseconds), and
the loop reads `perf_counter` rather than `time`.

## An audit hypothesis that did not survive

`enable = ["pypy"]` looked like it left free-threaded wheels unbuilt,
which would have made six statements false. It doesn't: PyPI serves eight
`cp314-cp314t` wheels for 0.7.1. In cibuildwheel 3.x free-threading is no
longer opt-in for stable versions. The prose is correct and no change was
needed.

## Verified

`uvx pre-commit run --all-files` exits 0, working tree clean afterwards.
Suite at 317, coverage 100%.

🤖 Generated with [Claude Code](https://claude.com/claude-code)

## Summary by Sourcery

Handle vendored vector drift more robustly, improve build-time error reporting, and ensure the benchmark actually measures btclib’s Python arithmetic with a reliable timer.

Bug Fixes:
- Treat upstream-deleted or renamed vendored paths as a distinct drift case instead of crashing when no commits are returned for a path.
- Add usage validation to the vendored-vector checker CLI to avoid IndexError when run with missing or extra README arguments.
- Report a clear RuntimeError when a cffi_modules entry refers to an extension object not defined in its build script.
- Guard Windows dynamic platform tag resolution with explicit mappings and a RuntimeError on unknown architectures instead of an unhandled KeyError.

Enhancements:
- Include detailed GONE/BEHIND drift messaging in both issue bodies and stdout for vendored-vector checks.
- Force btclib benchmarks to use pure Python arithmetic by disabling libsecp256k1 dispatch in all relevant namespaces.
- Switch benchmark timing to time.perf_counter and adjust iteration counts so Python-path measurements remain practical and meaningful.

Build:
- Clarify build hook behavior for missing cffi extension objects and unknown Windows architectures in hatch_build’s dynamic platform tag logic.

Documentation:
- Document the build-hook error handling and Windows platform tag behavior in the changelog.
- Document the improved vendored-vector drift handling and benchmark behavior in the changelog.

items.title: feat(benchmarks): land the A1 chunk-geometry measurement harness
items.body:
# 🧪 Make the A1 numbers reproducible

The offline measurements behind §4 A1 of the v1.2 plan — the ones that resolved the "are sliced spans first-class graph entities" fork — lived in a session scratch directory under `/private/tmp`. The knowledge graph recorded the code as **gone**. It wasn't; it was one reboot from being gone. This lands it.

## 💡 Why this is worth a PR rather than a gist

Protocol law §3 binds every Track A experiment to replay-before-paid. That contract is unenforceable if the replay harness is unauditable. Concretely, these scripts produced the zero-straddle rate across 31,244 triples, the 3-slice window hitting the fat-state ceiling, the 19%/12% header tax, and the selection-simulation result that redirected A1 away from "A2 must come first." Every one of those numbers is quoted in a locked plan doc and none of them could be re-derived.

There is also a live consumer. The plan adopted a contextualized-embedder offline arm that must run **before** a paid corpus rebuild locks an embedder. With this in the repo that arm is a `stage1.py` variant instead of a reconstruction from prose.

## 🛠️ What landed

`benchmarks/longmemeval_v2_chunk_geometry/` — 28 files, 284K. Nine stage scripts plus five support modules, and `out/` carrying every receipt.

**On the name:** it describes what is measured — size, boundaries, header overhead, retrievability of the indexed unit — and deliberately shares no token with `longmemeval_v2_*_slice*.py`, where "slice" already means *dataset subset*. The README fixes the vocabulary explicitly: **slice is the verb** (the algorithm), **passage is the noun** (`EntityType.PASSAGE`, the graph rows from #279).

**Four support modules had to be recovered separately.** `slicer.py`, `slicer_v2.py`, `corpus.py`, and `chunkparse.py` were missing from the first rescue pass, and they are where every boundary rule actually lives — without them nothing imports, let alone runs. A fifth, `summarize.py`, turned up alongside them.

## 🔍 Two portability fixes that were not optional

The scripts hardcoded absolute paths into one specific checkout. Run from a worktree, they would silently import a *different* checkout's benchmarks and read a *different* corpus — producing plausible numbers from the wrong inputs, which is the worst failure mode available to a measurement harness. Import paths now derive from `__file__`, and the two machine-local corpora plus the output directory resolve through `paths.py` with `SIBYL_A1_*` overrides, since a worktree does not inherit the primary checkout's `.moon/cache`.

Report writers now emit a trailing newline so re-runs stay byte-stable against the `end-of-file-fixer` hook instead of showing a phantom one-byte diff forever.

## 🧪 Validation

Behavior preservation was verified **by execution, not inspection**. The frozen catalogs were present locally, so `stage0c` and `stage0f` were re-run end to end, covering both import chains (the direct `slicer`/`stage0` path and the `corpus` path).

⚠️ **Stating this one precisely, because a one-byte gap deserves it.** The re-run reproduces the *original* receipt exactly — `stage0c_report.json`, 1215 bytes, `sha256 042424994e17a39b`. The **committed** copy is 1216 bytes (`dfe78838d3547a4a`) because of the deliberate trailing-newline fix above. The measurement is bit-identical; the serialization changed by one byte on purpose. The commit body's phrase "reproduce their committed receipts byte for byte" is therefore off by that newline, and this is the accurate version.

Lint gate:

\`\`\`
moon run root:inventory-lint
  All checks passed!   130 files already formatted
\`\`\`

`benchmarks/` is not globbed by ruff or ty — it is an explicit per-file allow-list — so the directory was added to both halves of `inventory-lint` plus the task inputs, following that existing convention. **The glob was confirmed live rather than silently skipped** by dropping a deliberately misformatted probe file in and watching the task fail. Everything ruff flagged that was not an intentional research-script pattern was fixed rather than ignored: two unclosed file handles, a closure capturing a loop variable, three dead locals.

## 📦 What is not here

`out/stage1_report.json` — 827 KB of per-question, per-arm, per-ranker recall curves. Its headline numbers survive in the generated `stage1_summary.txt`; the raw report regenerates by re-running `stage1.py`.

**Nothing in CI executes any of this.** The harness reads two large corpora under `.moon/cache` that are never committed, so no moon task may run it; `inventory-lint` only lints statically. Three dependency tiers are documented in the README — note that `stage1b.py` is *not* dependency-free as was first assumed: it needs `numpy`, and pulls `scipy` and `sklearn` transitively. Only `torch` and `sentence_transformers` are deferred behind a function-scope import.

## 📋 Five places the plan's prose disagrees with the code

Documented in the README, and worth a reviewer's eye because §4 A1 is a locked document whose rules would be implemented literally by someone who trusted it:

1. `TARGET_LO = 600` is **dead code in v1** — defined, exported, never read. The only band check is a greedy ceiling flush with no floor, which is why 29.47% of enterprise slices land under 600 chars. This is exactly what the v2 band-aware packing fix exists to correct — and that fix is **absent from the plan's rule list** despite being the largest change to the size distribution.
2. **No "shallowest depth" search exists**, despite the docstring. `_emit` greedily packs siblings at whatever level it is on and descends only when a subtree exceeds `HARD_MAX`. Cut depth is an outcome, not a search target.
3. The documented `reason` values are stale — two of the four documented names are never emitted.
4. The plan's **"line-count fallback" is a character-threshold fallback.** No line-count rule exists anywhere. The rate (0.14% / 0%) is right; the mechanism is not.
5. **URL path-extraction is already shipped**, not prospective — it was active in the v1 run that produced these numbers.

Plus two measurement traps documented so nobody re-derives them: `any_two_slices_same_state` counts *exactly two distinct* slices, so it reads lower than `window_1` without contradicting it; and `url_over_120_char_header_budget_pct` measures the **raw** URL, while shipped headers cannot exceed 120 by construction.

Every §4 A1 number checked reproduces: 31,244/31,244 zero-straddle triples, 92 measurable questions, window_3 at 0.9545/1.0 against fat 0.9545/1.0, header tax 0.1901/0.1197, goal-carry RRF 0.727/0.812 beating fat 0.682/0.792.

🤖 Generated with [Claude Code](https://claude.com/claude-code)

items.title: design: correct the ring, lead the badges with the licence, lock up the masthead
items.body: Three brand surfaces: the ring's geometry, the badge row, and the masthead composition. ## The ring was drawn to the wrong numbers Two independent faults, both visible at README size. **Round caps ate the gap.** `stroke-linecap="round"` extends `stroke-width/2` along the tangent past each endpoint — **12.7°** at `r=13.5, sw=6`. The source asked for a 34° gap and the screen showed **8.5°**. The mark read as a nearly-closed progress spinner rather than four separated arcs. Arcs now span 42.6° with a 47.4° geometric gap, which measures **22° on screen** once the caps are counted. **The two blues sat adjacent.** `#3c8cff` and `#0095fd` are near-identical. Side by side on a ring they merge into one lump split by a hairline, while cyan and green stay distinct opposite them — so the mark was visibly heavier on one half. The ramp now runs blue / cyan / blue / green so the two blues sit opposite. Sequence order is dropped on purpose: a ring has no first stop, so ordering the ramp for balance costs nothing a reader could have used. That reasoning does not carry to figures that read left to right, where the ramp should stay in sequence. ## The badge row leads with the licence Apache-2.0 moves to the front — the one fact in that row a reader comparing frameworks cannot skip, and it was sitting third in shields' default blue, a colour close enough to the ramp to read as unchosen rather than different. Now `#0095fd` with the OSI mark rather than the Apache feather, which would imply an ASF affiliation this project does not have. The documentation badge is gone: it pointed at the docs site, which the Documentation section already links, and the navigation strip sits directly beneath the badges. What is left answers three questions in descending order of how hard they block: may I use this, does it work, will it run here. Python keeps `#3776AB`, the language's own colour. Nothing was added — version, downloads and release badges would all be untrue today, since `rsihub` is not on PyPI and the repo has no releases. ## The masthead is one lockup, mark left and wordmark right Two `` tags side by side align on the text baseline rather than on each other, and GitHub strips the attributes that would correct it, so this composition has to be a single file to hold its proportions. `docs/rsihub-lockup.svg` welds them together. Everything derives from the mark box so the lockup scales as one object: cap height at 0.50 of the box, gap at 0.36, and the wordmark's cap height centred on the mark's centre rather than sharing a baseline — a ring has no baseline to share. items.title: Add search, indexes and explain; add an MCP benchmark arm; fix two scoring bugs
items.body:
Completes steps 6 and 7 of the design brief: the three remaining commands, and a third benchmark arm so the published table covers psql, MCP and `pg-axi` together.

## Commands

`search <pattern>`, `indexes [table]` and `explain "<sql>"`, bringing the CLI to the six commands in the brief.

Three decisions worth a reviewer's attention, since none were specified:

- **`explain` does not execute by default.** `--analyze` opts into real execution and wraps it in a transaction that is always rolled back. Explaining a `DELETE` must not delete anything. CI asserts this rather than trusting it.
- **`search` returns no row counts.** Mixing an estimate here against the exact counts the summary gives would be a quiet inconsistency; `table <name>` is one step away with the real number.
- **Primary keys and unique constraints are never listed as unused**, even at zero scans, because dropping them is not an option the reader has.

## Benchmark: three arms

| arm | success | avg input | avg turns | avg cost |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| psql | 98% (137/140) | 4,469 | 3.34 | $0.0059 |
| MCP (DBHub 1.2.0) | 95% (133/140) | 4,989 | 3.22 | $0.0065 |
| **pg-axi** | **100% (140/140)** | **3,629** | **3.05** | **$0.0048** |

14 tasks, 10 repeats, 420 runs under one set of conditions. 19% fewer input tokens than psql (95% CI -30% to -5%), 27% fewer than MCP (CI -43% to -10%).

DBHub was chosen because it is the Postgres MCP example in Anthropic's own Claude Code documentation. The obvious candidate, `@modelcontextprotocol/server-postgres`, is deprecated and archived with a published unpatched SQL-injection writeup.

### The accuracy result

On "which table has the most rows" the answer is `payment`, 16,049.

| arm | `payment` | `rental` |
|---|---|---|
| psql | 7/10 | 3/10 |
| MCP | 3/10 | **7/10** |
| **pg-axi** | **10/10** | 0/10 |

`payment` is partitioned, so `pg_stat_user_tables` shows the parent empty and `rental` looks largest. MCP does worst because `search_objects` is the natural tool to reach for and lists tables without row counts, routing the agent into the statistics views. `pg-axi` folds partitions into their root and counts exactly.

MCP also takes the single biggest win on the board, `email-columns` at 2,638 tokens against 5,435 and 7,000. That is in the README next to its failures.

## Two scoring bugs, both fixed

Found while investigating a `pg-axi` "failure":

- **`staff-count` demanded the word "staff"** while its prompt asked only for a count, so the correct answer `2` was scored wrong three times in ten. That penalty falls hardest on whichever arm encourages brevity, which is the arm under test.
- **`hasNumber` used `includes`**, so "12 staff" would have passed a check expecting 2. A wrong answer scored as a pass, worst where the expected numbers are small.

Now matched on digit boundaries and covered by `test/bench-checks.test.ts`. The harness had tests for the CLI but none for the code that decides pass or fail. All stored runs were re-scored offline against the corrected checks; only the definitive run changed, and only in `pg-axi`'s favour.

## Harness changes

- `Arm` now exposes a list of tools rather than one. An MCP server declares its own surface and usually exposes several; that is a real difference between these interfaces, not something to normalise away. Tool descriptions are passed through unmodified.
- `bench/trace.ts` had its own copy of the agent loop and system prompt. It is the tool used to establish the turn-count finding, so drift would have meant explaining a run that never happened. It now drives the real loop through a trace hook.
- Turn count added to the report. The whole finding is about turns and only tool calls were being shown.
- Arms are built lazily, so an arm nobody asked for never spawns a process. The MCP server version is pinned.

## A hypothesis that did not survive

The turn-count finding suggested `pg-axi`'s own next-step lines might be causing serial round trips. Tested with three variants of the disclosure block against 280 runs: turn count is flat at 2.97 / 2.99 / 2.97, moving by 0.00 turns paired across tasks. Disclosure costs about 46 input tokens per run, 1.3%, which is just the size of the block. Shipped behaviour unchanged.

## Reviewer notes

- The earlier README claimed 19% off a single 5-repeat run. Across three runs that figure ranged 7% to 20%, driven by one high-variance task. The table now carries bootstrapped intervals and says so explicitly.
- Raw results for every published figure are committed under `bench/results/`, force-added past the gitignore.
- Benchmark spend for this PR was about $7 of the $30 cap, on Claude Haiku 4.5 via Bedrock.
- Not done: step 8, packaging and npm publish.

items.title: Ask whether TensorRT ran, instead of whether the call succeeded
items.body:
Validates LM7's TensorRT path on Blackwell `sm120` across the axes that decide whether the backend is usable: four model families (MLP, ResNet18, BERT, SmolLM2 prefill), FP32/FP16/BF16/FP8, batch 1/8/32, dynamic sequence length, and artifact reload.

**106 cells, 32 artifact reloads, zero failures.** An Ada `sm89` control reproduces every defect below, so none of them is about Blackwell.

## Does it work on sm120?

Yes, with no code changes.

## Where does it win?

The serialized artifact, at small batch. Speedup of `tensorrt-export` over `inductor`, FP16:

| model | batch 1 | batch 8 | batch 32 |
| --- | ---: | ---: | ---: |
| bert | **4.37x** | 2.19x | 1.36x |
| smollm2 | **4.32x** | 3.62x | 2.49x |
| resnet18 | **3.09x** | 2.15x | 1.37x |

The monotonic decay is the point: the win is mostly launch-overhead elimination, which batching amortizes for everyone. Reload is cheap enough to justify the build — ResNet 0.48 s time-to-first-inference against a 13.5 s build.

## Where does it fail?

Four ways, **none of which raises**.

1. **`lm7.export(backend="tensorrt")` can write an artifact with no TensorRT in it.** The MLP does this at every precision and batch size: 0 engines, 3 PyTorch ops, a 0.3 s "build", output bit-identical to eager — and a manifest claiming `backend: tensorrt` with `device_bound: true` and a compute capability. The partitioner declines the 3-node exported graph because it is below `min_block_size=5`, and returns it unconverted without raising. `options={"min_block_size": 1}` fixes it and costs almost nothing on models that already convert.

2. **The JIT path returns wrong numbers on BERT.** Max abs diff **8.69** against eager, where `torch_tensorrt.dynamo.compile` on the same model, device and inputs gives 0.0097. Deterministic, all three dtypes, both GPU generations, survives `min_block_size=1`. A Torch-TensorRT defect rather than an LM7 one, but `lm7.compile(backend="tensorrt")` hands it over unflagged, and the greedy-token check that guards the causal-LM paths cannot see it. A minimal repro is in the doc and was run as written.

3. **Dynamic sequence length.** Export accepts `options={"dynamic": True}` and ignores it — artifacts stay shape-locked. Worse, a *statically* compiled JIT module handed a new length silently rebuilds an entire engine inside an ordinary inference call: 17.7 s, 15.0 s and 14.0 s for three new lengths. JIT `dynamic=True` does work, for 2.8x steady-state latency.

4. **FP8 is unreachable through this stack.** Torch-TensorRT 2.12.1 registers 230 converters and none for `aten._scaled_mm`; TensorRT 10.16 itself has the FP8 dtype. A four-layer `torch._scaled_mm` probe, deliberately large enough to clear `min_block_size`, converts to zero engines while reporting success. Via torchao, `fp8-dynamic` on SmolLM2 shatters into **91 engines around 752 PyTorch operators**, 13.6x slower than the unquantized artifact.

## What changed

- `benchmarks/tensorrt_matrix.py` — new harness, one cell per process, five plans (`core`, `fp8`, `batch`, `dynamic`, `min-block`), resumable with `--skip-existing`. Counts engine builds by wrapping `TRTInterpreter.run` and counts engines vs leftover PyTorch operators in the graph it is about to call, because "ran and matched eager" is satisfiable with no TensorRT.
- `docs/tensorrt-validation.md` — the write-up.
- Pointers and caveats added to `nvidia-blackwell.md`, `nvidia-tensorrt-evaluation.md`, `limitations.md`, `tested-hardware.md` and `docs/README.md`. The Blackwell page's "tensorrt — Verified" row now says what "verified" did and did not establish.

No `src/` changes: this is a validation pass. The obvious follow-up is making the backend warn or refuse when an export produces zero engines.

## Test plan

- `ruff check` and `ruff format --check` clean on the new harness.
- `pytest tests/test_tensorrt_backend.py` — 11 passed.
- Blackwell sweep: 106/106 cells and 32/32 reloads succeeded, zero crashes.
- The BERT repro in the doc was executed verbatim: max abs diff 8.6918.

Raw per-cell JSON is not committed (`artifacts/` is gitignored); every table here is reproducible with the commands in the doc.

items.title: Honor storage.compression on upgraded databases, and let a deployment select the codec
items.body:
`rocksdb-js` 2.6.1 (#2036) brought the codecs in and made lz4 the effective default. This fixes the case that default silently misses, and adds a way to choose a different codec.

## The bug: upgraded databases ignore `storage.compression`

`storage.compression` defaults to **`true`** (`config/defaultConfig.yaml`), so essentially every existing table's metadata records "compression enabled". `toRocksCompression` mapped that to *unset*, on the documented assumption that unset means "use the build default (lz4)".

It doesn't — not for a column family that already exists. RocksDB persists the codec per family, and a reopen that requests nothing **inherits what the family already has**; the build default applies only when the family is being created. Measured across separate processes:

```
5.1 instance, compression 'none'          -> 34.2M SST
5.2 instance, no option passed
    open -> engine reports {"algorithm":"none"}    <-- inherited, not lz4
                                          -> 68.4M SST   (new writes uncompressed too)
full compact()                            -> 68.4M SST   (unchanged)

control: same records, lz4 from scratch   ->  7.1M SST
```

So a brand-new 5.2 database gets lz4 while every database upgraded from 5.1 keeps writing uncompressed indefinitely — both having asked for exactly the same thing. New databases only worked by accident, because unset on a *non-existent* family does fall through to the build default.

An enabled setting now resolves to an explicit codec. On the real metadata path (`{ startingOffset, threshold }`, what `getDefaultCompression()` returns when `storage.compression` is true):

```
old:      opened 'none' -> reports none -> 31.6M SST
upgraded: opened 'lz4'  -> reports lz4  -> 33.9M SST   (the next 60k records cost 2.3M, not 31.6M)
```

**Existing data is deliberately left alone.** An explicit codec governs newly written files only, and `db.compact()` won't convert the rest: rocksdb-js calls `CompactRange` with default `CompactRangeOptions`, whose `bottommost_level_compaction` is `kIfHaveCompactionFilter`, and Harper installs no compaction filter — the bottommost level, holding the bulk of the data, is skipped. Converting in place needs a forced bottommost compaction, which is expensive enough to deserve an explicit operator decision rather than happening during an upgrade.

## Choosing a codec

`HARPER_STORAGE_ROCKS_COMPRESSION` selects the codec for every column family the process opens, validated against the build's `supportedCompression` so an unavailable name fails with a named error instead of a partial startup failure at the first open.

It's an env var and not a config key, and resolved once at module load, because RocksDB rejects reopening a family under a disagreeing codec and Harper's worker threads share one process-wide family registry — so every thread must agree. A config value doesn't achieve that; the main thread loads the storage layer during install, before the value is readable, while workers load it after:

```
pid=3591555 thread=0 resolved=undefined   <-- main thread, loads during install
pid=3591555 thread=1 resolved=zstd
pid=3591555 thread=2 resolved=zstd
```

`__dbis__` is then opened at the build default and reopened as the configured codec, and Harper dies with `The system database failed to load`. Reproduced on a fresh install with the value in config only; it fails on every boot. Making it a config key needs the value resolvable before the first family opens — a boot-ordering change, deliberately not in this PR, and the constraint is recorded in `DESIGN.md` so it doesn't get "improved" into one.

`copyDb`'s `openRocksDb` now resolves the codec the same way. `DESIGN.md` already called `openRocksDatabase` the single chokepoint and migration sat outside it — it creates the families the runtime later reopens.

## Benchmark

`benchmarks/compression/` compares codecs on identical data and workload, one instance per codec. On 1M document-shaped records:

| codec | data files | vs none |
| --- | --- | --- |
| none | 846 MB | 100% |
| snappy | 434 MB | 51% |
| lz4 | 454 MB | 54% |
| zstd | 351 MB | 41% |

Point reads get *faster* with compression — compressed blocks hold more records per block-cache slot and that outweighs decompression (lz4 nearly doubles point-read throughput at the storage layer). Sequential scans pay decompression with no cache-density offset and get slower.

Two traps the harness guards, both of which produce confidently wrong numbers: `@harperfast/integration-testing` installs under `os.tmpdir()`, which is tmpfs on most Linux hosts (every "on-disk" byte becomes a memory measurement); and Harper answers 503 once commits back up past `storage.maxTransactionQueueTime` — one run shed ~99% of its writes and still produced a throughput figure and a 67 MB "compressed" size, which reads as a spectacular win. Runs over an error-rate threshold are marked `INVALID`.

## Open concerns for the reviewer

- **The `toRocksCompression` change alters behavior for every existing table**, which is the point, but it's the line to scrutinize. `false`/`''` still map to `'none'`; an explicit `{ algorithm }` still passes through untouched; only "enabled, unspecified" changes meaning.
- **Benchmark sizes are as the workload left them, not a compacted steady state** — for the reason above, nothing outside the process can force a compaction. Codec-to-codec comparison is sound (identical workload each); the absolute ratio against logical bytes is inflated by update garbage. A storage-layer run using a real `db.compact()` agrees within 3 points.
- **Throughput numbers are single-sample, fixed codec order.** REST-layer variance swamps the codec differences; the size columns are the reliable output. Noted in the README.
- **Reads never touched a device** — the dataset fits in page cache. This measures decompression CPU and block-cache density, not I/O savings; an I/O-bound instance should look better.
- `openRocksDb` is a behavior change on the migration path — right side of the stated invariant, but worth a second pair of eyes.

Follow-up worth doing: expose forced bottommost compaction in rocksdb-js so an existing database can be converted on an explicit operator decision.

Cross-model review (Codex + Gemini + Grok + Harper-domain) ran pre-push; its findings on a no-op compaction step, a `scanBytesRead` race, the `copyDb` bypass, missing validation, committed result JSONs and missing docs are all addressed.
