items.title: Add voice engine quality benchmark and 2026-08 results
items.body:
Compares **Azure Voice Live** and **gpt-realtime-2** on the two things a small-business phone agent is actually judged on: did it understand the caller, and did it handle the call. 165 live calls plus 1200 conditioned ASR clips plus a 400-clip noise-suppression teardown, $22.29 spent.

Full write-up: `docs/research/voice-engine-quality-2026-08.md`. Datasets: `docs/research/voice-eval-datasets.md`.

## Recommendation

**Keep `kataleptic-realtime-hd` (Voice Live + gpt-4.1-mini) as the default, and never enable Azure's noise suppression.** Offer gpt-realtime-2 as an opt-in "more capable, slower" tier.

| | Voice Live + gpt-4.1-mini | gpt-realtime-2 |
|---|---|---|
| TTFA p50 / p95 | **1393 / 1654 ms** | 2079–2408 / 3468–3812 ms |
| Slots heard | **0.967** | 0.856–0.933 |
| Slots echoed back | 0.719 | **0.812–0.819** |
| Judge groundedness | 0.667 | **0.939** |
| pass^3 | 0.091 | **0.182–0.273** |
| Cost | **$0.03/min** | $0.07/min |

The two capabilities separate cleanly: Voice Live **hears** better (0.967 vs 0.856; it never lost a phone number) and answers ~690 ms sooner at p50 and two seconds sooner at p95 for 43% of the cost. gpt-realtime-2 **reasons** better — groundedness 0.939 vs 0.667, the largest single gap in the study. One mishears a name; the other invents an opening time.

`vl-native-brain` (Voice Live serving gpt-realtime-2) scores like gpt-realtime-2 on groundedness *and* has the worst p50 of any arm. **The difference is the brain, not the serving stack.**

## Two things worth acting on

- **`input_audio_noise_reduction` makes recognition worse under exactly the noise it exists to remove.** German degrades 6.05 → 7.47 WER at 10 dB cafe noise and 9.84 → 16.84 at 5 dB, with **zero** dropped utterances — so this is recognition damage, not plumbing. On English it *additionally* drops ~24% of utterances outright, even on clean audio. Reproduced at n=50 with the alternative explanations ruled out (locale, truncation, pairing drift, sample rate). `near_field` and `far_field` are byte-identical to off, so only the deep model does anything — and what it does is harmful. OpenFon doesn't set this knob, so this is a "don't turn it on later" finding.
- **`end_call` is unreliable on every arm** (23–27 of 33 runs). The `isFarewell` heuristic and the 15 s DO safety net are load-bearing — don't remove them.

## On recognition, the engines are close

Within one WER point in **12 of 16** language×condition cells. whisper-1 wins more cells (10/16) but by small margins (max 1.17 pt); azure-speech wins 6 but wins them big — including **20.5% vs 34.5% at 0 dB cafe noise in German**. On clean and moderately degraded audio there is no meaningful difference and the choice should not be made on WER.

## Review round 2 — fixture hygiene and scoring tests

- **Fixture phone numbers replaced** with ranges reserved for fiction (BNetzA `0152 288173xx` / `030 23125xxx`, `555-01xx`). Branch was rebuilt and force-pushed so the old Vodafone-prefix number is in no commit. README states plainly that all scenario audio, names and numbers are synthetic; a test fails the build if a fixture number leaves the reserved ranges.
- **Scoring tests added** and wired into CI as a `bench-scoring` job. They caught a time matcher that scored "2 PM" as a miss against `14:00`, and German scripts whose ASCII transliteration (`fuenfzehn`) Azure TTS read aloud as "fuer-enf-zehn" — a fixture defect masquerading as an engine failure. Both fixed by re-running 150 calls.

## Review round 3 — six scoring bugs

All scoring-side, so all corrected by **re-deriving from the existing raw logs — no calls re-run**.

| # | bug | effect on reported numbers |
|---|---|---|
| 1 | clock times compared as text (`normalize("14:00")` = "vierzehn null") | **grounded_ok 147/165 → 159/165**; strict success up on every arm |
| 2 | forbidden claims matched across turn boundaries | the study's **only `forbidden_hit` was a false positive** → 0 |
| 3 | `bargein_correct` read the caller transcript, not the agent | **24/30, not 30/30** — my "3/3 everywhere" claim was wrong |
| 4 | missing judge verdict counted as a pass | now aborts; `--allow-missing-judge` scores as failure |
| 5 | `run_all.sh` omitted `vl-gpt41mini-semvad` | default produced 132 calls vs the report's 165 |
| 6 | `end_call` double-counted on shared `call_id` | **`tool_ok` unchanged** (set comparison) — 23–25/33 stands; judge input cleaned and re-run |

**The corrected numbers widen the quality gap rather than closing it**, so the recommendation now splits by business type:

| | Voice Live + gpt-4.1-mini | gpt-realtime-2 |
|---|---|---|
| Strict success | 0.394 | **0.424–0.606** |
| pass^3 | 0.182 | **0.273–0.545** |
| Judge groundedness | 0.697 | **1.000** |
| TTFA p50 / p95 | **1393 / 1654 ms** | 2079–2408 / 3468–3812 ms |
| Cost | **$0.03/min** | $0.07/min |

gpt-realtime-2 made **zero unsupported claims in 66 runs** against 24 for the Voice Live arms — six of which are the agent promising a specific appointment slot *is available* when the prompt says "Do not promise a confirmed slot." **Keep Voice Live as the default for information-only businesses; route booking businesses to gpt-realtime-2.** `realtime_model` is already per-business, so it's a settings default.

39 tests, all six bugs pinned. Spend $23.19. Typecheck and tests green.

## Review round 4 — four more, and the class behind them

| # | bug | effect |
|---|---|---|
| 1 | `ttfa_p95_ms` was a percentile of **per-call medians** | **moves in both directions** — VL p95 1654 → **1748**, native 3812 → **3048** |
| 2 | `pass^k` ran `all()` over rows present | two trials satisfied pass^3; missing scenarios left the denominator |
| 3 | empty judge file read as "no judge supplied" | runs passed with zero verdicts |
| 4 | JSON `true` passed as a judge score | `bool` is an `int`; `float(True)` → 0.0 turned a **positive** verdict into a failure |

Per-turn TTFA was recoverable from the existing logs, so #1 is fixed properly rather than renamed. Percentiles are now over 96–106 individual turns per arm.

### The class — four more instances found by audit

You were right that this was a default, not a series of bugs. Auditing every `if x:` guard on a collection, every aggregate over "the rows present", and every vacuous conjunction turned up four beyond the ones reported:

- a run that **errored on the wire** could still satisfy the conjunction
- so could a call the **agent never joined** (zero agent turns)
- an unparseable `forbidden_hit` defaulted to **0** — "no forbidden claim"
- an unparseable `slots_all_heard` defaulted to **1** — "all slots captured"

**Ten places across three rounds, every one pushing the same way.** `summarize.py` now fails closed throughout: validates arm × scenario × k completeness, treats an empty `--judge` as an error, aborts on unparseable conjunction inputs, scores errored and agent-absent runs as failures, and prints `not measured` rather than a blank cell that reads as zero.

**None were firing on the final dataset** — all 165 runs are complete, judged and error-free — so every reported number is unchanged **except the latency percentiles**. The guards exist so the next run can't quietly report a partial one as a good one.

50 tests. `TestAbsentDataNeverPasses` invokes `summarize.py` as a subprocess per case, because what's pinned is that the *run refuses*, not that a helper returns False.

The README's synthetic-data section landed in round 2 (`bench/quality/README.md`, "No real call data is committed") — it names the reserved ranges and the test that enforces them.

## Review round 5 — the sweep's own misses, plus a percentile bug

**The sweep missed two instances of its own class**, because it matched the reported shapes instead of deriving the rule. The rule — *any place where the number of observations can differ from the number expected, and nothing compares the two* — catches both:

- `success_mean` averaged **only the rows present**, so under `--allow-incomplete` two successes out of an expected three reported **1.0**, which is precisely what that flag promises not to do. `pass_k` beside it handled the same gap correctly.
- `run_all.sh` neither stopped nor recorded a runner exiting non-zero, and the trailing `echo` made it exit 0, so a half-finished matrix scored as a whole one.

Re-running the pass against that statement, every aggregate now knows its denominator:

| aggregate | before | now |
|---|---|---|
| `success_mean`, `tool_ok`, `grounded_ok` | mean over rows present | rate over **expected** runs |
| `slot_heard`, `judge_*` | mean over rows present | carries n, flagged when short |
| `ttfa_*` | — | no a-priori denominator (a turn only yields a latency if the agent replied); run-level completeness carries it |
| `score_asr.py` | **no completeness check at all** | validates every (arm, lang, condition) cell, emits `complete` |
| `run_all.sh` | exit 0 regardless | collects failures, exits non-zero, says INCOMPLETE |

**Two more:**

- **`round()` is not nearest-rank.** Banker's rounding selects rank 20 of 20 and 96 of 100 where nearest-rank selects 19 and 95. Now `ceil(q*n) - 1`. The arms have 96–106 turns where `q*n` is non-integral, so **no published latency figure moves** — but at n=100 it would have. (`bench/realtime` isn't on `main` yet so I couldn't diff PR #2's implementation directly; adopted the `ceil` form you described.)
- **A late commit could bind a clip to the previous transcript.** On timeout `run_asr.py` recorded the clip without an item id and kept the socket, so a late `input_audio_buffer.committed` was consumed as the *next* clip's and every subsequent clip inherited its predecessor's hypothesis — silent WER corruption, no error on any affected row. It now aborts the batch so the existing retry reconnects.

**No reported number changes this round.** All 165 Track B runs and all 48 Track A cells are complete, judged and error-free, so the corrected guards agree with the published values exactly. 58 tests.

## Review round 6 (final) — two more of the class, and a written inventory

**Instance nine.** `run_scenarios.py` turned any exception into an error row and **exited zero**, so the shell taught last round to propagate child failures faithfully reported success from a runner that had swallowed its errors. Now exits non-zero listing failed scenarios.

**Instance ten.** `summarize.py` checked completeness by **counting rows**, so three copies of trial 1 satisfied `--trials 3` while trials 2 and 3 were missing, and `pass_k` reported success over duplicates. The runners append to JSONL, so any partial re-run reached this. Both the check and `pass_k` now key on the **set of trial ids**.

Since three sweeps each missed instances of the class they were sweeping for, the checks are now written down: **`bench/quality/COMPLETENESS.md`** — all twelve places the harness decides "this is complete", what each compares, how each can be fooled, and the three that cannot be verified at all. The rule in its final form: *every check compares what it got against what it expected, by identity rather than by count.*

### Cancellation — and barge-in withdrawn

An interrupted generation is `response.done` with `response.status == "cancelled"`; **zero** top-level `response.cancelled` events appear in any log, so the old check never fired. Re-derived from committed logs:

| arm | responses cancelled by the interruption |
|---|---|
| `native-gpt-realtime-2` | **6/6** |
| `vl-native-brain` | 1/6 |
| `vl-gpt41mini`, `-dns`, `-semvad` | **0/6** — nothing left to cancel |

That's the latency difference seen from the other side, and it's a direct observation.

**`bargein_stop_p50_ms` is withdrawn from the report rather than corrected a fourth time.** It measured when audio stopped arriving on the wire, not when the agent stopped speaking; that's not recoverable from this design. Cancellation counts and correction-adoption (24/30) survive because both are directly observable. The report marks barge-in as the weakest part of the study.

Also fixed: a closing turn burned **25 s of billed silence** when the response was only an `end_call` tool call.

**All headline numbers unchanged.** 67 tests.

### One self-inflicted incident

The `run_all.sh` test I added last round **truncated the committed results file** — `run_all.sh` does `cd "$HERE"` regardless of cwd, and `TRACK=b` begins by emptying `results/scenarios.jsonl`. It ran before I committed, so the commit captured the empty file. Restored from `4bfc79b` (165 runs, verified), and the output root is now overridable so no test can reach a finished run. The suite now asserts the results hash is unchanged.

### Fixture numbers, for the human reader

PR-Agent flags these because it cannot tell synthetic from real. They are: German **Bundesnetzagentur drama ranges** (`0152 288173xx` mobile, `030 23125xxx` Berlin landline) and the **`555-01xx`** convention for English. None can reach a subscriber. `bench/quality/README.md` § "No real call data is committed" states that every scenario, name, number and audio file is synthetic and TTS-generated, and `TestFixtureHygiene` fails the build if a fixture number leaves those ranges.

## Review round 7 (final) — barge-in withdrawn, three fixed

**Barge-in is no longer reported.** Applying your standard: four independent defects across four rounds in one metric.

1. stop latency timed when audio stopped arriving *on the wire*, not when the agent stopped speaking
2. adoption read the **caller's** transcript, not the agent's reply
3. cancellation watched for an event neither service emits
4. in-flight state recorded **after** the quiescence wait — and when the previous response was silent or tool-only, the barge-in turn's audio was **skipped entirely**, invalidating the rest of that scenario with no error raised

The two scenarios still run (transcripts are useful qualitatively); nothing is scored from them. The surviving qualitative finding — interruption is the client's job, and on Voice Live there is often no generation left to cancel — doesn't depend on any withdrawn number.

**Three fixes:**

- **`score_asr.py` validated by row count.** A duplicated clip id beside a missing one totals correctly, marks the cell complete, and double-weights the duplicate in the WER. Now compares clip **id sets**: no duplicates, expected size, identical across arms for the same (language, condition). **No published WER moves** — checked, and there are no duplicates: all 48 cells are exactly 25 clips with matching id sets.
- **`IndexError` on a condition-only run.** dWER and SNR50 are both relative to a clean baseline; without one it now emits no robustness rows and says why, instead of throwing after the detail CSV was written.
- **The inventory's one unfixed gap**: a scenario that connects, produces no agent turns and exits cleanly is now an error the runner reports.

## How much to trust these numbers

Now stated in the report itself, as plainly as you put it:

- **Eleven instances of one bug class** across six review rounds, where missing or unverified data read as a pass. Three sweeps each missed instances of the class they were sweeping for — hence `COMPLETENESS.md`.
- **One metric withdrawn** (barge-in, four defects).
- **The recommendation never moved.** Corrections changed magnitudes — the p95 gap narrowed substantially, strict success rose on every arm once time-valued facts became matchable — never the direction.

The report separates the figures that **survived unchanged** (WER table, slot capture, judge groundedness) from those that **moved under correction and could again** (latency percentiles, strict task success) from the one that **did not survive** (barge-in).

70 tests. Typecheck and tests green. Ready to merge.

## Review round 8 (final) — CI unblocked, four fixed

**[P1] CI was broken.** Reproduced on a clean env with only `jiwer` + `num2words`: collection died, `Ran 1 test, FAILED`. Took the refactor rather than adding the dependency — pure event helpers moved to `events.py`, and a test now asserts no scoring module reaches for `websockets` or the runner. **78 tests pass under the exact CI dependency set.**

**[P1] An outage was being published as a measurement.** An exhausted ASR batch wrote a full cell of error rows and exited zero, so the shell reported completion and the scorer saw a complete set of clip ids — a transport failure rendered as **100% WER**. Instance twelve, and the worst-consequence one: the others let a gap pass as success; this converts infrastructure failure into a number a reader would take for an engine that couldn't transcribe. Runner exits non-zero; `score_asr.py` refuses any cell whose rows are all errors.

**[P2] `final_language` — wrong in both directions, and it moved numbers.** Scored from the caller's transcript (testing what the *caller* said) with an echoed companion that joined all agent turns (earlier German drowning out a correct English reply). Scored from the agent's **final turn**:

| | was | now |
|---|---|---|
| code-switch followed | native 2/3 | **15/15, every arm** |
| `native-gpt-realtime-2` strict success | 0.606 | **0.636** |
| `native-gpt-realtime-2` slots heard | 0.856 | **0.911** |
| `vl-gpt41mini-dns` slots echoed | 0.651 | **0.706** |
| `vl-native-brain` slots echoed | 0.812 | **0.868** |

The earlier "native failed the switch once" was an artefact. `pass_k` unchanged everywhere; ordering unchanged.

**[P2] `--out` without an extension** silently overwrote the aggregate — `str.replace` returns the original when the pattern is absent. Both scorers derive companion paths properly and reject extensionless names.

`COMPLETENESS.md` now records that this class has been found **twelve times across seven rounds** — framed as the failure mode this code attracts, so the next person extending it expects to introduce it rather than assuming it's been designed out.

Ready to merge.

## Review round 9 (final) — barge-in excluded from scoring

**Fixed: the withdrawn metric's scenarios were still being scored.** You're right that leaving them running left them feeding `success`, `pass^k` and the slot aggregates — and when the preceding response produces no audio the runner never speaks the interrupting turn, so a row can exist for a call in which the scripted correction was never delivered.

Now marked `"scored": false` in the fixture and dropped from every aggregate *before* the completeness checks. They still run; their transcripts are still committed. **9 scored scenarios, 135 of 165 runs.**

**Checked rather than assumed — the recommendation does not move.** Every Track B figure shifts, and one within-family pair swaps (`vl-gpt41mini-dns` ↔ `vl-native-brain`), which was never a decision point:

| arm | success | pass^3 | slots heard | grounded |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| `native-gpt-realtime-2` | **0.593** | **0.556** | 0.893 | **1.000** |
| `vl-native-brain` | 0.407 | 0.222 | 0.920 | **1.000** |
| `vl-gpt41mini-dns` | 0.370 | 0.222 | **0.960** | 0.815 |
| `vl-gpt41mini` | 0.333 | 0.222 | **0.960** | 0.704 |
| `vl-gpt41mini-semvad` | 0.259 | 0.111 | 0.920 | 0.704 |

Both gpt-realtime-2 arms still lead both gpt-4.1-mini arms on strict success; groundedness is still 1.000 vs 0.704; Voice Live is still ~700 ms faster at p50 for 43% of the cost. The split recommendation stands unchanged.

## Documented, not fixed

Per your line — *silent contamination gets fixed, visible failure and debug-flag-only gets written down* — these are in `COMPLETENESS.md` with the shapes named:

- `--allow-incomplete` counts rows not identities: 4 rows against 3 trials → rate 1.333, `missing_runs` −1. The default path validates by identity, and that's what the published numbers rest on.
- `--allow-incomplete` omits entirely-missing ASR cells rather than reporting `complete=0`.
- A mid-stream `ws.send()` failure can leave the mic task without setting the event a turn awaits — hangs the run rather than corrupting it. Never fired.

80 tests, verified under the CI dependency set. Ready to merge.

## Review round 10 (final) — report now matches the CSV

**1. The VAD-control conclusion was wrong in both directions.** Recomputed on the final scored dataset, holding brain and stack constant:

| server → semantic VAD (gpt-4.1-mini, Voice Live) | change |
|---|---|
| strict success | 0.333 → 0.259 (**−0.074**) |
| pass^3 | 0.222 → 0.111 (**−0.111**) |
| TTFA p50 / p95 | 1315 → 1320 / 1719 → 1852 ms (**+5 / +133**) |
| judge groundedness | 0.704 → 0.704 (no change) |

The old "−69 ms, no effect on success" predated both the barge-in exclusion and the switch to turn-level percentiles — stale twice over. **Semantic VAD is marginally slower and scores slightly worse here.** At 27 runs/arm that's 2 runs and 1 scenario, so the magnitude is noise — but the direction is against it.

**The attribution survives via a cleaner cell than the control.** Holding stack *and* VAD constant — Voice Live, semantic VAD, brain varied — is the one fully-controlled comparison in the design: success **+0.148**, groundedness **+0.296**, TTFA p50 **+1049 ms**. The brain effect is twice the VAD effect on success, and it runs *opposite* to the confound (`vl-native-brain` is itself on the VAD that costs success, so its advantage is understated). The native-vs-Voice-Live comparison still crosses a VAD boundary and is now labelled directional.

**2. Groundedness denominator.** 24 was the all-run count. On the 135 scored rows it is **21**, all from gpt-4.1-mini arms, against **zero** for gpt-realtime-2 across 54 scored runs. The six over-promising cases are unchanged.

Swept the document for other pre-exclusion denominators and found three more: a stale worst-case p50 (2408 → 2369), `end_call` quoted as 23–25 of 33 rather than **17–19 of 27**, and a judge groundedness figure (0.697 → 0.704). A scripted check now verifies every Track B table cell against `summary.csv` and greps for stale tokens; it reports zero.

**3. `probe_session.py`** stopped at the first transcript-shaped event, which is truthy when empty — so on the noise-suppression arm it could report "no transcript" while the real one was queued. Keeps the longest text and drains for the duplicate; verified against `vl-gpt41mini-dns`.

80 tests, verified under the CI dependency set. Ready to merge.

### Rebased onto main

PR #4 and #6 landed while this was in review and rewrote the `deploy` job in `ci.yml`. Rebased onto `f627a08`; the conflict was resolved keeping **both** — main's expanded Cloudflare credential documentation and this branch's `bench-scoring` job. Validated the resulting YAML parses and still declares all three jobs (`check`, `bench-scoring`, `deploy`).

Re-verified after the rebase: 80 scoring tests under the CI dependency set, 138 repo tests, typecheck clean, report values still match `summary.csv`.

## Review round 11 — instance thirteen

**Fixed: the scenario universe was inferred from the results.** `summarize.py` built its scenario set from the rows it was given, so a scenario omitted across *every* arm disappeared from `expected_runs` and the `pass_k` denominator together — completeness passed and every aggregate was computed over a smaller matrix. You're right that this is the one gap the trial-identity checks can't see: they verify trials *within* a scenario, and this loses the scenario.

The set now comes from `fixtures/scenarios.json`. A fixture scenario with no rows aborts (or under `--allow-incomplete` scores as a failure for every arm while staying in the denominator); a results file containing a scenario the fixture doesn't declare is rejected. Three tests cover it, including the `--allow-incomplete` path where a missing scenario must give `pass_k` 0.5 rather than 1.0.

**Documented, not fixed** — both in `COMPLETENESS.md` with their shapes named:

- `response.done` with `status == "failed"` and no separate error event reads as a normal finish, so a partially failed call could enter scoring if another turn produced text.
- The final drain in `run_asr.py` catches `Exception`, so a websocket closure or decode error there is indistinguishable from the timeout that normally ends it, yielding an empty error-free hypothesis scored as a recognition miss rather than retried. The `CommitDesync` guard covers the same failure during the main loop; this is the tail.

Neither occurred in this run — all 165 runs error-free, all 48 ASR cells complete — and neither changes a reported number.

**No reported number changes.** 83 scoring tests under the CI dependency set, 138 repo tests, typecheck clean.

## Review round 12 — two matchers fixed, two fidelity limits stated

**Two P1 limitations now open the Confounds section**, ahead of everything else, because they change what the numbers *mean*:

- **The recogniser was told the caller's language.** Both tracks pass the scenario language to Azure Speech / whisper-1; `src/call-session.ts` leaves it unset in production. Every slot and success figure benefits from an oracle prior the product doesn't have — most of all German names, digit strings, and the 15/15 code-switching result. Both arms got it, so the comparison holds; the **levels are optimistic**.
- **Scripted turns continue after `end_call`.** Production begins hanging up. **Could it flip the ordering? No, on this dataset** — measured exposure is **two turns, both on `vl-gpt41mini`**, because the scripted `end_call` almost always lands on the closing turn. The gap it would need to close is seven runs, and it runs *against* the arm that would lose credit, so removing it would widen the gap. Stated with that number rather than as an open worry.

**Two matchers fixed**, and they cut opposite ways, so here's the net rather than an assumption:

| | effect |
|---|---|
| time matcher (inflating) | expected `14:00` matched `2:30`, `2 AM`, bare `2` → now parsed as (hour, minute) and compared |
| negation (deflating) | "not open on Saturday" matched forbidden `open on Saturday` → negation-window guard |

**Net:** seven false grounding credits removed, **all on gpt-4.1-mini arms** (`grounded_ok` 1.000→0.963, 0.963→0.852, 1.000→0.889) plus one echoed slot. gpt-realtime-2 arms untouched. **No success or pass^3 figure moved.** The negation guard changed nothing here — the study's only `forbidden_hit` had already been removed as a cross-turn artefact — so it's a guard for future runs.

One subtlety worth noting: the first fix needed a second one. `normalize("2:30")` is "two thirty", so a word scan over normalised text re-admitted the very times the digit pass had rejected. Spoken hours are now scanned only after digits are stripped.

90 tests. Ready to merge.

## Review round 13 — cancelled responses were attributed to the next turn

**The negative-TTFA count, and the real affected set.** Eight turns went negative — but that understates it: **every run containing a cancellation** has shifted attribution, whether or not the arithmetic crossed zero.

| | count |
|---|---|
| turns with negative TTFA | 8 (min **−5461.8 ms**) |
| runs containing ≥1 cancellation | **14 of 165** (7 in the scored set) |
| affected scenarios | `message-de-01` (6), `codeswitch-01` (1) |
| affected arms | `native-gpt-realtime-2` (4), `vl-native-brain` (3) |
| Voice Live gpt-4.1-mini arms | **0** — no cancellations at all |

`message-de-01`'s second caller turn has an internal pause, which is what trips the VAD.

**Fixed in the runner**: a cancelled response is discarded — its audio timings and the agent text it contributed — and the turn keeps waiting for the replacement.

**The committed runs can't be repaired.** Reconstructing the metric needs the moment the harness finished streaming the caller clip, which the log doesn't record. Those runs carry `ttfa_trustworthy=0` and are excluded from the percentiles:

| arm | p50 | p95 |
|---|---|---|
| `native-gpt-realtime-2` | 2022 → **2077** | 3262 → **3325** |
| `vl-native-brain` | 2369 → **2408** | 3474 → **3722** |
| Voice Live gpt-4.1-mini arms | unchanged | unchanged |

The mis-attribution had been **flattering the slower family**, so correcting it widens the latency gap. **Transcripts were never affected** — they append in arrival order, not per turn — so slots, grounding, success and pass^3 are unchanged.

**Contraction negation fixed.** You were right that the previous fix only handled phrasing nobody uses: the normaliser turns `aren't` into `aren t`, not `arent`. Split stems now listed, and the time path substitutes apostrophes in place so its offsets stay valid. Covers `aren't`, `don't`, `can't`, `couldn't`, `won't`, and the typographic apostrophe.

**Time matching documented as approximate.** No fourth regex. The report states both inflating failure modes — numeric strings parsing as clock mentions, and spoken composite times recording only the hour — names the affected metric (**strict success on the three booking scenarios**), notes that a single run is 0.037 at n=27, and points the reader at the WER table, slot capture and groundedness instead. Both modes hit every arm identically, so the comparison isn't skewed.

94 tests. Ready to merge.

## What's in here

- `bench/quality/` — harness, fixtures, scoring, raw event logs (audio redacted), CSV results.
- Track A streams conditioned FLEURS clips and scores each engine's own caller transcript. This measures **the STT front-end each stack ships** (whisper-1 vs azure-speech), not a free-standing ASR model, and is labelled that way throughout.
- Track B runs 11 Riverside Dental scenarios as live multi-turn calls against the **real** `buildSystemPrompt` output — `gen_prompt.ts` calls the product code, so the 21-day calendar block is genuine.
- Scoring is split by whether the question has an objectively right answer: slots, tool calls and language adherence are programmatic; the LLM judge sees only groundedness, resolution and tone, blind, with a seeded per-scenario shuffle. **Two seeds agree on groundedness 159/165 (96.4%)** — the judge is validated, not assumed.

## Confounds, stated

- Voice Live **rejects** `server_vad` on the gpt-realtime-2 brain, so that arm runs Azure semantic VAD while native runs server VAD. I added `vl-gpt41mini-semvad` as a control: on the same brain, VAD choice moves TTFA p50 by 69 ms and success not at all, so it is not driving the brain comparison — but the native-vs-Voice-Live comparison still crosses a VAD boundary.
- Caller audio is Azure neural TTS: more fluent than real callers, so Track B is optimistic in absolute terms but comparable between arms. Track A uses real human speech.
- **Barge-in cannot be measured server-side.** These engines deliver a whole response's audio faster than real time (`response.done` ~600 ms into a 4 s reply), so in 29 of 30 attempts there was nothing left to interrupt. Barge-in is entirely the client's job. All five arms did adopt the corrected value, 3/3.
- A collector bug was found and fixed mid-run; `vl-gpt41mini` was re-run as a control and produced **100/100 byte-identical** transcripts, confirming the fix is behaviour-preserving and the remaining empties are the service's.

Raw logs are committed so every number can be re-scored without spending again. Audio corpora are gitignored; `bench/quality/prepare/` regenerates them.

`npm run typecheck` and `npm test` pass.

items.title: docs: stop the plugin page keeping its own copy of the numbers
items.body:
`docs-site/claude-code-plugin.md` carried its own latency table and build time. Both had gone stale inside a day:

- **"344 Python files"** — written before the guard grew to eight languages. The index is 1135 files: 1009 `.py`, 60 `.ts`, 43 `.js`, 23 `.tsx`.
- **70 / 72 ms and 86 / 87 ms** — measured before #798 stopped the indexer walking nested checkouts, which is the fix that changed them.
- **"a 344-file repository takes about 6 seconds"** — measured today, 1135 files in 3.8 s.

Meanwhile the README had been updated properly: 1135-file index, a budget column, its own artifact in `benchmark_results/plugin_budget.json`, and a footnote about the pip-install path being faster than the plugin-only one. Two documents, two sets of numbers, one of them wrong.

## What changes

The page links to the README table and the artifact instead of restating them. The one figure it still names is measured today and is about this repository rather than about the guard's speed.

Same rule already applied to the self-analysis score after it appeared as 0.39, 0.63 and 0.36 in three places: **a number worth publishing gets exactly one home, or it drifts.**

## Verified

- `mkdocs build --strict` — no content warnings (remaining output is local cairo/PIL, absent on this machine only)
- `markdownlint-cli2` at the repo's pinned version — clean
- Figures re-measured on `main` today: 1135 files, 3815 ms build, `pre` p95 58 ms, `post` p95 75 ms

items.title: docs(benchmarks): report the agent-loop result, and separate it from the payload number
items.body:
## The cost claim is withdrawn, and the run refutes it itself

`§2` previously reported -33.5% cost per question, p = 0.007. The stratified run
contains a control that nobody had read as one.

**code-review-graph never called its server across all 15 questions.** It is
behaviourally a bare agent, carrying an extra 28,118 characters of tool schema
that should make it cost *more*. Measured on dollars it came out **43% cheaper
than the bare control**. A tool that did nothing produced a best-in-class saving.

The mechanism is prompt caching. Whichever arm runs first pays to warm the cache
and every arm after it reads it cheaply. In this run the bare control ran first
in **15 of 15** questions, and the correlation between an arm's position in the
cycle and its dollar cost is **-0.487**. That is a property of the schedule.

## What replaces it

Output tokens are never cached. Their correlation with run position is **+0.010**.

| Tool | Agent used it | Output tokens | vs bare | Leaner on | p |
|---|---:|---:|---:|---:|---:|
| **repowise** | **15 / 15** | **2,420** | **-15.9%** | **12 of 15** | **0.035** |
| CodeGraph | 13 / 15 | 2,540 | -11.7% | 10 of 15 | 0.302 |
| Serena | 4 / 15 | 2,551 | -11.3% | 8 of 15 | 1.000 |
| code-review-graph | 0 / 15 | 2,768 | -3.8% | 10 of 15 | 0.302 |
| Graphify | 3 / 15 | 2,878 | 0.0% | 7 of 15 | 1.000 |
| *bare agent* | n/a | 2,877 | baseline | n/a | n/a |

Only repowise reaches significance. It also reproduces: the same figure lands at
-12.9% on a two-arm run shape, where the dollar delta moves by 39 points.

Adoption and the loop numbers are now one table. Both answer the same question
and splitting them made a reader hold two tables to answer it.

## Also in this change

- The page opens on the JetBrains reruns of
  [Caveman](https://blog.jetbrains.com/ai/2026/07/speak-to-ai-agents-like-cavemen-tosave-tokens/)
  (65% advertised, 8.5% measured) and
  [RTK](https://blog.jetbrains.com/ai/2026/07/rtk-claude-code-token-savings/)
  (60-90% advertised, 7.6% *more expensive* at low reasoning effort). The gap
  between a one-context-load measurement and an agent loop is what this page
  exists to be careful about, so our own payload figure is now `§3` and is
  labelled the easy number.
- **New result:** the saving grows with task size. Split at the median, the
  harder half saves **722 tokens per question against 154**, permutation
  p = 0.013 over 200,000 shuffles. Both limits travel with it: the split is
  post-hoc, and every question is a single session of roughly nine turns, so
  nothing here measures a long task.
- `§6` says why indexing is slow in its first sentence rather than two
  paragraphs later.
- The per-shape breakdown is dropped at n=3 per row.
- Quality is stated as decoration rather than evidence: every per-arm effect is
  smaller than the 0.46 points the two graders disagree by on the same answers.

## README

The hero claimed "up to -96% tokens to load context, -89% file reads, -70% tool
calls" from paired runs that no longer appear on the benchmarks page, one leg of
which had never been rerun under the current harness. It now leads with the
measurement that has a committed CSV behind it, **-97% for a commit's context**,
with the agent-loop figure beside it.

Also fixed: two stale token figures (2,391 / 64,039 to 393 / 13,984), the cost
bullet, and one anchor that had begun resolving to the wrong section after the
retitle rather than failing visibly.

## Verification

No numbers were changed by hand. Every figure is recomputed from
`results/bakeoff_2026_08/rung6/layerb_stratified_django/swe_qa.jsonl` and the
committed token-efficiency CSV. Section 1 and section 5 are untouched.

items.title: Publication readiness: agnostic docs, a quick start that runs, a build that works elsewhere, v0.8.0
items.body:
Publication pass over the documentation. Two problems stood between this repository and a reader who does not already know it.

## The docs were written from a consumer's perspective

The README's quick start opened by telling the visitor that the interesting artefact lives in **another repository** — six links to a private one, at the most important position on the page. Every reference to a specific downstream consumer is now gone: README, `ROADMAP.md`, `docs/`, `tests/`, `examples/`, the `Makefile`, `include/geist.h` and `release.yml`.

An engine that stays application-neutral is one anyone can embed. Naming who links it, in the engine's own documentation, was the opposite of that claim.

## The quick start produced no output

It does now — verified by running the exact documented command:

```
make lib && make fetch-bench-model
make run ARGS='gguf_artifacts/bitnet-2b4t-i2_s.gguf "The capital of France is"'
-> The capital of France is Paris. Paris is a city that is known for its rich history...
```

It points at the 1.1 GB ternary model rather than the 3.1 GB test fixture, because a curious visitor should not wait for three gigabytes to find out whether the thing works.

`make bench` gets the section it earns (**Don't trust the numbers, run them**). It measures the competing engine in the same run, against the byte-identical GGUF, after the board has cooled back to the temperature geist started from — that is the claim that survives scrutiny, not the ratio.

## One number was wrong

The full-numbers table listed BitNet decode on a Pi 5 as **17.4 vs 8.2 t/s with no context length**. The recorded run (`benchmark/reference_runs.json`, 2026-08-01) reads **17.9 vs 9.1 at 32 tokens** and **15.0 at 512**. A throughput figure without a sequence length cannot be compared to anything; all three lengths are listed now.

## Also

- **Removed the tracked `geist` symlink** at the repository root. It pointed at the CLI that 0.7.0 deleted, so a fresh clone got a dangling link in the first directory listing a visitor sees.
- `ROADMAP.md` lost the two tracks and the protocol phase that belong to an agent layer, and gained a `## Scope` statement instead.
- Stale instructions fixed: `QUICKSTART.md` still claimed `make` drops a `./geist` symlink (no rule creates one), `DEPLOY.md` pointed at a fetch script in a repository nobody can read, the Makefile's default-goal comment described a CLI.
- Dead links: `README.md#where-this-is-going` now resolves; every relative link in the repository was checked.

## Verification

- `make lib` — green
- `make test-unit` — 27 passed, 17 skipped, 0 failed
- `make agent-contract-smoke` — 17 contract symbols present
- `make format-check` — all 285 files conform
- Quick start executed end to end, output above

No source behaviour changes: the only non-documentation edits are comments.

items.title: Phase 11: release
items.body:
Makes the repository readable by someone who has thirty seconds, five minutes or
an afternoon, and closes the plan.

## What was built

**`README.md`, cut from 784 lines to 133.** What this is in two sentences, the
headline result as one table, the pipeline as a mermaid diagram, four commands,
the layout of the code, and the limitations. The diagram is mermaid rather than
a committed image so that the repository still commits no plots.

**`docs/results.md`.** Every result with the run id behind each number. Per
system: accuracy against horizon, invariant behaviour, the held out regime gap,
resolution generalisation for the fluid, speed at matched accuracy, the break
even rollout count and the calibration result. Then the diagnosis agent scores
and a run index.

**`docs/architecture.md`.** What was built rather than what was planned, and it
now holds the harness, model and training loop detail the README was carrying.

**`docs/reproduction.md`.** One path from a clean checkout to the headline
numbers with a measured runtime at each step.

## What the results were

No surrogate here is faster than the solver at matched accuracy. The N-body
graph network runs at 0.056 of the cheapest solver setting that matches it. The
fluid operator is the one undecided case at 1.23 with a range of 0.81 to 1.63,
which does not establish a speedup. The neural operator lost to its own
convolutional control at a matched parameter count on every accuracy number and
won only on resolution consistency. Neither surrogate generalises to its held
out regime. The fluid ensemble's spread warns 0.4 of simulated time before the
error crosses the trust threshold; the N-body ensemble warns 0.088 too late.

Two numbers the README carried were wrong and are corrected against the records.
The N-body graph network completes 0 of 4 held out rollouts rather than 3, and
the ensemble diverges later than the single network rather than sooner, at steps
154 to 163 against 153 to 159. A comment in `configs/fluid.yaml` claimed 1,941 s
and about 5,800 s of training; the epoch timings give 2,010 s and 5,286 s.

## One test fixed

`test_both_momenta_are_conserved_for_a_many_body_cluster` failed in CI on the
first push, at a relative drift of 1.1e-14 against a bound of 1e-14, having held
on Windows at 4.9e-15. Same seed and same code, differing only in the order the
runner accumulated the sums in. A bound with a factor of two of headroom is a
statement about one machine rather than about the solver, so both linear
momentum bounds are now derived from what they measure: 2000 steps each able to
lose an epsilon. Checked that this is not vacuous, since scaling one body's
reaction force by one part in 10^12 drifts 700 times past the new bound.

## What the limitations are

Stated in full at the top of `docs/results.md` and in the README. One machine,
eight CPU cores, no CUDA. Small systems and small datasets. Both surrogates stop
being physical well inside their horizons. Timings are not reproducible and
neither is the third significant figure of a chaotic error. Calibration was
bought with vagueness on the held out regimes. The diagnosis agent's 86 per cent
was not produced by the shipped command, because no API credential was
available.

## What was left out

**The eight repeat benchmark medians were not regenerated.** Each benchmark
invocation overwrites `benchmark.json` in its run directory, so only the last of
the eight survives. The speed tables now give both the phase 09 median and the
retained repeat and say which is which. Regenerating would have produced
different absolute timings on a machine the section already documents as
drifting by a factor of two. This happened once more during the phase, to a
solver only repeat no document cites.

**No results image is committed.** `CLAUDE.md` forbids committing plots and the
brief asked for one image. The mermaid diagram satisfies both.

**No metric was cut.** The brief anticipated metrics that could not be made to
fail. All seven have sentinel tests asserting both what they catch and what they
do not, so there was nothing to cut, and that is recorded rather than left as an
empty section.

## Checks

`ruff check`, `ruff format --check` and `mypy --strict` clean over 207 source
files. Full suite including slow and integration: 1,401 passed, 2 skipped, 96
per cent branch coverage. Both skips are the live API tests, which need an
`ANTHROPIC_API_KEY`. No dead code, no unused configuration keys, no stale to-do
notes, no em-dashes and no US spellings outside PyTorch API names.

items.title: docs(changelog): record the measured fixes under Unreleased
items.body:
Changelog entry for the work merged in #103. CHANGELOG.md only — no code.

## Contents

Four `Fixed` entries (YAML block-scalar detection, `find` deleting its payload, the TOML filter shadowing the test distiller, `cargo test` recounting collapsed lines), one `Removed` (`est_cost_usd` / `ModelPricing`), and two `Changed` (the measured numbers; the determinism and latency costs, now stated rather than hidden).

## One thing worth a reviewer's eye

The `[0.6.1]` entry currently credits the `find` distiller with:

> strips out raw file path samples entirely and emits a highly compressed, AI-friendly key-value summary … maximizing token reduction (**up to 99.8% savings**)

That behaviour *was* the bug. It reported ~99% by discarding the file paths that were the answer to the question, and it is where the retired **97.3%** all-time headline came from.

I did not rewrite the 0.6.1 entry — published history should stay as published — so the new `Unreleased` entry names it explicitly instead, and the old claim no longer stands as the only account of that change. The replacement is lossless prefix factoring: ~72% on the same output, every path round-tripping byte-for-byte.

## Note on the numbers quoted here

They are the measured ones from #103: **58.9% net** across 1,810 replayed traces, **63.6% of calls saving nothing** and adding zero bytes, and a `65.3% → 58.9%` *drop* caused by fixing the YAML sniffer — six of those points were destroyed manifests, not removed noise. Nothing in this entry is projected.

<!-- AI-PR-DESCRIPTION-START -->
## PR Auto Describe


## Summary
Critical data integrity and accuracy fixes: format-safe compression now passes JSON/YAML/CSV through byte-for-byte; the YAML sniffer no longer misclassifies block scalars (fixes manifests seen as docker logs); the `find` distiller replaced payload deletion with lossless prefix factoring (~72% savings, nothing lost). Removed the `ModelPricing` dead code that couldn't know cache vs. input costs. Replaced all published benchmarks with measurements from 1,810 real traces (net 58.9% reduction, not the claimed 97.3%).

---

## Key Changes
- **Format gate**: JSON, NDJSON, YAML, TSV, CSV bypass collapse markers entirely
- **YAML sniffer**: block scalar bodies (`|`, `>`, etc.) now skipped, not judged — prevents manifests misidentified as docker logs
- **`find`/`grep` distillers**: lossless prefix factoring replaces lossy deletion; same ~72% savings, fully reversible
- **TOML filter guardrail**: filter only wins if it beats `MIN_REDUCTION_PCT`; `TestDistiller` shadowing fixed
- **`cargo test` totals**: quotes runner's own summary line (cargo, pytest, jest) instead of recounting collapsed lines
- **Removed**: `est_cost_usd`, `ModelPricing`, `_cached`/`_cache_creation` fields (dead code, wrong numbers)
- **Benchmarks**: replaced all published claims with 1,810 real replay traces; actual savings: 58.9% net (was 97.3%), `git` 91.3%, `cargo` 96.8%

---

## Detailed Breakdown

### Data Integrity Fixes
| Issue | Symptom | Fix |
|-------|---------|-----|
| Format-agnostic collapse | JSON dashboard output had 14 collapse markers; `jq` failed | Format sniffer gates both hook points; structured formats pass through |
| YAML block scalar misdetection | 608-line ConfigMap with HCL block scalar → 13,463 bytes as "docker logs" | Sniffer skips block scalar bodies; `|` is YAML's own signal |
| `find` deleting its answer | ~99% "savings" = discarded file paths (the actual answer) | Lossless prefix factoring: hoist shared prefix to header, paths relative; round-trips byte-for-byte |
| `grep` per-match path repetition | Path printed per match (wasteful) | Path hoisted once per file, offsets for matches |

### Distiller Selection Fixes
- **TOML filter shadowing**: `sys_build_domain` was winning race but only cutting 1% (below `MIN_REDUCTION_PCT`); its phantom cut still discarded `TestDistiller`'s 94% reduction. Filter now only short-circuits if it *actually* beat the guardrail.
- **`cargo test` recounting**: `CollapseMode::Test` folds `... ok` lines before distiller sees them → reported `1 passed` for `490 passed`. Now quotes runner's summary; falls back to counting only when no summary printed.

### Removed Dead Code
- `ModelPricing` used only `.input`; `_cached`/`_cache_creation` were always zero; every dollar figure was a fresh-input guess presented as session cost. Removed from `stats`, `diff`, `guard::config`. Unknown keys in existing `config.toml` still parse.

### Benchmark Corrections
| Claim | Actual |
|-------|--------|
| 97.3% all-time | 58.9% net (15.0 MB → 6.2 MB) — previous figure was manufactured by `find` deleting its payload |
| `docker build` 99.5% | 37.2% (5,783 bytes from 9.2 KB fixture) |
| `git diff` 50.0% | 44.6% |
| `~40% faster TTFT` | Never measured |
| `$35+ USD/month` | Used removed estimator |

Real benchmarks from **1,810 execution traces** on release binary with fresh `HOME` per invocation: `git` 91.3%, `cargo` 96.8%, `cat` 9.1%.

### New Documentation
- **Non-determinism**: warm `~/.omni/omni.db` causes scorer variance; same binary/input gave 1,835 bytes then 433 on identical runs (21/30 differed). A/B tests must isolate state per invocation.
- **Latency cost**: ~82 ms for 496-byte `git status` against fresh DB → **~308 ms** against 97 MB DB, per hooked command.

---

## Notes
- YAML sniffer fix **reduced** reported savings (65.3% → 58.9%) because six previously "saved" data points were actually destroyed manifests being misread as noise.
- All i18n READMEs carry the same corrected numbers.

---

## Breaking Changes
- **`ModelPricing` removed**: unknown config keys still parse (backward compat), but dollar figures no longer printed in `stats`/`diff` output. Users relying on `est_cost_usd` output will see nothing.
- **Benchmark numbers changed significantly**: any docs/landing pages hardcoding old figures are now inaccurate.

items.title: test(conformance): add a Bowtie harness for the JSON Schema engine
items.body:
Adds a [Bowtie](https://docs.bowtie.report/) harness at
`conformance/bowtie`. Bowtie drives every JSON Schema implementation
through the official suite over one protocol, which gives us something
`run-json-schema-suite.ts` cannot: other implementations' verdicts on
the same case, so a divergence can be read against what the ecosystem
does rather than against the suite alone.

It does not replace the existing runner. That one stays the committed
baseline CI ratchets against; this is the outward comparison, and it is
not wired into any gate.

## What it found

Run against eight other JS/TS implementations plus boon (Rust),
go-jsonschema and python-jsonschema:

| Implementation | Rate |
| --- | --- |
| json-schema-library 11.6.2 | 100.00% |
| hyperjump 1.17.7 | 99.69% |
| **oaverify 5.4.0** | **99.54%** |
| schemasafe 1.3.0 | 96.77% |
| ajv 8.20.0 | 80.45% |

Every remaining divergence is a documented gap. Before #663 the count
was 20 and matched `REPORT.md` exactly, one for one, in both
directions; that agreement is what gave the harness its credibility as
a cross-check. It is now 5.

One reading note on that table: ajv's number is mostly strict-mode
compile refusals rather than wrong verdicts, so raw pass rates reward
permissive defaults and should not be quoted as a quality ranking
without that caveat.

## Design

`harness.ts` speaks version 1 of the harness protocol over stdin/stdout.
The compile/validate path mirrors `run-json-schema-suite.ts`, feeding
each case's `registry` through `compileSchema`'s `external` map the way
that runner feeds the suite's `remotes/`. `build.mjs` bundles harness
and engine into one dependency-free ESM file with esbuild, reading
aliases from `workspace-aliases.ts`, so the image needs no `pnpm
install` and no prior build. Only `core`, `schema` and `formats` are
copied in, which is the whole transitive source closure of the compile
path.

**Only 2020-12 is advertised.** The engine ships three dialects and the
other two are OpenAPI flavours rather than JSON Schema drafts.
Advertising a draft the engine does not compile would report harness
lies as validator failures.

## Two traps recorded in the README

Both cost time to find and would cost it again.

Two of `bowtie perf`'s four default benchmarks (`Draft2020-12_MetaSchema`
and `nested_schemas`) `$ref` the 2020-12 metaschema, which oaverify does
not ship. `compileSchema` throws, and every timed iteration measures the
error path instead of validation. On `nested_schemas` that reads as
second place and an 8x win over ajv, so the artifact flatters us and is
easy to quote by mistake. The README gives the command to check a
benchmark before trusting it, and says explicitly that registering the
metaschema in the harness to make the numbers appear is the wrong fix,
since it would give the harness a capability the library lacks.

The keyword benchmarks (`-k`) are all self-contained and do measure real
work, verified by running all 53 cases through the harness with zero
errored results. They are still compile-throughput numbers rather than
validation-speed ones, because the harness compiles per case.
`additionalProperties` is our only last place, and its schema carries
99,999 properties: in-process that shape costs ~364ms to compile against
~15ms per validate.

## Not included

No CI wiring. A gate that can turn red because another project shipped a
release is one people learn to ignore. A scheduled job that diffs the
divergence set against `json-schema-results.json` is the shape worth
having, and it is a separate change.

`conformance/bowtie` is deliberately absent from AGENTS.md's sub-root
table: it is not a pnpm root, so it has no lockfile and the dependabot
rule for new roots does not reach it. That is stated where the table is,
because its absence otherwise reads as an oversight.

No dependency on #665; either can merge first.

items.title: Catch removed magusfile calls at load; derive target conventions from the graph
items.body:
Two plan sessions: magusfile API migration tracking, and convention drift derived from the knowledge graph.

## Magusfile API migrations

Enumerating what had actually shipped closed this plan rather than sizing it. Four removed calls, not fifteen, so no codemod.

The failure mode was worse than "a confusing parse error". Buzz reads a missing member as `null`, so a magusfile calling `magus.needs` parsed, loaded, and passed `magus ls` - and because the static target graph is built by reading `ctx.needs` out of the source, it reported NO dependency edge. `magus run build` silently never scheduled the prerequisite.

- **MGS1025** rejects the four removed calls at load, reading the AST so a mention in a comment is not a call, with a textual fallback only for the shape that cannot parse (`magus.project.register` predates required parameter annotations, so it dies in the parser).
- **`magus-api.lock` + `TestMagusSurfaceLocked`** make the NEXT removal loud. The table behind MGS1025 is hand-maintained; the lock snapshots all 38 members a magusfile can reach and fails naming the member and the table that has to describe it. Verified by simulating a removal, in both directions.
- Two premises in the original plan were wrong and are corrected in the notes: dot-to-backslash was never a breaking change, and ctx-threading was already handled well by MGS1008 - it was the model to copy, not a gap.

## Benchmark fixtures

The rot was four layers deep, each invisible until the one above it was fixed: the removed API, then spell renames (`ts` -> `typescript`, `py` -> `python`), then a cross-project import written workspace-relative where magus resolves it dot-relative, then the spell op contract itself (callback-returning-bool -> returning a `Command`).

All four generators now produce workspaces that load, verified by execution. `benchmarks/README.md` claimed the go fixture "is what's in CI"; nothing runs these, which is exactly why they rotted, so the claim is replaced with the consequence and a load check.

## Convention drift

Two advisors, both silent by default, both derived from the corpus rather than declared.

| | groups | on | the question |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| `conformance` | targets | op set | do these do the same work (needs precision) |
| `missing-target` | projects | spell set | are these the same kind of project (needs generality) |

Deliberately opposite keys. Loosening conformance to spells collapses every Go target into one bucket with an 18% majority; tightening missing-target to ops splits two Go services with different toolchains and sees nothing.

Verified both directions on real graphs, including the false positive that killed the first attempt at the second axis (a `buf` schema project is not a Go service short of a test):

- This workspace: **0 findings from both, at every threshold tried**, down to far more permissive than the shipped defaults. There is no convention here to violate.
- Planted drift: `checkout:unit-test -> should be 'test' (6 of 7)` and `svc-new is missing 'test' (5 of 6 of kind go)`, without flagging the schema project.

Thresholds (cohort 5, share 0.8) are defensible but uncalibrated - this workspace cannot distinguish them from any other pair. They are action inputs, and every finding reports its own numbers, so a wrong threshold is visible in the output rather than hidden in it.

## Notes for review

- The advisors have never posted a real comment. Their analysis path runs end-to-end locally, but the `gh api` publish/silence paths have only been exercised by `advice.buzz`'s own tests. This PR is the first real run.
- `c92f6d2f` on `add-profiling-gate` attributes bespoke tooling in the graph and both advisors benefit from it for free. A duplicate implementation on this branch was reverted in favour of it; no Go conflicts remain.
- `benchmarks/large-monorepo` is fixed and its spell contract verified against a scratch mirror, but the clone path needs network and is unverified.

items.title: 0.4.0 — the honest reframe: a checklist, not a benchmark
items.body:
## 0.4.0 — the honest reframe: a checklist, not a benchmark

> **This description was rewritten.** The original argued from a corpus study that has since been **withdrawn** — we audited it ourselves and it did not hold up. Details below, because how that happened matters more than the numbers did.

### The claim, and the proof

**CrewScore measures coverage, not quality.** You can prove it from the shipped rule catalog in ten seconds, with no corpus and no trust required:

```python
from crewscore.scoring import DIMENSION_KEYS, overall_score
from crewscore.scorers.structural_analysis import SCORER_MAP
dim = lambda m, t: 0 if not m else min(100, round(15 + 85 * m / t))
per = {k: dim(1, len(SCORER_MAP[k])) for k in DIMENSION_KEYS}
print(per, overall_score(per))
```

A prompt that states **all eight governance controls clearly, once each, scores 28/100** — below the lowest tier boundary of 50. Stating every control *twice* still reaches only 41. Getting to 70 requires restating one control four to six different ways, which is exactly the redundancy our own Context Bloat detector flags as a defect.

A metric a well-written prompt cannot pass is not measuring quality. It is measuring coverage — and coverage is genuinely useful, which is what the docs now say.

This is pinned by tests, so a rule-count change cannot silently move it.

### What we withdrew

An earlier draft of `docs/validation.md` reported a 1,368-prompt discrimination study. A claims audit found numbers in it that are not merely wrong but **impossible**:

- 60.0% recall reported for a dimension present in **2** prompts — only 0/50/100 are achievable
- a matching-line total **below the minimum its own distributions require**
- a confidence interval implying p=0.281 against a stated p=0.36, with no statistical test named anywhere
- "each alternative made the tool look *better*" introducing two effect sizes both **lower** than baseline
- "1 prompt in 283 (2.1%)" — 1/283 is 0.35%
- a claim of reproducibility "from `scripts/`", where no such harness is committed

It is withdrawn pending a committed, executable harness. Publishing unreliable statistics to demonstrate rigor is self-defeating — and "a hostile reader will reproduce this in an afternoon" was the original argument *for* publishing. That cuts both ways. The conclusion never depended on the study; the formula establishes it deterministically.

Every one of those figures has been swept from the README, the site, the CHANGELOG and the issue template, and a test now forbids their return.

### Also fixed: the browser and the CLI disagreed

`score-engine.js` compiled rules with `new RegExp(p, "i")`. JavaScript's `\b` is ASCII-only; Python's is Unicode-aware. So `确保hipaa合规性` scored compliance **0 in the CLI and 24 in the browser** — CJK has no inter-word spaces, so an English acronym flush against native script is ordinary prose, not an edge case. Confirmed on Chinese, Greek and Cyrillic.

Note for reviewers: the `u` flag does **not** fix this (JS `\w` stays ASCII-only in Unicode mode). The patterns are rebuilt with explicit Unicode lookarounds.

### Also fixed: `fix --apply` generated unbounded context bloat

The guard tested for `## Guardrails` while the writer emitted `# Guardrails`, so it never matched its own output. Three runs took a one-line prompt to 123 lines. The tool that exists to flag Context Bloat was manufacturing it.

### Breaking

1. **`--json` for coding-agent config** drops `overall`, `dimensions`, `findings`, `transparency` — keys *absent*, not zeroed. Branch on `governance_applicable`.
2. **`crewscore fix` exits `1`** rather than injecting governance templates into an `AGENTS.md`.

### Everything else

Artifact profiles (config judged on smells, never a governance grade); configuration-smell detectors replicating [arXiv:2606.15828](https://arxiv.org/abs/2606.15828); a **script-injection fix in `action.yml`** proven live against the unfixed manifest; the `scored` Action output, because an empty `score` cannot guard itself; and crash-hardening so a UTF-16, latin-1 or binary file errors cleanly instead of raising a traceback under `--json`.

### How this was validated

Human review was explicitly not the gate. Six independent gates ran instead:

| Gate | Result |
| --- | --- |
| Clean-room install | Wheel installs and honors both contracts outside the source tree. Found that **0.3.0 was never published either** — PyPI stops at 0.2.7 — falsifying a claim in our own CHANGELOG. |
| Offline-claim falsification | **Holds.** `socket` patched *before* import, every command driven: zero egress. 20 runs byte-identical. |
| Claims audit | **Found the false study.** Every figure re-derived independently before acting. |
| Python/JS parity | 199 inputs + regex-dialect probes. **34 divergences**, now fixed. |
| Adversarial robustness | **FRAGILE** → four crash classes fixed. |
| Mutation testing | Suite scored **64%**; survivors clustered at tier boundaries and file discovery. Gaps closed, each verified by re-applying the mutant. |

CI now runs on Linux (3.11/3.12/3.13), Windows and macOS — the first macOS run in this project's history, and the first CI execution of the Windows cp1252 path.

`release.yml` publishes via PyPI Trusted Publishing (OIDC), so no long-lived token exists in this repo. It gates on tag-equals-version, a non-stale `score-engine.js`, and a clean-venv wheel asserted against the published contracts.

**Not included:** PyPI publish and the GitHub release. No credentials exist here, and trusted publishing needs a one-time browser-side configuration by the project owner.

items.title: Stale-comment sweep: the non-destructive half of #30
items.body:
Per #30's step 0, **every deletion is held pending sign-off**. This PR is the half that cannot
lose anything: comments and docs that actively describe a harness we do not have. My full plan,
with each of the five "confidently dead" items re-verified as still dead, is
[on the issue](https://github.com/BenEpstein/caching-in-llms/issues/30#issuecomment-5196401970).

## The big one: `benchmarks/README.md`

It is the operator's manual a grader follows, and it described a different experiment:

| Claim | Reality |
|---|---|
| 6 cells × 6 seeds | **5 cells × 20 seeds** (`BETA_GRID="0 0.5 1.0 2.0"`) |
| Grid lists `b0.25`, `b4.0` | `b0.25` was dropped; `b4.0` never existed |
| "n=6 per cell" | n=20, every cell |
| Headline cell `loadaware-b0.1` | Cannot be generated — retired per-rate β calibration |
| Layout table | Omitted **seven** executables, including `plot_results.py`, which makes every committed figure and was named nowhere in the file |

Retired cell names are now listed **as un-generatable** rather than quietly corrected — they
still appear in older `results/` directories and a reader will meet them.

## Everything else

- `run_cell.sh` claimed the β-sweep cells replay a 3-seed subset; `run_sweep.sh:85` says n=20 on
  every cell.
- `plot_results.py`'s `--cand` help said β is calibrated per-rate "so the cell name is not a
  fixed literal" — contradicting its own docstring. It now states the real constraint.
- `plot_results.py` documented 5 figures while writing 10; `analyze.py` still described "the 6
  paired per-seed differences" at p<0.05 (it is 20 at a Bonferroni 0.025).
- `values-baseline-kvaware.yaml` justified `gpuMemoryUtilization: 0.45` with arithmetic over a
  retired 64-prefix s=1.2 hot set. **The value is right and is kept** — the comment now marks the
  derivation historical, and says to re-derive before changing it rather than to justify it.
- `apply-router-patch.sh` + `deploy/dev/README.md` referenced a `PATCH_TARGETS` map that is a
  `case` (bash 3.2 has no `declare -A`); `deploy/README.md` cited a line that moved 58 → 74.

## Held for your call

- **The five deletions** — closed-loop mode, the no-op `sys.path.insert`, the
  `registration_controller` patch target, `dcgm_poll --duration`, the `load_gate` β echo.
- **`plot_results.py`'s `--cand` inference.** Not theoretical: I hit it today regenerating
  figures. With the standard grid it sees three non-`b0` cells and raises every time. I'd delete
  the inference and make `--cand` required — a default that cannot fire reads as supported.
- **The triplicated `job=vllm-engines` parse.** Proposing to defer: the copies genuinely differ
  (one windows by seed, one does not), only one is tested, and *this parse already corrupted 17
  of 74 seed rows once*. Changing analysis code while #31 is about to produce the final numbers
  is the wrong order.

168 tests green.

items.title: Add real-time ClickHouse/Flink analytics pipeline and Iceberg lakehouse module
items.body:
Adds two modules and closes an open backlog item. 95 files, ~10.6k lines.

## `realtime_analytics/` — Kafka → PyFlink → ClickHouse → FastAPI

Real-time analytics over AI agent conversation events, with the ClickHouse
tuning measured stage by stage rather than asserted.

**Measured** (12M events, p95 over 15 interleaved rounds):

| Query | Naive | Tuned | Rows read |
| --- | ---: | ---: | --- |
| Tenant dashboard | 181 ms | **2.4 ms** (75×) | 12,000,000 → 128 |
| Platform-wide health | 286 ms | **2.0 ms** (143×) | 12,000,000 → 91 |
| Slow-response triage | 204 ms | **4.8 ms** (42×) | 12,000,000 → 90,112 |
| Conversation drill-down | 26 ms | **3.7 ms** (7×) | 12,000,000 → 186,479 |
| Storage | 1003 MB | **405 MB** (2.5× smaller) | — |

API holds **8.5 ms p95 over HTTP** against a 100 ms SLO.

Staged schemas (`00`–`06`) isolate one decision each — types/codecs, sorting
key, partitioning, skipping indexes, materialized views, and projections as
the alternative. Every stage is verified to return results **identical** to
the naive baseline before any speedup is reported.

Ingest has three paths, and the PR is explicit about when each is right: a
batching Python consumer, ClickHouse's own Kafka table engine, and Flink for
the event-time rollup only. Flink's official JDBC connector ships **no
ClickHouse dialect at any released version**, so the rollup goes over Kafka
and is ingested by the Kafka engine.

## `iceberg_deployment/` — Apache Iceberg on Spark 3.5

Closes the `Tasks.md` item *"Adopt Delta/Iceberg with column mapping and a
deliberate schema-evolution policy."*

Field-ID schema evolution (a rename preserves data where a Hive table
silently returns NULLs), partition-spec evolution without rewriting data,
time travel and rollback, MERGE upserts that make at-least-once replay
converge, and the maintenance procedures — compaction, snapshot expiry,
orphan cleanup — that keep a table healthy.

## Housekeeping

Untracks `.env` (kept as `.env.example`; all values were already
placeholders) and 22 stale `.pyc` files that predate the `.gitignore`. Both
index-only; local files untouched.

## What is verified, and what is not

**Verified on this machine:**
- 70 tests (`realtime_analytics`) + 22 tests (`iceberg_deployment`), all
  against real engines — ClickHouse embedded via `chdb`, real Iceberg tables.
  No mocks.
- Full stack on Docker: 106,106 events Kafka → ClickHouse with **exact**
  materialized-view reconciliation; every API endpoint exercised.
- PyFlink job running on the cluster: 1,321 windows emitted and ingested, all
  minute-aligned, counters internally consistent.

**Not verified:**
- Flink under sustained load — no throughput-per-parallelism numbers, and the
  backpressure section describes diagnosis rather than a regression driven to
  ground.
- The Iceberg REST-catalog-on-MinIO compose stack. Configured and sharing
  `session.py` with the tested path, but the containers were not started.

Both limits are stated in the module READMEs rather than left implied.

## Notable negative results (documented, not hidden)

- A `minmax` skipping index that prunes **nothing** — latency's tail is
  uniform across granules. Removed from the shipped schema, kept in the
  benchmark so it keeps demonstrating that.
- An aggregate projection the planner **never selects**, because the query
  filters on a column it does not materialize.
- A materialized view that was **slower** than the scan it replaced, twice:
  default `index_granularity` on a small wide table, and a tenant-keyed view
  answering a fleet-wide query via 1,400 sketch merges.
- Weekly partitioning, which measurement showed was the wrong call (~0.8 ms
  fixed cost per part; daily was 11× slower). Schema changed to monthly.
- Two measurement bugs that nearly published wrong numbers: sequential
  measurement creating a phantom 2.6× regression, and ClickHouse's query
  condition cache making an *unindexed* table look indexed.

## Test plan

```bash
cd realtime_analytics && ./deploy.sh test    # 70 passed
cd iceberg_deployment && ./deploy.sh test    # 22 passed
cd iceberg_deployment && ./deploy.sh demo    # six-step walkthrough

# reproduce the numbers (no Docker needed)
cd realtime_analytics && ./deploy.sh bench && ./deploy.sh explain
```
