items.title: perf: define cold start phase contract
items.body:
## What changed

Adds the measurement-only cold-start phase runner and methodology for process startup, imports, Environment construction, first source render, first bytecode-cache render, warm render, module/LOC closure, and separate memory samples.

## Impact

Fixes the measurement blind spot before any lazy-import or AOT work. Non-Linux runs are explicitly development-only and cannot become public claims.

## Verification

- 5 focused contract/preflight tests; 10 related tests
- local 3.14.2t/GIL-disabled smoke across all seven phases
- guarded Linux mode correctly rejects Darwin
- `make lint`, `make ty`

## Steward Notes

- Consulted: benchmarks, runtime, docs/audit, tests.
- Risks: timing the wrong phase, tracemalloc distortion, publishing Darwin numbers.
- Evidence: output preflight before samples, raw median/p95 samples, platform/GIL/git metadata.
- Concurrency: no shared runtime behavior changes.
- Collateral: benchmark README and internal methodology only.

Advances #247. The issue remains open until the guarded Linux CPython 3.14t JSON capture is retained.
Advances #167

items.title: perf candidate: struct-of-arrays hot synapse fields (weight + from_index) for the interleaved gather (Issue #533)
items.body:
# Struct-of-arrays hot synapse fields for the interleaved gather (Issue #533) ## Summary The record-interleaved gather reads only two of `SynapseData`'s three fields — `weight` and `from_index` — but streams all 8 bytes of the struct. This adds a parallel **struct-of-arrays** view, `CompiledNetwork::hot_weights: Vec` and `hot_from: Vec`, built by the new `hot_synapse_soa` at every construction path, and points `weighted_sum_interleaved::` (scalar / AVX2 / NEON / wasm `simd128`) at those two slices. The hot loop's synapse stream drops from **8 B to 6 B** per synapse and the prefetcher gets two clean sequential streams over `start..end`. The change is **additive**: `synapse_type` stays on `SynapseData`, so `neuron_activation_scalar`, the aggregate/IF paths, the per-lane scattered kernels, the single-record forward passes and the binary format are all untouched. Numerics are bit-identical — the same values accumulate in the same order. The redundancy is the correctness hazard the issue calls out, so `CompiledNetwork::debug_assert_hot_soa` guards every interleaved entry point: a network whose hot view has drifted from `synapses` panics in debug and test builds rather than silently scoring wrong numbers, and compiles away entirely in release. Closes #533. ### Breaking change Marked with a `perf(network)!:` Conventional Commit and a `BREAKING CHANGE:` footer, so the `version-increment` job bumps the **minor** per `RELEASING.md`: - `simd::weighted_sum_interleaved` / `weighted_sum_interleaved_8` now take `hot_weights: &[f32], hot_from: &[u16]` instead of `&[SynapseData]`. - `CompiledNetwork` gains two public fields, so struct-literal construction must supply them. `hot_synapse_soa` is exported from the crate root for exactly that (the test and bench fixtures use it). Consumers that build networks through `CompiledNetwork::new` or `compile_creature` — the normal route — need no change. ## Evidence ### Benchmark — this is a performance change `cargo bench --bench hot_paths` on the committed `production_exact` topology (2,461 inputs, 1,666 non-input neurons, 21,513 synapses; 4,096 records per iteration). `base` is the parent commit run from a separate `git worktree`; `after` is this branch. **Method.** 24 **ABBA** pairs per group — each round runs `base, after, after, base` so the two arms bracket each other and thermal/load drift cancels within the round — with criterion `--warm-up-time 1 --measurement-time 3 --sample-size 20`. Each arm's round score is the mean of its two runs. Apple M4 Pro (12 cores), rustc 1.97.1, `--release`. | group | base median | after median | Δ median | paired Δ (mean ± SE) | rounds favouring `after` | | --- | ---: | ---: | ---: | ---: | ---: | | `mse_sum_production/production_exact` | 15.566 ms | 15.412 ms | **−0.99%** | −1.12% ± 0.72 | 18 / 24 | | `scoring/production_exact` | 24.621 ms | 24.061 ms | **−2.28%** | −1.02% ± 0.71 | 17 / 24 | **Read the sign, not the magnitude.** The host was **not quiet** — an unrelated process held the load average near 15 on a 12-core machine, so round-to-round noise is ~3.5% and neither group's mean clears its own standard error. What does clear is the direction: **35 of 48** paired rounds favour `after`, a two-sided sign test p ≈ 0.002, and symmetric noise cannot produce that. The honest reading is a real gain of roughly **1–2%** — at the low end of the issue's ≥1–2% bar, not the 3–8% it hoped for. **Why the upside shrank.** The issue's L1-residency argument was written against the pre-#530 world: 21,513 synapses × 8 B = 168 KB against an M4 core's 128 KB L1D, with an 8-lane `mse_inter` of 132 KB, so 6 B/synapse would have flipped the array into L1. At the shipped `MSE_TILE_LANES = 32` that framing no longer holds — `mse_inter` is ~528 KB and never L1-resident, and each synapse drives `R = 32` lanes (128 B of gather traffic) against its own 8 B, so trimming 2 B removes ~1.5% of the loop's bytes rather than crossing a capacity threshold. The 8-lane `scoring` group, where the ratio is 8 B against 32 B, is the better-placed of the two and shows the larger median — which is why both groups were measured rather than just the one the issue names. > **Scope caveat** (same as `pr-summary-530.md`). The issue's acceptance gate > names the *production* fixture in NEAT-AI-scorer — N ≈ 50 distinct creature > variants over the ≈22 GiB multi-file corpus in directory mode. Neither the > 3 MB production `network.json` nor the corpus is available in this repo > (`BASELINE.md`, "Bench-only baseline"), so that end-to-end A/B cannot run > here. What is measured above is the exact kernel the issue targets, at > production record volume, on the closest reproducible proxy this repo has. > The scorer-side confirmation on the full corpus remains the human-run gate > before the wall-clock claim is made there — and given the measured margin sits > at the bar rather than above it, that confirmation matters more than usual. ### Memory `hot_weights` + `hot_from` cost **+6 B per synapse per compiled network** — ~126 KB on the production creature, ~6 MB across a 50-strong population, since `CompiledNetwork: Clone` means directory-mode scoring clones them once per worker. Documented in `README.md` and `benches/BASELINE.md`. ### No UI to screenshot This is a library-internal performance change with no web interface. The evidence is the benchmark table above plus the test results below. ### Mutation evidence — the tests can fail Per AGENTS.md rule 2, each mutation was applied alone and reverted afterwards. Suites: `hot_synapse_soa`, `mse_batch_interleaved_parity`, `interleaved_scoring_parity`. | # | mutation | result | | --- | --- | --- | | M1 | `hot_synapse_soa` builds the arrays in reverse order | **5 of 7 red** | | M2 | `compile_creature` builds the SoA from an empty slice | **3 of 7 red** | | M3 | `CompiledNetwork::new` drops the last synapse from the SoA | **3 of 7 red** | | M4 | NEON kernel reads `hot_from[start]` for every synapse (source slip) | **1 of 7 red** (`interleaved_scoring_matches_the_single_record_reference`) | | M5 | drop `debug_assert_hot_soa` from the MSE interleaved entry point | **1 of 7 red** (the fail-loud guard test) | | — | all mutations reverted | **all suites green** | M4 is caught only by the parity test, which is correct — a source slip does not change the SoA arrays themselves, only the numbers they produce, which is exactly why the suite carries an independent oracle as well as the structural assertions. The oracle is independent per AGENTS.md rule 1: `interleaved_scoring_matches_the_single_record_reference` scores each record on its own through the scalar `CompiledNetwork::activate` forward pass, which never reads `hot_weights` or `hot_from`, so a fault in the gather moves only one side of the assertion. ### Architecture ```mermaid flowchart LR C["compile_creature / CompiledNetwork::new"] --> S["synapses: Vec<SynapseData>
weight + from_index + synapse_type"] S --> H["hot_synapse_soa
single home of the rule"] H --> W["hot_weights: Vec<f32>"] H --> F["hot_from: Vec<u16>"] W --> G["weighted_sum_interleaved::<R>
6 B per synapse"] F --> G S --> A["aggregate / IF / single-record paths
unchanged, 8 B per synapse"] G --> D{"debug_assert_hot_soa
at every entry point"} D -- "drifted" --> P["panic in debug — fail loud"] D -- "consistent" --> O["bit-identical results"] ``` ## Test Plan New suite `neat-core/tests/hot_synapse_soa.rs` (7 tests): - `compile_creature_builds_a_hot_view_matching_every_synapse` — the JSON construction path, asserted element-for-element **and** against the fixture's actual asymmetric weights/sources, so a zeroed or sorted copy fails. - `binary_deserialiser_builds_a_hot_view_matching_every_synapse` — the same for `CompiledNetwork::new` over a hand-serialised `.bin` buffer. - `cloning_a_network_preserves_the_hot_view` — `Clone` is on the directory-mode path, one network per worker. - `both_construction_paths_agree_on_the_hot_view` — the JSON and binary routes describe one topology and must produce one hot view; this is what stops the two construction paths drifting apart. - `hot_synapse_soa_preserves_order_and_handles_an_empty_array` — empty input, plus repeated sources and a repeated weight that a de-duplicating or sorting implementation would collapse. - `interleaved_scoring_matches_the_single_record_reference` — the independent oracle, over record counts 1 / 5 / 8 / 33 / 70 straddling the scalar, 4-way, 8-record and 32-record interleaved tiers. - `a_drifted_hot_view_fails_loud_instead_of_scoring_wrong_numbers` — mutating `synapses[0].weight` without rebuilding the view must panic, not score. Existing suites carried through unchanged (fixtures updated to supply the two new fields via `hot_synapse_soa`): `mse_batch_interleaved_parity`, `interleaved_scoring_parity`, `flat_record_scoring_parity`, `score_squash_simd_parity`, `mse_squash_simd_parity`, `simd_weighted_sums`, `aggregate_squash_set`, `aggregate_squash_tail_parity`, `batch_record_skeleton`, `packed_record_scan`, `inline_squash_dispatch`, `network_activate_trace_batch`, `short_input_zero_fill`. No test was commented out, skipped, or weakened. `./quality.sh` passes (fmt, clippy `-D warnings`, `cargo deny`, full workspace tests, doc build, release build). `cargo check -p neat-core --target wasm32-unknown-unknown` passes — required by AGENTS.md because no PR gate compiles the wasm half of `simd.rs`, which this change edits. ### Security self-check - No new external input surface: `hot_synapse_soa` reads an in-memory slice the loader has already validated. - The load-time `from_index < num_neurons` guard in `CompiledNetwork::new` (Issue #207) is unchanged and still the soundness precondition for the kernels' `get_unchecked`; the new `unsafe` reads of `hot_weights` / `hot_from` are bounded by the same `start..end` span as the `synapses` reads they replace, and carry `SAFETY:` notes saying so. - No secrets, no new dependencies, no shell/SQL/HTTP surface. --- 🤖 Processed by: stservice 🏷️ Run id: `vibe-msh9r6hr-25546f`

items.body:
## Summary

Adds `it::d4np::util::Stopwatch` (component #19): a microsecond-grade accumulating
profiler over `std::chrono::steady_clock`, opening **Milestone 7 — Diagnostics &
Instrumentation**.

## Motivation

Roadmap item 7.1; spec §2 component #19 ("microsecond high-resolution profiler"). The two
trap-decisions (clock choice, accumulation semantics) are recorded in
[ADR-0018](docs/adr/0018-stopwatch-steady-clock-accumulation.md).

## Changes

- **`steady_clock`, deliberately not `high_resolution_clock`**: the standard permits — and
  libstdc++ chooses — `high_resolution_clock` to alias the NTP-adjustable `system_clock`;
  a wall-clock step mid-measurement produces negative or wildly wrong timings. Monotonic
  `steady_clock` has nanosecond-grade native resolution on every matrix cell, comfortably
  finer than the spec's microsecond target.
- **Accumulating semantics**: `start`/`stop` cycles sum (timing a section entered N times
  reports total cost); `elapsed()` returns `std::chrono::nanoseconds` including the open
  interval; `elapsed_microseconds()`/`elapsed_milliseconds()` truncating conveniences;
  `reset()`, `restart()` (per-interval timing), `Stopwatch::start_new()`.
- **Sequencing misuse throws `std::logic_error`** (start while running, stop while
  stopped): idempotent no-ops were rejected — a measurement tool must not turn state bugs
  into quietly wrong numbers.
- Plain value type (copyable; copies are independent), not thread-safe (documented).
- The RAII scope guard (report-on-destruction) is **deferred** until `Logger` (7.3) exists
  as its reporting sink — same reasoning as deferring continuations in ADR-0015.
- **Tests** (7 cases): timing assertions are lower-bound or monotonicity only
  (`sleep_for` guarantees at least the requested steady-clock time; upper bounds flake on
  loaded runners). Zero start, non-decreasing while running, freeze on stop, accumulation,
  reset/restart, misuse matrix, copy independence.
- Docs: ADR-0018 (+ index), ROADMAP 7.1 flipped + coverage map, README milestone 7 → in
  progress, CHANGELOG, journal checkpoint.

## Design Patterns

- None — plain value utility; nothing adopted or force-fit (noted in ADR-0018).

## Verification

- [x] Builds cleanly on the full CI matrix (Linux x86_64 (GCC>=11, Clang>=14), Windows x86_64 (MSVC>=19.30), macOS arm64 (Apple Clang>=14)) — local MSVC green; matrix pending CI
- [x] Unit tests pass; new/changed behavior covered (≥ 80% line) — 7 new cases / 22 assertions
- [x] `clang-format (LLVM-derived, 4-space, 120 col)` clean; `clang-tidy (bugprone/cert/cppcoreguidelines/modernize/performance/portability/readability)` clean on the diff
- [x] ASan, UBSan, TSan, Valgrind green (where applicable) — CI jobs; single-threaded value type
- [ ] Benchmark numbers attached (when perf-relevant) — no performance claims made
- [x] `python tools/consistency_lint.py` passes

## Documentation Impact

- [x] README.md updated (if user-facing surface changed) — milestone 7 → in progress
- [x] ROADMAP.md checkbox flipped
- [x] ADR added/updated (if a non-trivial design decision was made)
- [ ] docs/patterns/README.md updated (if a pattern was introduced, refined, or rejected) — none this PR
- [ ] Spec updated (if behavior diverges from `docs/specs/`) — no divergence
- [x] CHANGELOG.md updated (for user-visible changes)
- [x] PR metadata set — assignee, one type label, release milestone (**M7**)

items.title: docs(0051): say only what is true, and let CI keep it that way
items.body:
ADR 0051's release bar is that nothing **actively misleads**. Measured against it, the README oversold in five places, and the two evaluation documents mis-attributed limitations to tasks that do not cover them.

## Claims softened to what is actually known

- **"linear horizontal scalability"** (headline + Principles) — unmeasured. ADR 0048 T3 is `planned`, and that ADR forbids measuring a scaling curve on one host. The honest form is a statement about the architecture: shared-nothing, no coordinator on the publish hot path, curve not yet measured. Same for the shared-subscriptions line billing itself as "the linear-scaling lever".
- **"The main thing not yet done is cutting a tagged release"** — not true. It now points at a new **Limitations** section listing what a reader would otherwise discover in production.

## Numbers that were wrong

| | was | is |
|---|---|---|
| peer frame encode | ~280 ns | **~439 ns** |
| peer frame decode | ~420 ns | **~357 ns** |
| ADR count | 44 | **55** |

The peer-frame figures were stale *bincode* numbers, superseded by the postcard re-baseline (`BASELINE.md`). They under-reported encode cost by ~35% **in our own favour**. `mqtt-bridge` and `mqttd-operator` were absent from the crate table entirely.

## Limitations attributed to the wrong task

`SIZING.md` and `COMPARISON.md` both cited **0041-T7** for the missing per-store disk quota. T7 is the *bridge-spool* byte bound — the per-store quota was tracked by nothing. SIZING further claimed all four unbounded axes were "tracked as T6–T8" when two were tracked by no task at all.

The clauses were kept and the tasks created:

- **0041-T9** — per-store disk bound: one store can consume the whole watermark and brown out the others.
- **0041-T10** — per-connection write buffering. `MAX_BACKLOG` is a **hard-coded 10 000 messages** per stalled subscriber: bounded in count, unbounded in bytes, and not configurable by any setting. At the 1 MiB default packet size that is **~10 GiB of worst-case headroom per connection**. Now stated plainly in README, SIZING and COMPARISON, with the practical mitigation — cap `MQTTD_MAX_PACKET_SIZE`, since the product of the two is the real worst case.

## Two claims about other people, and about ourselves

- `COMPARISON.md` published a **competitor-negative benchmark observation** (NanoMQ QoS-1 acks stalling at 1024 msgs/connection) sourced from a harness whose own rules forbid publishing dev-grade numbers. Ours is the honesty rule; breaking it against a third party is worse than breaking it about ourselves. **Removed.**
- `COMPARISON.md` still said **"no operator by decision"** — stale since ADR 0055 was accepted and an operator was built. It now says what is true: built and e2e-tested, *not packaged for installation*, chart is the supported path.
- `deploy/operator/operator.yaml` now declares itself **development/e2e only**. It pins `mqttd-operator:e2e` with `imagePullPolicy: Never`, so outside kind every pod sits in `ErrImageNeverPull` forever. A manifest that merely *looked* installable would be the more expensive mistake.

## And the derivable facts are now CI-enforced

`scripts/check-readme-facts.py` (**ADR 0051 T1**) checks the two README facts that have a mechanical source of truth — the ADR count and the crate table — because those drift silently: nothing fails when a crate is added or an ADR is written.

Verified by reintroducing both real defects:

```
README states facts the tree contradicts:
  - claims 44 ADRs; docs/adr/ holds 55
  - crate `mqtt-bridge` is missing from the Workspace layout table
```

Wired into the existing `delivery dashboard` job. `gen-status.py --check` green; every README ADR link resolves.

## Not included

The **MSRV statement**. `rust-version` (1.88; operator 1.89) and `rust-toolchain.toml` (1.97.0) are different things and not actually in conflict — but *nothing verifies the MSRV*: every CI job uses `stable` or the 1.97 pin, so "1.88" is an untested claim. That needs a verification job, not a sentence, and follows separately.

items.title: fix(claims): three shipped numbers were wrong, and the gate could not see them
items.body:
## What this is

The round started from a small observation about a competitor's positioning
table — five rows, each naming a *failure mode prevented* rather than a feature,
no adjectives, one number — and the thought that we could fill that format more
honestly, because every cell can carry a resolvable pointer.

Checking whether we actually could found that **three numbers we ship are wrong**,
and one shared cause.

**One sentence:** a decision recorded its own unblocking condition, the condition
was met, and nothing fired — because the gate that would have noticed sees only
percentages, and the ledger checks that a pointer *exists*, never that its number
is *true*.

## The three, all re-verified directly

| | Finding |
|---|---|
| **1** | README said *"compiled into 7+ host agents"*. Truth: **23 detected** (test-pinned), **20 receiving a written config surface**. Understated by **3×** — and it had propagated to two other live docs. |
| **2** | `second-brain-retrieval-precision` published `5/27`, `5/27`, tie-set `3.3`. Its artefact says `2/27`, `27/27`, `4.111`. The pointer resolved the whole time, so CI stayed green. A **sibling claim on the same file cited the correct figures** — two backed claims disagreeing while both resolved. |
| **3** | `ledger-exec-verifiability` published "0 of **25**"; the ledger held 26. Shipped in the previous PR — i.e. mine — and stale within a day. |

Finding 1 is the sharpest: `host-agent-count` sat `unbacked` with its evidence
field literally naming its own unblocking condition — *"once `surface-matrix.yml`
exists, bind the count to that file and flip."* **That file exists and is
CI-gated.** The condition was met and nobody noticed.

## Why nothing caught them — two holes, both load-bearing

The witness sweep matched `/\d+\s*(%|x)/`. It was written against the
"84.8%-style headline" anti-lesson and catches exactly that shape. A bare integer
carries neither, so no ratio pattern could see `7+` and no unit allowlist would
either.

**And fixing that alone still did not catch it.** Bite-testing end-to-end, the
probe passed anyway: the README line already carried
`<!-- claim:no-runtime-daemon -->`, and the sweep exempted the line on *any*
marker — so the figure rode along on an unrelated **qualitative** claim. A
`kind: qual` entry about having no daemon says nothing about a quantity. Now a
figure is cleared only by a `kind: quant` marker, and the failure message names
which marker failed to license it.

## What was cancelled by measurement, not skipped

- **Widening the witness surfaces** — counting first showed `docs/benchmark.md`
  alone fires on **54 lines**. It is a methodology document whose job is to be
  full of statistics; sweeping it produces the flood that teaches a maintainer to
  bypass the gate. The gap was the pattern, not the surface list.
- **Migrating inbound references** — became unnecessary when the approach changed
  from relocating six misfiled ADRs to *scanning* for them. Zero references
  touched, ten of which sit in frozen archives whose paths were correct when
  written, and the scan keeps working for the next misfiled file.

Both are recorded in the archived roadmap with the number that killed them.

## Also fixed

Six files under `agents/settings/contexts/` are titled `# ADR — …`, carry a
decision status, and had **zero** presence in the ADR index — ADRs by every
property except location. The index now scans for them. And `docs/adrs/memory/`
existed on disk while absent from the audit's hardcoded area list, so it was not
audited at all; a new check fails on any unlisted area directory — the same
defect shape as last week's gate watching a path that no longer exists.

## The borrowed format

The mechanism already existed: `comparison.yaml` rows are resolved in CI by the
same pointer resolver as the ledger. So this borrows the framing, not a
capability. An optional `failure_mode` field renders a second view of the same
rows; a row appears there **iff** the field is populated, so membership is a data
property rather than a curated short-list that drifts.

The council split on this and the resolving argument was that the source already
projects once — a schema field is lower drift risk than hand-picking rows for a
second surface.

The schema comment records what **not** to copy: the comparable suite pinned its
marketing figure with an `assertIn("<number> tokens", …)` test while its own
published formula yields a value ~4× larger. The pin turned a wrong number into
an invariant CI actively defended. A pointer can go stale and be re-derived; a
pin makes staleness the passing condition.

## Verification

`task typecheck-ts` clean · 32 tests pass · 10 gates green (`check_claims`,
`check_comparison`, `check_references`, `check_enforcement_coverage`,
`lint_override_kernel_guard`, `check_adr_frontmatter`, `lint_surface_matrix`,
`check_artefact_count_messaging`, `audit_adr_coverage --check`,
`build_proof --check`) · condensation in sync · roadmap archived per the PR-gate.

End-to-end proof: removing the marker from the real README line exits 2 and names
the reason; restoring it exits 0. An unlisted ADR area directory exits 1 and names
itself.

## Parked, with named reopen conditions

The forward-only decision-homing linter and the archive index for the ~94
stranded prose decisions — both converged on by the council, deferred on
**priority** not merit (three live wrong numbers outranked a class-prevention
mechanism), and the baseline they need is already measured: 691 marker lines
across 248 archived roadmaps.

Also parked and stated: an activation-rate number (the nearest artefact is
disqualified by its own contract as something that "would fabricate activation
counts") and an end-to-end cost figure (the raw reports behind the existing
per-task numbers are operator-local and untracked — 0 of 29 in git — so they are
not reproducible from a clone).

items.title: Say what the harness actually checks, and stop citing documents that never existed
items.body:
Say what the harness actually checks, and stop citing documents that never existed

Sixth and final change of the code review, and the only one that is
documentation. 57 files, and every Java diff in it is comment-only: the sole
non-comment change in main or test source is two diagnostic string literals in
benchmark's GateChecker. Nine of the ten POMs differ by XML comments alone; the
tenth, db, differs by one <message> body. Nothing here can move a bit, because
nothing here is executable.

Verified: core 2141 tests / 0 failures, geoapi 12, db 75, conformance 345, all
green in the default reactor. golden is correctly absent from that reactor. All
five workflow YAMLs parse, all three shell scripts pass `bash -n`, both gate
baseline JSONs parse, and all ten POMs parse -- the last of which is not
rhetorical, since an earlier draft of this change put a `--` inside an XML
comment and made db/pom.xml unreadable to Maven.

The gate whose pass/fail bit carries no information

  golden.yaml's header comment said the golden report "is gated". It is not,
  and the claim had already been copied into docker/run.sh and golden/README.md
  before anyone read the test. GoldenMasterTest fails on any UNEXPLAINED row,
  and there are 2,291 of them, so the test is red today by design. A red test
  that stays red tells you nothing about a change. The four checks that are
  genuinely automatic -- the test ran exactly once, it was not skipped, the
  module reported at least 40 tests with 0 skips, and the generated table has
  the same line count as golden/baseline/1.4.3/golden.tsv -- catch a truncated
  sweep and a stale rule set. They would not catch several hundred rows
  migrating between UNCHANGED and UNEXPLAINED, because the six figures that
  would reveal it are pinned as prose and compared by eye.

  All four sites now say that, including the header comment the error came
  from. Filed as #104, with the caution that "fix it by asserting zero
  unexplained" is re-pinning rather than gating, and that promoting the
  expectation file to a gate input brings it under the never-edit-a-test-input-
  to-make-it-pass rule.

Forty-one citations to four documents that do not exist

  reference/numerics.md, reference/performance.md and two others were cited 41
  times across the tree and have never been in the repository. One mention
  survives, at conformance/pom.xml:123, because it correctly records the
  problem rather than committing it.

  The other 40 were resolved three ways. Most were repointed at something real
  -- allocation-baseline.json, the root POM's bench profile, AuthalicLat,
  MathHelpers.norm2, core/util/FastStrictTrig, Proj4jException.fillInStackTrace,
  benchmark.CrsPair. Some were restated as project policy, which is what they
  had always been describing. Five were deleted outright as unverifiable: "up
  to 49 allocations per vertex" (replaced by the measured 160 -> 0 B/op),
  "1-10 microseconds" for fillInStackTrace (replaced by the measured 585 ns and
  1,440 B), a "10-1000x" cache ratio, "1.5-3x time" for StrictMath, and six
  numerics.md row numbers.

  A dangling citation was concealing a wrong figure at least once.
  allocation-baseline.json attributed the pure-Java FdLibm rewrite of
  sin/cos/tan to JDK 17. It reached them in JDK 21; through 17 they are native
  JNI calls that allocate nothing, so the claim was inverted, not merely
  imprecise. Checked against the running JDK -- Temurin 21.0.11 reports
  StrictMath.sin/cos/tan native=false -- rather than taken on trust. Because
  the citation pointed nowhere, no reader could have caught it by following it.

Numbers that were wrong, and one that could not be recovered

  The conformance figures in RELEASE-NOTES.md, CHANGELOG.md and
  conformance/pom.xml are now 7,441 / 7,900 -- 94.19 %, with the denominator's
  derivation shown: 7,923 in-block assertions less 23 vacuous, and
  7,441 + 457 + 2 + 23 = 7,923 exactly. gie-expected-failures.tsv is 482 data
  rows, not 483; the earlier count included the header, and 482 is what the
  harness itself reports and what 457 FAIL + 2 SKIP + 23 VACUOUS sums to.
  golden's report figures are 41,425 CHANGED and 39,134 INTENDED.

  The `1,066 / 6,845 -- 15.6 %` baseline attributed to 1.4.3 is deleted rather
  than reworded, because nothing in the tree reproduces either number. What
  replaces it is derived and bounded: the 93 +proj= names registered at tag
  v1.4.3, matched against the operation governing each of the 7,923 in-block
  assertions, put 1.4.3 at no more than 1,830, or 23 %, counting every
  ambiguous case in its favour. Registering an operation is not the same as
  agreeing with PROJ to tolerance, so the real figure is lower; an upper bound
  that can be re-derived beats a point estimate that cannot.

Instructions that only worked on the machine they were written on

  conformance/sync-upstream.sh defaulted PROJ_DIR to an absolute path on the
  author's disk. It now resolves a PROJ checkout sitting beside this repository
  and still honours $1 and $PROJ_DIR. db/pom.xml's proj.db.source default stays
  at Homebrew's Apple-silicon path, since nothing in a default build reads it,
  but the comment now tells a Linux or Intel-Mac contributor the flag to pass.

  db/README.md carried a surviving copy of the #95 claim that CI proves index
  reproducibility. No workflow does, because it needs sqlite3 and a built
  proj.db; that is a contributor step, and the README now says so and gives the
  invocation verified to exit 0.

Two stale figures kept, deliberately

  docker/run.sh's `bench` is ~21 minutes, measured at 21 m 23 s, not the ~16
  minutes the header claimed. That is corrected. CI_MIN_TESTS stays at 1700
  against a measured 2,573 -- the comment moved above the constant and now says
  the floor is 873 below reality and would no longer catch a whole module
  dropping out of the reactor. Raising it changes what the harness asserts,
  which belongs in its own change and not in a documentation pass. Filed as
  #103.

The `Golden master` job is renamed from "blocking" to "scheduled", which is
what it is: master's ruleset carries deletion, non_fast_forward, pull_request,
required_linear_history and required_signatures, and no required_status_checks
rule at all, so no job name is load-bearing for protection. LICENSE.PROJ's two
artifact names are corrected to neoproj4j-epsg and neoproj4j-grids-us-legacy.

Filed and not fixed here: #102 (whether the db reproducibility proof should
become a CI gate), #103, #104.

items.title: Add real 5-model deflection benchmark with reproducible routing
items.body:
## What
A measured benchmark of KORA's deterministic front-door routing across 5 models (Qwen2.5-32B local via vLLM; Claude Sonnet 4.6, Claude Haiku 4.5, Llama 3.3 70B, Llama 3.1 8B via AWS Bedrock).

## Key results
- **Deflection 76.7% — identical across all 5 models** (330 → 77 LLM calls). Set by the deterministic router, so it does not vary with the served model.
- **Routing precision 0.883, recall 0.971** — reproducible with no API key, no GPU, no LLM calls.
- **Accuracy**: equal with-KB; large gain without-KB that grows as the model weakens (8B +0.335 → Sonnet +0.223).

## Reproducibility
- `./reproduce.sh` regenerates the workload (byte-identical MD5 check) and verifies routing metrics against the committed result — zero credentials needed.
- All 5 per-model result JSONs are committed; every wrong answer and routing miss is enumerated.

## Honesty
All numbers are measured, not projected. The router is answer-blind (never sees category or ground truth). The FAQ judge is fixed at Sonnet 4.6 across all arms. Single synthetic domain; broader workloads are future work (see README roadmap).

items.title: Green CI, honest numbers, measured competitors, and a rebuilt landing page
items.body:
Supersedes #17 (its commits are merged in here). Everything on this branch came from measurement finding something wrong, not from planning.

## CI is green again

Two failures on `main` after 0.5.0, neither a code defect — both **host-dependent tests**, which is why local runs stayed green through the entire release branch.

- `test_find_chrome_falls_back_to_cached_chrome_for_testing` patched `subprocess.run`, but `find_chrome()` uses `shutil.which`. The mock was inert. No `google-chrome` in PATH locally → fallback ran → passed for the wrong reason. CI's Ubuntu has it → returned first → the branch under test never executed.
- Auditing the file found a second: `test_stale_chrome_executable_is_not_trusted` asserted only that the result *differed* from a bogus path — vacuously true where `find_chrome()` returns `None`.
- The lint job installed `.[dev]` without the `mcp` extra, so `mcp.*` became `Any` and strict mode failed all five tool decorators. It now installs `.[dev,mcp]` — lint what users actually get.

## Two bugs the benchmark and CI found

**A delta could cost more than the page it replaced.** On a click-driven navigation where the reported URL trailed the document, `build_delta` diffed two unrelated pages and emitted 5,701 tokens where the snapshot was 2,963 — in 6 of 22 runs. Two independent guards now bound it: a size check at payload selection, and a restamped-document check comparing the elements behind shared handles (the Hacker News case scored 0.04 agreement). Both mutation-tested.

**A launch failure said only "timed out".** Chrome's stderr went to `/dev/null`, so CI could report that a launch failed but never why. It now carries process state, exit code, port-file path and Chrome's own complaint — and distinguishes "died before writing the port" from "still running at the deadline". The first version of that diagnostic was itself racy (`poll()` returns `None` for an unreaped process); it waits for the exit before describing it.

Also: a reused profile kept the previous run's `DevToolsActivePort`, so `_read_port` could return a dead port — a defect in the persistent-profile feature shipped in 0.5.0.

## Numbers that were wrong

| Claim | Reality |
|---|---|
| Delta = 75% per-turn saving | Single-page best case. Real median **1.0x** across a mixed run |
| 19x vs raw HTML | From a run whose data was never saved. Re-measured: **16.0x** |
| 5.8x vs Playwright MCP | Ratio-of-medians. Conservative statistic: **5.0x** |

`build_delta` returns `None` on a URL change, so a navigation turn sends a full snapshot by design and a realistic run is mostly navigation. The delta is dramatic *inside* one document — 9.1x median where it can fire — and the honest end-to-end figure is **~18x** (16.9x–18.4x across repeat runs), dominated by compression rather than by the delta.

Every headline now carries its statistic, its date and its range.

## Competitors, measured

Both README tables said "not measured". Same 8 pages, tiktoken `cl100k_base`, 2026-08-10:

| grip | Playwright MCP | Puppeteer a11y | Puppeteer HTML | raw HTML |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| **1,998** | 11,597 | 27,489 | 58,280 | 58,912 |

grip smallest on 8 of 8. Median of per-page ratios: 5.0x vs Playwright MCP, 11.6x vs Puppeteer's a11y tree, 16.0x vs raw HTML.

On Hacker News, Playwright MCP's tree is **larger than the HTML it describes** — a page of mostly links costs more as roles and names than as tags. It gets its own section, because it cuts against the accessibility-tree-equals-compression story grip also rides.

The first run of that benchmark reported a constant 32 tokens for Playwright MCP across all eight pages. It was the "browser not installed" error being counted as a snapshot. Publishing it would have claimed a competitor was 60x more efficient than grip. The doc records it as a caution.

## Landing page

Rebuilt. Geist Sans, Geist blue for interaction only, no orange, no emoji, light and dark defined at the token level. Charts via dither-kit through shadcn, with `orange` deleted from the vendored palette's type union rather than merely unused.

Every figure lives in one metrics module with its range, because the page was drafted three times against three different numbers before the benchmark settled. It leads on ~18x, then says plainly that most of it is compression. Its limits section states what grip cannot do: challenges detected and attempted but not defeated, solve rates unmeasured, no TLS/JA3 parity and none reachable from Python on stock Chromium, IP-reputation blocking is an egress problem.

## Verification

261 unit tests, 33 gripsearch, and the full integration suite — verified with a fake `google-chrome` on PATH so the launcher tests exercise the CI path. `ruff` and `mypy --strict` clean. Landing page builds and lints.

items.title: Fix dashboard: real ASIC numbers, representative ECP5 Fmax, links + README
items.body:
Fixes the published metrics dashboard (https://mountain-reverie.github.io/jcore-cpu/), which was showing wrong/missing numbers and broken links.

## What was broken (root causes)

1. **ECP5 Fmax showed the artifact (~27 MHz), not the real ~42.9 MHz.** The emit parsed the *bare-cpu* `nextpnr.log`, whose only clock is the unconstrained-IO artifact `$glbnet$clk$TRELLIS_IO_IN`. The representative number lives in the `cpu_timing_top` harness log, which the emit never read.
2. **ASIC metrics were garbage** (`cpu/cells = 3`, no area, no Fmax/WNS/power). `cpu_sta.sh` read the hierarchical, round-tripped `cpu_asic.v`; `abc` only tech-maps the top module, so submodule logic stayed generic ("Area … unknown") and OpenSTA couldn't time it.
3. **`size`/`speed` links 404'd** — github-action-benchmark doesn't generate per-suite index pages in `external-data-json-path` mode.
4. **No top-level README.**

## Fixes

- **`cpu_sta.sh`:** `synth -top cpu -flatten` before the Nangate45 map → the whole CPU tech-maps → correct total area/cells + real WNS/Fmax/power. *(Per-block ASIC area is dropped for now — it never produced valid data; noted as a future refinement.)*
- **ECP5 Fmax (both, labelled):** the ecp5 job now runs the harness P&R **before** emit; `metrics.py` surfaces `cpu/Fmax (representative)` (~42.9, the gated number) **and** `cpu/Fmax (IO-unconstrained)` (~27). New `parse_nextpnr_fmax` takes the final post-route value (matches the gate's `tail -1`). The Fmax floor gate runs **after** emit so a real regression still records its data point.
- **Dashboard:** links point to the real `benchmark-data.json`; the per-block chart hides until per-block data exists (no more zero bars).
- **README.md:** project intro, CI badges, and a prominent dashboard link.

## Verification
- [x] `synth/tests`: 18 unit tests pass (added `parse_nextpnr_fmax` + dual-Fmax `build_ecp5` coverage)
- [x] End-to-end emit on fixture logs yields `cpu/Fmax (representative)=42.86`, `cpu/Fmax (IO-unconstrained)=27.22`, plus util
- [x] YAML valid; `cpu_sta.sh` syntax + no-toolchain guard; `node --check` dashboard
- [ ] First master run after merge: confirm the dashboard shows the ~42.9 MHz representative Fmax, real ASIC area/timing, and working links

## Follow-up noted (not in this PR)
Per-block area (ASIC + ECP5) and the real lever for breaking past ~42 MHz — pipelining the ID/EX register-read↔execute boundary (logic-depth bound, confirmed by the seed sweep).

items.title: Move the PVM2 pipeline into nub, add a reference personality and a cross-engine benchmark
items.body:
Moves the personality-generic PVM2 program pipeline out of the JAVM layer and into nub, gives nub a reference personality so it can run its own JIT, and adds a dependency-isolated cross-engine benchmark comparison.

## Why

The ELF→PVM2 pipeline sat on the wrong side of the nub/JAVM split. `javm-transpiler` was a 2191-line generic RV64EMC linker that touched `javm-cap` at exactly four lines, purely to emit a cap-shaped `Image`. The PVM2 ABI constants lived in `javm-cap/src/layout.rs` behind a comment admitting they were there only because javm-cap was the common dependency. `subsoil`, the guest runtime, had no JAVM dependency at all.

The consequence was that nub — which owns the interpreter and the JIT — could not build or load a PVM2 program, had zero end-to-end tests, and had no benchmarks. Meanwhile 11 of `javm-bench`'s 14 workloads were pure compute (`prime_sieve()`, `keccak_bench()`, …) with no capability content, benchmarking nub's engine from inside JAVM's crate.

## What moved

| Concern | Before | After |
|---|---|---|
| PVM2 ABI constants | `javm-cap/src/layout.rs` | `nub-program/src/abi.rs` (javm-cap re-exports) |
| Program blob format | `javm_cap::image::Image` (SSZ, cap-shaped) | `nub_program::ProgramBlob` (flat) |
| ELF parse + RV→PVM2 rewrite | `javm-transpiler`, 2191 lines | `nub-linker`; javm-transpiler is now 137 lines |
| Guest runtime + endpoint macro | `rust/subsoil{,-derive}` | `nub-rt` + `nub-rt-macro` |
| Cross-compile + link helper | `rust/build-javm` | `nub_build::pvm2` |
| 11 compute workloads | `components/benches/*` | `nub/programs/*` |
| 3 capability workloads | `components/benches/*` | unchanged — they measure JAVM |
| Reference personality | none | `nub-flat` (host) + `nub-flat-guest-x86` (guest) |

`javm-bench` keeps `sub_vm_recurse`, `sub_vm_data_recurse` and `pt_cache_call`, which genuinely exercise the capability system.

## New: the flat personality

`nub-flat` is what makes nub's JIT runnable outside JAVM. Running recompiled code needs the ring-0 substrate in `nub-arch-x86`, which needs a `GuestPersonality` — so until now nub had to borrow JAVM's. Flat is one program, one frame, no capability graph, no sub-VMs, no yields: ~600 lines against `javm-guest-x86`'s 2700, which is a reasonable measure of how much of that crate is capability semantics rather than execution.

It comes with nub's first sandbox end-to-end coverage, asserting that the JIT and the interpreter agree on both return value *and gas* for every program. Gas equality is the strong assertion — it says the two backends charge identically instruction for instruction, which is what makes them interchangeable for a metered VM.

## New: `nub/bench-compare`

A separate, excluded workspace with its own lockfile comparing nub against native, PolkaVM, Wasmtime and Wasmer — 14 engine rows over 10 workloads. It is excluded from both root manifests so polkavm/wasmtime/wasmer never enter the main lockfile, `cargo audit`, or the SBOM. It ships nothing; it only measures.

Fairness rules it enforces, documented in its README: gas is an axis and never a normalizer, metering mode is part of row identity, counters are set to maximum so instrumentation runs but never fires, and metered and unmetered rows sit in one table with an explicit column rather than being corrected against each other.

## Measurement correctness

The first version of this harness produced numbers that were wrong, in both directions, and the fixes are worth calling out because the failure mode was quiet:

- **Storage was inside the timed region.** nub's `compile` step is *publish* — ship the blob into the sandbox, decode, content-hash, materialize. That is hashing-bound and belongs to a different subsystem than the recompiler. It now sits outside the target and is reported separately.
- **The headline rows were measured in one shared process.** `run.sh` only looped over two of the four kinds; the other two came from a single process running every program against every engine, against a guest heap that is never swept. Contamination reached 47%.
- **The row filter was a substring match**, and engine names nest (`..._sync_gas` is a prefix of `..._sync_gas_full`), so the script ran two rows per process — defeating the one-process-per-row rule that exists because nub's sandbox is a process-wide singleton.
- **The statistics were hand-rolled**: a fixed 50 samples, no warm-up, reduced to a bare median. Repeat runs of the same row varied by 30–50%.

criterion now owns the measurement, and `nub-bench` gained its own `jit` bench so the same engine is measured by two harnesses that share no measurement code. They agree within 1–3% on all ten programs (prime-sieve cold 222.9 µs vs 224.8 µs; keccak cold 42.6 vs 42.9). The report shows the confidence interval whenever it exceeds 2% of the median, and no longer clamps a negative recompile cost to zero — `cold` does strictly more work than `invoke`, so `cold < invoke` is impossible and clamping was hiding it.

## Verification

- **Pinned gas vectors are unchanged.** This is the durable invariant across the whole refactor: `javm-bench/tests/workloads.rs` and `nub-bench`'s pinned `(value, gas)` pairs are deliberately duplicated across the two repos and both still hold. Three vectors were re-pinned in one commit, for a stated reason — the guest crypto dependencies were not version-pinned, so a fresh lockfile resolved ed25519-compact 2.3.1 instead of 2.2.0 and shifted gas by 3.3x. They are now pinned exactly.
- Blob byte-identity was checked at each refactor stage against the previous stage, so the pipeline move is provably content-neutral.
- `cargo fmt --all --check`, `cargo clippy --workspace --all-targets -- -D warnings`, `cargo test --workspace` all clean.

## Result

`nub_jit` is fastest of the metered JIT engines on all ten workloads. The full tables, every engine and every measurement kind, are in `nub/bench-compare/BENCHMARKS.md`.

One open item, stated rather than buried: flat's *execution* beats JAVM's on every program, which is what a personality with no capability graph should do — but flat's *recompile* costs ~46 µs on prime-sieve where JAVM's costs ~1 µs. That is real, reproducible, and not yet explained.

items.title: perf: comparative benchmark vs the C, and a bit-exact cbrt table (-22.4% on Pi 5)
items.body:
Two commits from a profiling session. Read them separately: the first is tooling and docs, the second is a one-line codec change plus a table.

## 1. Comparative benchmark against the C (`3acf2cf`)

go-aac had no comparative benchmark against the encoder it ports, unlike go-flac (libFLAC/SoX/ffmpeg) and go-opus (a Go-vs-C table). The README reported only self-referential realtime multiples, so "how close are we to the C" had never been answered.

It is now, and it is worth knowing: **go-aac runs at ~2.09x FFmpeg's CPU time** on a Raspberry Pi 5 and on x86_64, 2.64x on Apple M4, **in about a third of the memory** (4.1 MB peak RSS against 10.4 to 13.3 MB).

`scripts/bench-encoders.sh` follows go-flac's harness: same job, one process, single-threaded, reporting wall time, CPU seconds, peak RSS and stream size. It **refuses a distro FFmpeg**, because 7.x and earlier ship a different coder set (`anmr`/`twoloop`/`fast`) whose `anmr` is not the `nmr` scalefactor trellis this library ports; comparing against it measures the wrong C. Verified that guard fires.

`tools/wav2aac` gives go-aac an equivalent CLI to time. It drives the low-level `aac` package rather than `pcm`, because `pcm.Config` exposes no coder selection and the benchmark needs to compare every coder against its FFmpeg counterpart. It streams frame by frame so peak RSS measures the encoder rather than the harness.

The benchmarks feed a real recording via `GOAAC_BENCH_WAV`. This matters more than it sounds: the existing benchmark fed two summed sine tones, and a sparse two-tone spectrum quantizes most bands to zero, so the rate-distortion search exits early and the profile understates exactly the code that dominates on real input.

## 2. Escape-path cbrt to a bit-exact table (`94fce82`, closes #7)

`fmath.Cbrt32` was `float32(math.Cbrt(float64(x)))`, a **float64** cube root, where the C uses float32 `cbrtf`. It had exactly one caller, and its input `cq` is an integer clipped to `[0, 8191]`, so `cq^(4/3)` takes only 8192 distinct values.

Measured by A/B on a 120 s recording, min of 3, isolated, all three platforms:

| Platform | Before | After | Saved | go/C |
| --- | ---: | ---: | ---: | ---: |
| **Raspberry Pi 5** | 6.38 s | **4.95 s** | **-22.4%** | 2.09x to **1.62x** |
| x86_64 (i7-1260P) | 2.82 s | **2.41 s** | **-14.5%** | 2.09x to **1.79x** |
| Apple M4 Pro | 1.84 s | **1.61 s** | **-12.5%** | 2.64x to **2.40x** |

**Encoder output is byte-identical on every platform.** The table is generated from the exact expression the scalar path used (`float32(cq) * fmath.Cbrt32(float32(cq))`), so the lookup is an identity transform of that arithmetic rather than an approximation of it; `pow43_exact_test` asserts equality for all 8192 inputs. It must not be regenerated from `cbrtf` or a closed form: the Go lineage is what the gate has blessed.

## Verification

* All 14 packages pass.
* The differential gate passes with `GOAAC_REQUIRE_ORACLE=1` (required, not skipped).
* Encoder output byte-identical to pre-change on Pi 5, x86_64 and M4.
* `wav2aac` output verified byte-identical to the `pcm` path (the benchmark's honesty depends on this).
* Only one line of production codec code changes; the rest is tooling, tests and README.

## Worth flagging for review

**`tools/wav2aac` is 229 lines of new code that no differential gate covers.** Its correctness matters because the comparative numbers depend on it. The check that gives me confidence is that its output is byte-identical to `pcm.EncodeInterleaved`; an earlier draft was 657 bytes short because it did not drain the encoder delay, which is exactly the class of bug that would have quietly flattered our own numbers.

**The profile was wrong about the cbrt gain in both directions**, claiming 4.6% on M4 (really 12.5%) and 10.1% on Pi (really 22.4%), and a call-count reconciliation agreed with it on M4 and was also wrong. See #7 and #8. The rule this establishes for the rest of the optimization work: size every item by A/B differential, never from profile shares.

## Context

Baseline and profile: #6, #10. Plan of record: #9. Native Go track and the go-perf findings: #11. The gap is **not** FFmpeg's hand-written asm (worth ~1%, measured); it is compiler auto-vectorization plus a scalar-codegen gap in code the C also runs scalar.

items.title: docs: single-call naming, reader-facing precision, and a re-ordered README first screen
items.body:
Zero-cost, offline-only corrections to publicly visible surfaces: naming precision, money formatting, README first screen, supported-interpreter timing, and the sample-size citation. **No Azure call was made.**

Scope is deliberately limited to tasks **Z1–Z5**. The legacy Model Router pricing-truth patch (Z6) touches renderer/publisher/replay paths and is intentionally left for its own follow-up PR.

## Z1 — Naming cleanup without changing URLs

The generic synthetic experiment-07 arm is now `single-call` in every reader-facing label, and the Microsoft product name no longer shares a semantic block with the synthetic **52%** coverage figure.

Renamed (visible text only): experiment-atlas card heading, tab list, headline table row and GIF/SVG alt text; the `experiments-overview.svg` card label; the dashboard frontier chart legend; `docs/index.md`, `docs/lab-notebook/{index,story-arc,story-arc-en,devlog,07-model-router}.md`, and the README routing-layer paragraph.

**Preserved exactly as-is:** page slugs (`07-model-router.md`), asset filenames (`model-router.gif`), in-page anchors (the atlas heading pins its old anchor via `attr_list`), and the *real* Azure deployment id `model-router` used in experiments 09/10 and the setup guide. URL migration belongs to a later slice.

A dated note was added to the 2026-07-16 devlog entry so readers don't copy the now-dead `experiment run model-router` command; the historical text itself is untouched.

### Enforcement — semantic, not line-based

`scripts/check_naming_surfaces.py` splits every reader-facing surface into **semantic blocks** — headings, paragraphs, list items, table rows, whole admonition cards, figure alt text, dashboard UI blocks and experiment metadata — and fails if any single block contains both the product name and the synthetic figure. Code fences are stripped (they legitimately contain the real deployment name), and link targets are stripped so preserved slugs never match.

It currently checks **2,092 blocks**. `tests/test_naming_surfaces.py` covers it with fixtures for wrapped lines, table rows, cards and alt text — cases a same-line `rg` would miss — plus negative cases proving slugs, deployment names and the real-product experiments 09/10 are not flagged.

## Z2 — Reader-facing precision

`router.pricing` now declares the contract explicitly:

* `READER_FACING_USD_RENDERERS` — human-readable renderers; totals show 2 decimals, sub-cent amounts up to 4 (`format_usd` / `format_usd_avg`, mirrored by the dashboard's `usdSmart` / `usdAvg`).
* `CANONICAL_PRECISION_SURFACES` — `--json`, the audit ledger, replay reports and run-record fields keep canonical full precision.

`tests/test_reader_facing_precision.py` renders the declared surfaces from real runs and inspects every emitted money token, and separately asserts that machine JSON and ledger records are *not* rounded and still agree with the rendered total before rounding. No repository-wide decimal regex is used.

While re-capturing examples, the README before/after transcript turned out to be attributed to the wrong command — the shown numbers come from a `--synth` replay over the 100-row workload, not from `make replay` (which prints a 5-task run). The prose now names the exact reproducing command.

## Z3 — README first screen

Re-ordered to: (1) two-sentence value proposition, (2) one compact visual generated from verified repository data (`docs/assets/gif/hero.gif`, produced deterministically by `scripts/build_experiment_gifs.py`), (3) the strongest honest evidence explicitly labelled a **five-prompt wiring proof** with its sample-size caveat, (4) the free offline quickstart stated in **seconds**, (5) links to methodology, benchmark evidence and the full manual.

The public static page is called an **interactive offline demo** (README and `docs/index.md`), never a live paid dashboard. The existing-Foundry path moved below the first screen and is labelled **target / in progress** until its release gate exists.

## Z4 — Timing re-baselined on supported interpreters

Measured a real fresh clone → install → first result on **CPython 3.11.15 and 3.12.13** (the previously cited ~17.5 s figure was taken on 3.14, outside the supported set, and is no longer used).

| Segment | 3.11.15 | 3.12.13 | Nature |
|---|---|---|---|
| `git clone --depth 1` | 1.17 s | 1.37 s | telemetry |
| venv + `pip install -e .` (cold cache) | 7.18 s | 4.83 s | telemetry |
| venv + `pip install -e .` (warm cache) | 6.59 s | 4.60 s | telemetry |
| **post-install `cost-router hero --json`** | **0.12 s** | **0.12 s** | product promise |

`docs/manual/install.md` records the numbers with full environment metadata (OS, arch, vCPU, interpreter builds, cache state, network) and labels them an observed target — not p95, not an SLA. It also states that the offline path is never described as "10 minutes".

## Z5 — Sample-size citation pinned

Microsoft's guidance (≥100 prompts for statistically reliable results; fewer than 30 is directional only) is now cited with its official URL and the **2026-07-29** access date in `docs/manual/measurement-protocol.md` §3.4, `docs/manual/workload-inventory.md` and `samples/workloads/README.md`. `curated-24` is marked `evidence_tier=directional`; `hero-100-prompts` is noted as the first candidate for a stronger tier.

## Verification

```
python -m pytest -q                              # all pass (3 new test modules)
python -m ruff check .                           # All checks passed!
mkdocs build --strict --site-dir /tmp/site-z     # exit 0
python scripts/check_naming_surfaces.py          # OK — 2092 blocks checked
bash scripts/validate-local.sh                   # PASSED (secret scan + tests + lint)
```

## Reviewer focus

* `scripts/check_naming_surfaces.py` — is the block-splitting strict enough for "card" and "figure metadata"?
* `README.md` first screen — order and the wiring-proof caveat wording.
* `docs/manual/install.md` timing table — the numbers come from one Linux machine; they are labelled as observations, not guarantees.

## Not in this PR

Z6 (legacy Model Router pricing-truth annotation and fail-closed enforcement in renderer/publisher/replay) is deliberately excluded and left for a follow-up.

items.title: Release 0.15.0: dart-sass JS-API parity fix (breaking), honest benchmarks, Node 24 LTS
items.body:
30 commits. One breaking change, one shipped-bug fix, and a substantial correction to how we measure and publish performance.

## Breaking (npm packages only)

**`result.css` no longer ends with a trailing newline** (`4cbb353f`). grass's JS API was appending one; dart-sass's JS API does not — so every result differed from dart-sass by a single byte. This was a real bug in the shipped npm package, found by a benchmark's byte-equality assertion (the CLI-level parity corpus is structurally incapable of seeing JS-API divergences).

The CLI and the Rust API are **unchanged** — both still end with a newline, matching dart-sass's CLI. dart-sass deliberately has different trailing-newline behavior for its CLI and its JS API; grass now matches both.

Consumers writing `result.css` straight to a file and needing the previous bytes should append `"\n"` themselves. Version bumped **0.14.6 → 0.15.0** (minor, not patch — it is breaking).

## Benchmarks: measured honestly, and several claims came down

The performance numbers on the README were wrong in ways that all flattered us. Fixed:

- **Corpus speed ratios were startup-inflated.** The 14-project corpus timed dart via `npx sass` (npx resolution + Dart VM boot — ~0.7s just to compile a one-line file) against grass as a native binary, producing 12x–134x "speedups". Removed at the generator; the corpus now times both engines **warm and in-process**. Honest result: **2.5x–18.1x, median 6.37x**, all 14 still byte-identical to dart-sass 1.101.0.
- **Peak memory was inflated ~3x.** We compared grass's *native* binary against dart-sass's *pure-JS npm CLI*, which carries an entire Node runtime. Both dart CLIs emit byte-identical CSS — the gap was packaging, not memory. Corrected to a like-for-like native comparison: **3.3x less** (was claiming 8.90x).
- **We were benchmarking a stale dart-sass** (sass-embedded 1.97.3) while claiming parity against 1.101.0. Bumped to the latest; the newer dart-sass narrowed our lead and we published the smaller numbers.
- **We were benchmarking on Node 23** — an odd-numbered, non-LTS release nobody runs in production. Everything re-measured on **Node 24 LTS**; `.nvmrc` pins it.

The README now carries the full 14-project table, WASM figures, and a footnote naming the method for every row.

## CI: Node 20 → 24 LTS

Node 20 reached end of life in April 2026. Every Node reference bumped: `setup-node` pins, the x86_64 Rosetta test's Node tarball (and its SHA-256), and the `node:*-alpine` images used for the musl napi tests. Safe for consumers — `crates/napi` targets `napi4` and N-API is ABI-stable, so the build Node does not constrain the runtime.

Note: Node 22 is still a supported LTS and is now untested. A `[22, 24]` matrix would cover it cheaply; deliberately not done here.

## Also in this release

- Release CLI binaries are now PGO-trained on a multi-project corpus.
- N-API concurrency documented: `compileAsync` parallelizes on the libuv threadpool. Raise `UV_THREADPOOL_SIZE` before the first async call — 3.76x at the default pool of 4, 6.63x at 8 (8 concurrent Bootstrap compiles).
- New bench harnesses: `bench/scripts/napi-concurrent.mjs`, `bench/scripts/wasm-compare.mjs` (four-engine, raw byte-equality gate — the one that found the newline bug).

## Gates

sass-spec 13,849/13,888; real-world corpus 14/14 byte-identical to dart-sass 1.101.0; Bootstrap/USWDS byte-zero; `cargo test`, fmt, clippy clean; napi + pkg-publish suites green. CLI output verified byte-identical to `npx sass@1.101.0`.

items.title: Add index benchmarks against a generated 50k-row indexed table
items.body:
## Summary
Adds benchmarks demonstrating what automatic index use (v2.0.0–v2.1.0) buys, restores the historical cross-library comparison, and makes the benchmarked **DbfDataReader package version switchable** — everything measured against published packages (the project keeps its benchmark-the-release philosophy).

## Cross-library comparison (v1.1.0 and v2.1.0 sections in benchmarks.md)
Recreates the Sylvan / NDbf / DbfDataReader comparison in the style of [MarkPflug/Benchmarks](https://github.com/MarkPflug/Benchmarks/blob/main/source/Benchmarks/DbfDataReaderBenchmarks.cs) — same method names as the old v0.5.x tables — reading every field of every record of the `tl_2019_01_place` census fixture. The package version is an MSBuild property, so any release is one flag away:

```
dotnet run -c Release --project test/DbfDataReader.Benchmarks -p:DbfDataReaderVersion=1.1.0 -- --filter "*DbfDataReaderBenchmarks*"
```

Findings: the sequential read path is **unchanged from 1.1.0 to 2.1.0** (~1.15× NDbf, identical allocations) — the whole SQL/typed-query/index feature set is additive — and both improve markedly on the 0.5.x-era ratios (1.8–1.9× with 4× allocations). The 2.x-only index benchmarks are excluded from compilation when benchmarking 1.x. A project README documents the commands.

## Index benchmarks
The repository fixtures are 3–16 rows — useless for index benchmarks — so `BenchmarkTableGenerator` writes a 50,000-row DBF **plus a matching compound index**: the CDX writer produces the simplest structure the library's strict reader accepts (uncompressed leaf entries, max-key interior entries, sibling-linked levels, a two-tag directory), with tags on `ID` (unique integers, exercising the #298 key transform) and `CODE` (character keys, ~100 rows per value). Before anything is measured, `GlobalSetup` verifies through the public API that indexed and scanned executions return identical rows for every benchmarked shape — a wrong writer fails the run rather than producing pretty-but-false numbers.

### Results (Apple M3 Max, .NET 10, ShortRun; full tables in benchmarks.md)

| Scenario | Full scan | Index | Speed-up | Allocations |
|---|---:|---:|---:|---|
| Equality seek (1 of 50k rows) | 23.0 ms | **50 µs** | ~459× | 17.9 MB → 32 KB |
| Range scan (100 rows) | 23.8 ms | **102 µs** | ~233× | 17.9 MB → 81 KB |
| Character seek (100 rows) | 22.2 ms | **157 µs** | ~141× | 16.8 MB → 81 KB |
| `top 10 … order by ID desc` | 60.6 ms | **3.0 ms** | ~20× | 66.4 MB → 5.7 MB |
| `count(*)` filtered (10k rows) | 23.6 ms | **973 µs** | ~24× | 18.0 MB → 1.2 MB |
| `count(*)` all rows | 21.8 ms (read rows) | 15.1 ms (status scan) | 1.4× | **16.8 MB → 10 KB** |

The last row is the honest one: a whole-table count still reads every record, so the win is modest in time but ~1,600× in allocations — value parsing is what it skips.

items.title: feat(bench): reproducible benchmark harness (efficacy, latency, false positives)
items.body: ## Summary Adds `bench/`, a reproducible harness that runs the **real firewall** over a labelled corpus and prints the three numbers a security buyer asks about. No values are hardcoded; change the corpus and the numbers change. Run with `npm run bench`. This is the credibility layer for selling Carapace: it produces measured efficacy/latency/false-positive figures and prints its own honesty caveats so the eventual numbers are defensible. ### What it measures 1. **Efficacy** — how many MINJA-style memory-injection attacks reach durable memory, comparing `undefended` vs a `naive keyword filter` vs `Carapace`. "Reached" means the promotion verdict is `allow`. Anchored to MINJA (arXiv:2601.05504, ~95% undefended success). 2. **Latency** — added per-op cost (p50/p95/p99/mean, microseconds) via `process.hrtime.bigint()` over 20k iterations: `baseline store` vs `Carapace ingress` vs `Carapace full write`. 3. **False positives** — detector flag rate on a benign corpus that *includes adversarially-hard items* (trigger words in innocent contexts), plus how often legitimate **trusted** memory is wrongly blocked. ### Measured numbers on this run ``` EFFICACY (reached durable memory, lower better) undefended 30/30 100.0% naive keyword filter 25/30 83.3% Carapace 0/30 0.0% fast-detector recall 14/30 46.7% <- detection misses paraphrase/multilingual/bridging, yet 0/30 reach memory: the provenance gate is the backstop LATENCY (microseconds, in-process) baseline store p50 0.86 p95 3.56 Carapace full write p50 16.34 p95 31.60 -> added p50 ~+15us, p95 ~+28us; ~49k ops/sec single-thread FALSE POSITIVES all benign 1/25 (4.0%) hard subset 1/10 (10.0%) legit trusted memory wrongly blocked 0/16 (0.0%) ``` (Latency is machine-dependent and not committed to any doc; the harness prints it live.) ### Honesty (enforced in output + `bench/README.md`) - Attacks are **MINJA-style reproductions**, not the paper's exact dataset. - The fast detector is a deterministic heuristic; it misses paraphrase, several languages, and subtle bridging records. Shown, not hidden. - Carapace's strength is the **provenance gate, not detection**: untrusted content cannot become durable memory even when detection misses it. - The PromptGuard 2 model detector seam is **not wired**; these are the heuristic-only floor. - If an attacker controls a trusted (T0/T1) channel, detection becomes load-bearing. Stated plainly. ### Provenance model used by the harness Attacks arrive unauthenticated on untrusted channels (an attacker can't authenticate as the principal); benign first-party content (`direct`/`filesystem`/`tool`) is authenticated. This is the asymmetry the firewall is built around. ### Files - `bench/corpus.ts` — 30 labelled attacks (by evasion family) + 25 benign (10 hard). - `bench/harness.ts` — firewall builder, provenance helpers, timing/percentiles. - `bench/run.ts` — orchestrates the three measurements + prints the report. - `bench/README.md` — methodology + honesty notes. - `package.json` — adds `"bench": "tsx bench/run.ts"`. ### Verification Existing gate stays green: `typecheck` clean, **33/33 tests**, `demo` ledger `verify()->{valid:true}`, `redteam` 5/7 detect / 0/7 reached. `bench/` typechecks strict-clean (run via `tsx`, same convention as `examples/`). Link to Devin session: https://app.devin.ai/sessions/354d50bfa1c3408dbbfe9237c7510335 Requested by: @JoeProAI ---

items.title: docs(250): ratify the extraction contract — R1/R2/R3, plus two corrections to its own numbers
items.body:
Closes the design half of #250. The GM has ruled on D1–D3; this records the rulings, the measured cost of each, and two places where the proposal's own numbers were wrong.

## The rulings

| | ruling | measured cost on ch46 |
|---|---|---|
| **R1** (D1) | **Refuse and flag** — a conflict the VTT cannot settle renders as neither copy. **A span verbatim in both copies is never a conflict.** | **2** interruptions/session |
| **R2** (D2) | **A transcription garble is a ground-truth defect and gets fixed** — per-cue, in the `.cleaned.vtt`, authored by the GM. Never a global replace, never a model judgement. | 3 cues this session |
| **R3** (D3) | **Refuse and flag** on editorial brackets inside a verbatim span; binds any *new* one. | **7–10** spans/session |

R1's exclusion is the load-bearing part. Without it the rule fires on two similar-but-distinct *real* utterances and wakes the GM to adjudicate between two facts.

## Two corrections to the proposal's own numbers

**Class-4 brackets were reported as 3. They are 10 per layer.** The first pass classified by *token identity*, so `[Lathander]` was bucketed as a speaker label (it is one — three times, plus a fourth inside a verbatim blockquote) and every marker carrying a comment (`[inaudible — probable "…"]`) matched no known token and fell through uncounted. Reclassified by *position* — every bracket inside a `> "…"` span — the count is 10, identical in `new/` and `smoothed/`. R3 was ruled against the old figure and re-confirmed at 7–10.

**D1's cost was never measured before the ruling was requested.** It is not the 34/79 per-quote unverified figures — most unverified quotes have no second copy to conflict with. Pairing the two sections against each other and classifying both copies gives 8 paired spans in `new/`, 3 settled by the tape, 2 that R1 must refuse.

## What R2 corrected in its own framing

- **The registry does not know.** `Vukradin`'s registry entry carries exactly one alias, `Bard`. It has never heard of `Vucherdin` — so the option "permit canonical spelling when the registry is confident" would never have fired. The model laundered the name on its own initiative, which is the defect, not a policy gap.
- **This is not the alias rule.** An alias is a *spoken variant*; the standing rule that an alias is identity and never a text substitution is untouched. An ASR mishearing is a defect in the tape. Evidence for the latter here: `Vukradin` 11×, `Vucherdin` 3×, `Vukra Din` 1× in one session, with every mangled form from a single speaker and none from a player.

## Why the model is not the flagger

Recorded because it will be proposed again. Both #245 benchmark arms had the Vucherdin span in front of them: Fable kept the garble with no audit entry, Opus silently reclassified it. Neither flagged anything, in opposite directions. `sd_verify_quotes` still surfaces any drifted span as `near` — the discovery path stays open and deterministic; what is dropped is the model pre-filtering the GM's list.

## Also

- Adds the doc to `docs/README.md`, which #257 missed.
- Records three open implementation questions: clarifying-vs-replacing brackets, where R2 corrections live long-term (`corrections.yaml` exists but `sd_verify_quotes` doesn't read it and it keys on doc-path globs, not cue indices), and C4's two options.

Docs-only — no code, no tests affected. The filename still says `_proposal`; left alone so #257's links don't break.
