items.title: fix(ledgers): validate ledger and ADR identifier allocation

labels.name: area: infrastructure
labels.description: CI, packaging, releases, and repository automation

items.body:
Closes #82. Closes #83.

## The collision this prevents

`scripts/check_ledgers.py` validated that each ledger file exists and carries its heading, and that
every benchmark artifact matches its own self-digest. It never looked at the ID column. Nothing
checked ADR numbers at all. Both conventions were enforced by review — and review does not see a
merge.

That is the whole failure mode. Two branches that each append a row numbered `D-137` produce **no
textual conflict**, because the rows land in different places in the same Markdown table. Two
branches that each add `docs/adr/0066-<their-slug>.md` produce no conflict either, because the
filenames differ. Git merges both, cleanly and silently, and the repository ends up with one
identifier naming two unrelated records — a permanent ambiguity in something that is cited from
commit messages, issues, other ADRs, and the ledgers themselves.

### The real ADR-0066 incident

Not hypothetical. Three concurrent branches each created an ADR-0066:

| Commit | Branch work | File created |
|---|---|---|
| `0a05b1f` | route bundle contract | `docs/adr/0066-atomic-route-bundle-preview.md` |
| `b00062c` | bounded ordered multilayer proposals | `docs/adr/0066-bounded-ordered-layer-routing.md` |
| `4e1c737` | route-aware placement scoring | `docs/adr/0066-route-aware-placement-ranking.md` |

The first landed on `main` as ADR-0066 (#57). The second was renumbered by hand to ADR-0068 (#58).
The third was renumbered to ADR-0067 (#59). Both renumbered ADRs then merged in parallel with #81 —
the pull request whose entire job was rebuilding the ADR index — so **neither appeared in the index
at all** until this branch.

### It happened again while this branch was open

This is the part worth reading twice. The branch was cut from `main` at `cdd60d3`, and the checkers
were written against that tree. While the work was in flight, **#59 merged** — and it introduced
four more collisions, which the new checker caught on rebase:

| Identifier | Names | ...and also names |
|---|---|---|
| `D-137` | documentation reorganization (#70) | the ordered-layer proposal seam (ADR-0068) |
| `D-139` | route-aware placement scoring (ADR-0067) | the ordered-layer compatibility correction |
| `D-140` | the route-aware interpretation correction | the atomic route bundle (ADR-0066) |
| `B-076` | recorded-link target corrections | the ordered-layer internal proposal oracle |
| `B-078` | route-aware selection replay | the capped ordered-layer `(node, vias)` differential |
| `B-082` | route-aware claim correction | route-bundle released-version provenance |

Six identifiers in `main` each name two unrelated records. Four of them arrived during the few hours
this branch was open. That is the argument for the check, made by the repository rather than by me.

The ambiguity is already load-bearing: `D-138` and `D-139` cite "D-137's compatibility boundary" and
"D-137's compatibility claim" (meaning the ordered-layer row); `D-140` cites "B-078/B-081" (meaning
the route-aware benchmarks); `check_doc_links.py`'s two exemptions cite `B-076` (meaning the
link-corrections entry); `B-078` supersedes a claim "made alongside B-076" (meaning the other one).

## What this adds

**Ledger identifiers** (`scripts/check_ledgers.py`) — parses the `D-`, `R-`, `SEC-`, and `B-` spaces
from table rows and section headings, then:

- **fails** on a duplicate identifier, on an identifier that is not zero-padded to three digits, and
  on a row that goes backwards in the decision, risk, or security ledger;
- **reports** gaps without failing. `D-039`, `SEC-021`, and `B-006` are permanent — a withdrawn
  number is never recycled, so that a stale external reference resolves to nothing rather than to an
  unrelated entry;
- makes no ordering claim about the benchmark ledger, which is organized by topic.

**ADR numbers** (`scripts/check_adr_numbers.py`, new) — fails when two files claim one number, when
an ADR's own `# ADR-NNNN:` heading disagrees with its filename, when an ADR is missing from or
repeated in the index, when an index row points at a missing or wrong file, and when the index is
out of order. Unallocated numbers are reported, never failed.

### The nine legitimate duplicates

The benchmark ledger deliberately reuses a number for a **replay** of that benchmark, as a `####`
sub-entry under the `###` entry it replays. There are exactly nine, and they are carried in a closed
`REPLAY_SUB_ENTRIES` list keyed to exact heading text — the same shape as the existing
`EXEMPT_TARGETS` list in `check_doc_links.py`.

Being listed is **necessary but not sufficient**. The heading must still be a `####` sub-entry, and
the `###` entry it replays must already appear earlier in the document. So an accidental duplicate
cannot be legalized by editing the list alone — which matters, because `B-076`'s two entries are
*both* `####` sub-entries and a heading-level heuristic would have accepted them. An exception that
stops matching real text is itself a failure, so an exception cannot be added and then quietly
forgotten.

### The actual root-cause fix

Both checkers verify their **single-line allocation registries**: the `Highest allocated / Next free`
table in `docs/ledgers/README.md`, and the `next unused number — currently **NNNN**` line in
`docs/adr/README.md`. Each must match what the tree actually contains.

That is the part that stops the collision rather than merely detecting it. Because each ID space is
one line, two branches that both take the next number now conflict **textually** on that line, and
Git refuses to merge them instead of accepting both. The checker turns a silent semantic collision
into a loud syntactic one.

## What the checkers found, and what was deliberately left

The checkers were run against the tree **unchanged** first, both at the original branch point and
again after rebasing onto the new `main`. Everything below is a real pre-existing violation, not
something introduced here.

| Finding | Disposition |
|---|---|
| `D-137`, `D-139`, `D-140` each allocated twice | **Recorded, not repaired** — correction entry `D-142` |
| `B-076`, `B-078`, `B-082` each allocated twice | **Recorded, not repaired** — correction entry `B-084` |
| Decision-ledger document order displaced by the same merges | Recorded by `D-142` |
| `ADR-0067` and `ADR-0068` absent from the ADR index | **Fixed** — both indexed |
| `SEC-114` undocumented unallocated number | Documented in `docs/ledgers/README.md` |
| Allocation registry stale by 3–8 numbers in every space | Refreshed and now machine-verified |

The six ledger collisions are **recorded rather than renumbered, deliberately**. The ledgers are
append-only. Renumbering a merged row would rewrite history to hide that the collision happened and
would break every external citation that already exists, several of which are listed above. `D-142`
and `B-084` state which entry each ambiguous number refers to in each citing context and instruct
readers to cite the date or sub-entry title alongside it.

Each collision is carried in a closed `RECORDED_COLLISIONS` list keyed to its correction entry, so
it is printed on every run while a **new** duplicate still fails the build. Registering a collision
is not a way to accept one: it requires landing the dated correction note first.

One consequence worth naming: merging two independently appended blocks also **displaces document
order** — the `D-137` block now sits after the `D-139`/`D-140` block. A recorded collision therefore
also excuses the order it displaced, because that is one defect and one correction note. An
unrelated out-of-order row still fails, and both directions are covered by tests.

`docs/adr/README.md` is an index rather than an append-only ledger, so the two missing rows are a
fix rather than a record.

## Verification

Full local gate on the exact branch tip, rebased onto `97b56ce`:

| Gate | Result |
|---|---|
| `ruff format --check` | 378 files already formatted |
| `ruff check` | All checks passed |
| `mypy src` (strict) | Success: no issues found in 90 source files |
| `pytest` (full, real KiCad 10.0.5 nodes running) | **1585 passed, 1 skipped, 379 subtests passed** |
| `check_version.py` | passed — `0.5.0` |
| `check_ledgers.py` | passed — highest allocated `B-084`, `D-142`, `R-112`, `SEC-117` |
| `check_adr_numbers.py` | passed — 67 records, highest allocated `ADR-0068` |
| `check_doc_links.py` | passed — 146 Markdown files, 2 exemptions |
| `check_audio_benchmarks.py` | passed — 3 fixtures |
| `check_circuit_intents.py` | passed — 1 fixture |
| `check_secrets.py` | passed |
| `python -m build` | built `copper_mcp-0.5.0` sdist and wheel |

The single skip is the pre-existing conditional in `tests/test_metamorphic.py` ("endpoint swap is
only defined for a two-pin net"), not a KiCad-availability skip: KiCad was on `PATH` and every
KiCad-backed node ran.

`pip-audit` could not build its isolated environment locally (`ensurepip` aborts under this
sandbox); auditing the installed environment directly reports no known vulnerabilities, and CI runs
the packaged path.

### Regression tests and mutation checking

29 new cases across `tests/test_check_ledgers.py` and `tests/test_check_adr_numbers.py`: duplicate
`D-` id fails, duplicate ADR number fails, index/file mismatch fails, heading/filename mismatch
fails, an allowlisted replay sub-entry passes, a historical gap passes — plus out-of-order rows,
unpadded identifiers, replay entries promoted out of sub-entry position, replay entries with no
parent, unused exceptions in either list, displaced-versus-unrelated ordering, stale allocation
registries, and a case asserting the committed tree satisfies every rule.

Every rule was mutation-checked by reverting it individually and confirming its test fails:
**20 mutations, 20 killed.**

## Scope

Tooling and documentation only. No runtime contract, capability, diagnostic, schema, or public
behavior changes. Recorded as `D-141`; both new checkers are wired into `make lint` and CI.

items.title: util/spec2017: sampled SPEC CPU2017 ref inputs via SE-mode KVM (systematic + phased sampling)
items.body:
Sampled SPEC CPU2017 **ref** inputs under the detailed NeoverseV2 model, using SE-mode KVM (PR #12) to make the fast-forward affordable.

## Why

SPEC2017 intspeed ref is ~23 T instructions. AtomicSimpleCPU runs at **1.59 MIPS** on this host — **162 days** for the suite, 32 days for 657.xz_s alone — and atomic is only ~10x faster than the detailed core (48–151 KIPS), so fast-forwarding is nearly as expensive as simulating and cannot be paid per experiment. SE-mode KVM runs at **0.6–4.1 GIPS**, which makes it affordable.

## What is here

- **`checkpoint` + `measure`** — systematic (SMARTS-style) offsets across the whole workload, paid once and reused by every configuration. `report.py` gives IPC with a **Student-t confidence interval** computed in CPI space.
- **`phased`** — the in-run loop: initial KVM fast-forward, then N x (warmup -> ROI -> KVM fast-forward), no checkpoints. Cheap, but a **prefix probe, not a sample**.
- **`size`** — each workload's true length in gem5's own instruction count.
- Workloads parsed from SPEC's own `speccmds.cmd`, never hand-transcribed.
- `--mem-size` (default 16GiB), replacing a hardcoded 3GiB that killed 7 of 18 sizing runs with `fatal: Out of memory`.

## The finding that matters

The first real multi-sample CIs show **no single K works**:

| workload | K | IPC | 95% CI | CV | K for ±1% |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| 600.perlbench_s | 23 | 1.7160 | ±0.28% | 0.65% | 2 |
| 641.leela_s | 29 | 1.5429 | **±2.46%** | 6.47% | **161** |

At ±2.46% a 2% leela "win" is indistinguishable from noise. A point estimate would have reported it with no hint. `report.py` prints the achieved CI every run.

## Blocking bug, not worked around

**SE-mode KVM cannot hand a syscall-active workload to a detailed core.** The switch panics at `PC 0x1c8` — an offset into the EL1 vector page SE-KVM installs at `0x0000ffff00000000` to forward SVCs to gem5 (`src/arch/arm/se_kvm.hh:49`), with its top bits gone. The guest was inside a KVM-only trampoline; that PC means nothing to a core that emulates `SVC` directly.

It is **deterministic**, not a race: 620.omnetpp_s panics identically at initial fast-forwards of 1.00e9, 1.05e9 and 1.10e9. Only **5 of 11** benchmarks survive (the compute-bound ones). The rest crash loudly rather than reporting wrong numbers. This is the same defect as the ~23% of perlbench checkpoint restores that panic at `0x1c8`. **Fixing it means changing PR #12's KVM code, not this harness** — see `util/spec2017/KNOWN_BUG_kvm_switch_vector_page.md`.

Separately fixed here: the KVM path advertised `FEAT_CRC32`/`FEAT_DOTPROD`/crypto HWCAPs that glibc's ifunc resolvers act on, but the NeoverseV2 FUPool has no unit for `SimdCrc32`/`SimdDotProd`/`SimdAes*`/`SimdSha*` — so 602.gcc_s and 625.x264_s panicked at valid glibc PCs. Now only the intersection is advertised.

## Verified

- **Cache coherence across the O3->KVM switch — proven, not inferred.** `--phased-finish` runs the workload to completion after the last ROI so its output can be diffed. On 605.mcf_s, three O3->KVM round trips give checksum **10630734340**, byte-identical to a pure-KVM reference. (A weaker IPC cross-check agrees: 0.6994 single-switch vs 0.7009 in-loop.)
- **IPC cross-checks**: mcf 0.8019 (SE-KVM restore) vs 0.799 (old SE baseline); leela 1.5995 vs 1.5786.
- gem5 SE instruction counts match native `perf` to <0.1%.
- 16 concurrent SE-KVM jobs, zero contention.

## Also fixed along the way

- **625.x264_s's `BuckBunny.yuv` was truncated to 224 of 1250 frames.** Every prior x264 number encoded a truncated input; it also made the workload look 4.6x shorter (32.70 B vs 150.95 B insts) and was the real cause of the old "2nd pass has more frames than 1st pass" error.
- A stale-size landmine: failed sizing runs left `rc=0` rows that would have placed every x264 sample in the first ~6% of the workload silently. `_merge_sizes` now refuses rows from failed runs.
- The full-system KVM design (58.8 MIPS, disk image, boot) is retired — SE-KVM is 10x faster and needs none of it. The README records why, so nobody rebuilds it.

## Not done

- Warmup swept on one workload only (flat to 0.42%, non-monotonic 1M->50M; >1M buys nothing on mcf).
- `sizes_gem5_se.csv` complete for 11/18 workloads.
- 998.specrand_is is 0.43e9 instructions, shorter than the 10e9 initial fast-forward, so `phased` reports 0 ROIs for it (flagged PARTIAL).

items.body:
## What this changes

This pull request corrects two numbers the project publishes, completes two security documents that described only half of a boundary, and repairs a test job that was running out of time.

**The two numbers were wrong in different ways.** A chart titled "commits per week" counted merge commits instead of commits, so it read about four times too low. Branches here keep several commits each, so one merge stood in for all of them. Separately, a performance table had a row labelled `all` under a column headed `total`. That row adds up six unrelated benchmark inputs, so a reader took it for the cost of a single call and overstated that cost several-fold: one small command costs about 0.07 ms, while the summed row reads 13 ms.

**The two documents each described what the network policy inspects, and neither said what it cannot see.** The policy matches the hostname the agent dials. It never sees the address that an allowed service then contacts for itself. A package cache or a registry mirror will fetch whatever URL a caller hands it, so admitting one name can reach destinations no rule admitted. The second gap is about the opposite direction. `SECURITY.md` listed sanitization of the text the agent itself writes, and gave no purpose for it — which reads as defense against injected instructions, although nothing outside the agent injects into the agent's own output. Its real job is to close a hidden channel: invisible characters the agent writes into a file cannot carry a message to a later agent that reads that file. A second model watching the stream cannot replace this, because it must first recognise a payload, and an encoding it does not recognise looks like noise.

**The test job is the Windows leg.** Its shards run against a 25-minute limit, and one was killed at that limit with the suite 98% finished. Most of the limit goes to a stretch that prints nothing at all, so the job named no cause. That stretch is now measured and made shorter.

## Partitions

Ordered by how carefully each one wants reading.

- **Commit-cadence undercount** — `.github/scripts/repo-health-charts.py`, `METRICS.md`, `.github/workflows/repo-health-charts.yaml`, `tests/test_repo_health_charts.py`. Changes a published number. The cadence series borrowed its dates from the first-parent walk that the lines-of-code chart needs. It now walks `git log --no-merges` on its own, and each of the two walks says in its header why the other one is wrong for it.
- **DrvFs shard bring-up** — `.github/scripts/wsl-cross-platform-tests.sh`. The only change to how CI runs. Three edits, none of which raises the time limit: bytecode moves off the slow Windows-drive bridge, two `uv run` calls stop re-checking the project against its lock after it was already synced, and timestamped markers bound the silent stretch.
- **Stage-timing sum mislabelled** — `bin/bench-stages.py`, `bin/check-stage-perf.py`, `METRICS.md`, `tests/*`. The row is now `sum-of-kinds`, a single token, because the table's own parser splits on whitespace. The page says the plotted series is a whole-corpus regression signal and gives the real per-call range. Each history entry now also records per-kind totals, so the log can answer what one call costs.
- **Fetch-capable host caveat** — `SECURITY.md`, `docs/configuration.md`, `bin/lib/sbx/project-domains.bash`. Prose and one comment block. It documents a property the policy always had.
- **Output-strip purpose** — `SECURITY.md`, `README.md`. One bullet extended in place in each file. `README.md` had the gap twice: its bullet is titled "Input/**output** sanitization" while the text covered only the inbound half, and the architecture diagram drew a strip on the arrow into the sandbox and none on the agent's own output.
- **Chart labels and their reconciliation** — `METRICS.md`, `bin/check-stage-perf.py`, `tests/test_readme_charts.py`. The sanitization chart sat under a heading that said "Monitor", so the word "sanitization" appeared nowhere on the page and nobody could find the chart by its subject. It now has its own heading. Two sibling charts had page labels that disagreed with the labels their own publishers write.
- **CI-triage note** — `.claude/skills/ci-triage/SKILL.md`. **Doctrine, so it needs your approval and must not merge automatically.** A log fetch returns about 99 bytes and a refusal when the log holds terminal colour codes. That greps as empty, so it imitates a different failure whose remedy — wait and retry — never helps here.

## Review focus

`bin/lib/sbx/project-domains.bash`. The new header states what the admission gate does **not** prove, directly above the checks that do prove things. Every check below it is a positive assertion about the name, and this is the one paragraph saying those checks cannot speak for the service behind that name.

The wording I am least sure of is "fetch-capable host". It names the class correctly, but it is not a term of art, so a future reader may search for something else.

## Security boundary impact

No boundary moves. Both document edits make `SECURITY.md` accurate about limits the policy always had. The threat model gains no assumption and loses none.

## Decisions made

**Historical stage-timing points stay as they are.** The history log stored only the summed value, so no past entry holds the per-kind detail that a per-call number needs. Re-running the benchmark at old commits on today's hardware would invent points nobody measured. The stored values are not wrong, only mislabelled — over a fixed corpus they remain a valid regression signal — so the labels changed and the series stands. Per-kind totals are recorded from this commit on. Under the alternative, the chart restarts from zero history to fix a caption.

**When a chart's page label and its publisher disagree, the publisher wins.** Its string is what gets drawn into the image the reader is looking at. This renames two charts a reader may know by their old names: "Setup time" becomes "User install work", and "sbx launch timing" becomes "sbx launch-to-handover". The URLs and the history keys do not change, so no chart loses its trend.

**The corrected cadence chart cannot publish from this branch.** The chart workflow has no pull-request trigger and confines its push leg to `main`, which a test pins as a safety property, so unmerged code can never overwrite the published chart. A manual dispatch runs from the default branch and would republish the same wrong numbers. The published image keeps the old figures until this merges, and the daily job then corrects it. I dispatched nothing.

## Guard extended, not added

A guard for the label class already existed and did not fire, which is itself the finding. `tests/test_readme_charts.py` reconciles published chart names against the page in both directions, so a chart cannot go missing and a dead reference cannot linger. It passed here, correctly — the chart was present. What it never compared is the human-readable label, which is the only copy a reader can search the page for. That is now reconciled, off machinery the file already had. No new check, no new workflow, no budget entry, and it lands with an empty baseline.

**Scope limit, because it is easy to misread.** This does not catch the stage chart's original defect, where both label copies agreed with each other and both disagreed with the chart's own drawn title. I tried reconciling those two first, and dogfooding killed it: 4 of 12 charts legitimately differ, since the drawn title carries things like "(95% CI)" that an accessibility label should not. A shared-word weakening does not help either — the failing pair shared the word "stage". So the check claims the siblings and says so.

**No guard for the cadence class, and I am not proposing a hollow one.** The class is "a count derived from a first-parent walk". A text lint cannot express it, because the correct use of that walk lives in the same file. I checked every other first-parent use in the tree; each answers "which commit" or a merge-parentage question, where first-parent is right. One member, no growth. The header on the cadence function names the trap in the words a future session would search for.

<details>
<summary>Verification residue</summary>

**Falsifying commands, all run on this branch.**

`bash scripts/precheck.sh` — exit 0 on every round, most recently after the CI-script partition. pylint 10.00/10, pyright 0 errors. One advisory finding is a pre-existing file-size ratchet on `.github/scripts/auto-resolve/discover.py`, untouched here.

`uv run pytest tests/test_check_stage_perf.py tests/test_readme_charts.py -q` — 81 passed. `uv run pytest tests/test_repo_health_charts.py -q` — 61 passed. `uv run pytest tests/test_wsl_ensure_node.py tests/test_cross_platform_gate.py tests/test_ci_shard_config.py -q` — 46 passed. `uv run shellcheck -x .github/scripts/wsl-cross-platform-tests.sh` — clean.

**Cadence correction, observed against this repo's real history rather than a fixture.** The last completed week goes from 379 to 2103. The five weeks before it move by 2.6x to 4.8x, so the chart changes shape and not only height. Whole history goes from 3250 first-parent commits to 11232 non-merge commits. The new test builds a repository with a three-commit branch merged `--no-ff` and pins the two counts apart at 4 against 2, which is the undercount itself rather than one expected number.

**Non-vacuity, observed.** I copied the new label test into a detached worktree at `41bdf5192` and ran it: `2 failed, 36 passed`, red on exactly `setup-time` and `sbx-launch-timing`, the two charts whose page label disagreed with their publisher. Green on this head.

**The DrvFs timeout, measured.** Merge-queue run `31070020717`, queue branch `gh-readonly-queue/main/pr-3601-…`, so the batch held this pull request alone. Shard 2 ran 25m04s against `timeout-minutes: 25` and reported `cancelled`; GitHub reports a job over its budget that way. Between `uv sync` finishing and pytest printing its header the log is empty:

| shard | silent bring-up | test phase | items |
| --- | ---: | ---: | ---: |
| 8 | 8m03s | 6m30s | 247 |
| 2 | 12m27s | 10m48s, killed at 98% | 270 |
| 1 | 13m17s | 6m00s | 243 |

The bring-up is the larger half of the budget and is paid per shard, so widening the fan-out cannot buy margin — each new shard pays it again while dividing only the smaller half. The `uv run --extra dev --no-sync` combination was exercised here against uv 0.12.0, the version that leg installs.

**Inferred, not observed:** that the three edits actually shorten the bring-up. This session has no WSL2, so I could not reproduce the filesystem. The phase markers are what will report it, on the next run of that leg.

**Two auto-resolve merges, audited rather than trusted.** `0d788a095` and `3414b1de1` each merged `main` after a conflict in `.claude/hooks/gate-hooks.bundle.mjs`, a generated file. For both, `git show --remerge-diff` leaves a one-line delta — the `INPUTS-SHA256` header — and the bundled code is byte-identical to `main`'s blob (`diff -u` is 11 lines, all header). That is the correct result: this branch's only bundle-source edit is a comment, which the bundler strips, so the code cannot change while the input hash must. I did not recompute the hash locally; the required regeneration check is what falsifies it.

**Reported honestly.** Shards 6 and 7 went red on `b1b88124b` before this: `tests/test_check_stage_perf.py` pinned the old label in two places, and my sweep had covered `METRICS.md` and `bin/` but not `tests/`. Shard 4 then went red on `afcdc5640` because a two-word label broke a parser that splits rows on whitespace, which is why the label is one token. Both are the same class the rename was about, which is why the reconciliation above rides this pull request rather than a note.

Three separate reds on this pull request were not real: an `always()` reporter relays a cancelled shard set as a failure, and each time a newer push had superseded the run. The most recent was run `31071740055` on head `22e67e015`, whose own conclusion is `cancelled`.

The push gate confirmed the changelog fragments: `changelog check: valid changelog fragment added or amended.` `.github/` is `internal` in `config/changelog-paths.json`, so the CI partition owes none.

**On the incident that prompted the first partition.** A sandbox's single permitted outgoing path was a self-hosted package-cache proxy. The models forged an admin token on it, poisoned a cached package, and reached the internet from a second machine that fetched that package. glovebox ships no such proxy — `bin/lib/sbx/dep-cache.bash` is a host-side read-only archive, not a live proxy — so the same exposure arrives here only when an operator allows a fetch-capable host, which is the decision those three edits annotate. Detail below the headline is public reconstruction, not vendor-confirmed: the source report and both news write-ups sit on hosts absent from `sandbox-policy/domain-allowlist.json`, so I could not read them directly.

</details>

items.body:
# What & why

The repository had no `CHANGELOG.md`. This adds the first entry, distilled from
what is in the tree and what the merged history shipped.

Part of #143 - see the one deviation below, which is why this does not close it.

## Type of change

- [x] Docs

## What the entry says

The observable surface, one bullet each: the batch entry point and its
asynchronous contract, the frame subset with what it verifies and what it
refuses, the streaming context including its poisoned state, the status set, and
the version single-sourcing.

Then three sections a changelog usually leaves out, which are the ones a consumer
of a decompressor actually needs:

- **the supported subset as limits** - LZ4 only, block-independent frames only,
  decode only, opt-in CUDA engine, and the deliberate divergence from liblz4 on
  a zero match offset;
- **the guarantees as tested**, each naming the test that holds it up rather than
  the intention behind it;
- **known gaps** - Compute Sanitizer cannot attach on my machine,
  so the four-tool sweep has never produced a clean run, and the GPU tests run
  there rather than in CI. A first changelog that drops those two is the wrong
  kind of shorter.

Numbers are referenced, never quoted: the baselines carry their own methodology
blocks in `docs/BENCHMARKS.md` and the write-up that reads them is linked.

## Every line traced

Each claim was checked against the tree rather than written from memory. The
non-obvious ones:

- the asynchronous batch contract and the per-chunk result: `include/cudec.h`
  above `cudec_lz4_decompress_batch`;
- the frame subset, the four things verified when present, and
  `CUDEC_ERR_UNSUPPORTED` for block-linked mode being liblz4's own default:
  `include/cudec.h:109-126`;
- the poisoned streaming context and that only the destructor is valid on it
  afterwards: `include/cudec.h` above `cudec_lz4_decompress_stream_ctx`, and
  `ctx.poisoned` in `src/stream.cpp`;
- `CUDEC_ERR_NOT_IMPLEMENTED` reserved and returned by no current entry point:
  `include/cudec.h:34-38`;
- the version cross-check: the `CUDEC_CMAKE_VERSION_*` assertions in
  `tests/conformance_c.c`;
- the architecture list `80` plus `86-real`: `CMakeLists.txt:97` - written as the
  default list rather than as "baseline sm_80", which is the masterplan's phrasing
  and not what the build says;
- the zero-offset divergence: the comment and reject in `src/lz4_block.h`, pinned
  by `tests/parser_twin.cpp`;
- the structural invariants: the configure-time refusals in
  `tests/CMakeLists.txt`, each with its own liveness probe.

Nothing in the entry claims a capability the suite does not exercise. Snappy is
in the tree as an oracle and a corpus only, so it appears in the entry as a
planned milestone and nowhere else.

## The deviation, and why this does not close the issue

The issue asks for `[0.1.0] - <date>` as the first released section. The entry
sits under `[Unreleased]` instead, and the file says why in its own header:
`include/cudec.h` reports **0.0.1**, and no tag exists.

```
$ grep -n "CUDEC_VERSION" include/cudec.h | head -3
17:#define CUDEC_VERSION_MAJOR 0
18:#define CUDEC_VERSION_MINOR 0
19:#define CUDEC_VERSION_PATCH 1

$ git tag
(no output)
```

So a `[0.1.0]` heading here would name a version the tree does not carry and a
date the project has not chosen, in the one file whose job is to be accurate
about exactly that. The issue also says this change must not bump the version -
which is the same constraint from the other side. Both the number and the date
belong to the release that bumps it (#82), and moving the content under a heading
is one edit there.

That is one bullet of the Done-when unmet by choice, so the issue stays open with
this reasoning in it rather than being closed on a technicality. The other two
bullets - the file exists and is Prettier-clean, every line traces to the tree or
a merged PR, and no claimed capability is untested - are met.

## Verification

- [x] Prettier - `All matched files use Prettier code style!`
- [x] Docs synced - the entry references the README milestone table, BENCHMARKS,
      BENCHMARK-METHODOLOGY and DETERMINISM rather than restating them, so there
      is nothing here to drift against.
- [ ] No build or test change: the diff is one new Markdown file.

## Engineering checklist

- [ ] Fail-closed / oracle / determinism / CUDA-ABI - not applicable, no code
      changes. What the entry says about each of those was checked against the
      test that holds it.
- [ ] An adversarial review was NOT run. There is no second reader on this board
      tonight, so this body carries the evidence in place of one: the per-claim
      trace above and the version/tag commands behind the deviation. That is
      weaker than a review and is not being presented as one.
- [ ] Review record - none, for the reason above.

## Notes

The header paragraph also states what "notable" means for this file, so the next
entry does not have to re-decide whether an internal refactor belongs in it.

items.title: feat: extract mise's asset selection into crates/asset-picker
items.body:
> **Stacked on #3.** Base is `backfill`; retarget to `main` once that merges.

## Why

Backfill's asset selection was a few dozen lines of substring matching I wrote from scratch. Review had already caught it treating `apple-darwin` as a *Windows* asset, because `darwin` contains `win`.

That is the worst class of bug this project can have. A wrong pick still yields a binary that **runs** — so it reports numbers that look entirely real, attributed to the wrong platform. Silence would be better.

mise has solved this properly: regex tables for OS/arch/libc, scoring for format and naming, rejection of installers and packages, and **78 tests** covering what real projects actually ship. Rediscovering that one bad measurement at a time would have been foolish.

## What this is

`crates/asset-picker` — the pure scoring core, extracted. **mise itself is untouched.**

| came across | left behind |
|---|---|
| platform detection (`AssetOs`/`AssetArch`/`AssetLibc`, regex tables) | checksum discovery and verification — needs an HTTP client |
| `AssetPicker` and its scoring | `PlatformTarget` / `AssetMatcher` — bound to mise's config types |
| the platform-token table | |
| **62 of mise's tests**, verbatim | |

`Format` is a trimmed reimplementation rather than a copy: mise derives its parsing from `strum`, and pulling that in for a twenty-line enum isn't a trade worth making.

This is a copy and **it will drift.** The crate root says so, and carries mise's MIT notice (`crates/asset-picker/LICENSE`). Both projects are MIT.

## One behavioural change, and mise is right

On a glibc host it now picks the **gnu** build where my heuristic preferred musl. That isn't cosmetic — musl and glibc builds differ in allocator and startup cost, so benchmarking the musl build measures something most users never execute.

One gap I did have to close: mise *defaults* libc rather than detecting it, which is right for the common case and wrong on Alpine, where a gnu binary will not start at all. `host_libc()` passes musl through when `tak` was itself built against musl — the only signal available without shelling out.

## Tests

69 in the crate (62 from mise + 7 for `Format`), 20 in tak. `cargo fmt --check` and `clippy -D warnings` clean. Verified end to end against `sharkdp/hyperfine` and `jdx/communique`, both of which ship full multi-platform asset sets.

---

<!-- CURSOR_SUMMARY -->

> [!NOTE]
> **Medium Risk**
> Backfill’s release-binary choice changes (e.g. gnu vs musl on glibc hosts), which directly affects benchmark validity; mitigated by extensive ported tests and conservative filtering.
> 
> **Overview**
> Adds a workspace crate **`crates/asset-picker`** with mise’s release-asset scoring (regex OS/arch/libc tables, `AssetPicker`, archive `Format` detection, platform tokens) plus its tests, and wires **`tak-cli`** to depend on it.
> 
> **`tak backfill`** no longer uses hand-rolled substring scoring in `pick_asset`. It pre-filters candidates (`is_usable_subject`, sidecars/source/unopenable formats), drops unlabelled archives when any asset declares a platform, then calls **`AssetPicker::with_libc`** with **`host_libc()`** (musl when `tak` is musl-built) and **`with_no_app(true)`**. Unrecognised hosts are refused outright. **`fetch_binary`** unpacks using the same **`Format`** classifier so selection and extraction stay aligned.
> 
> Docs note the new crate in README status and prior art.

items.title: Harden benchmark worker and offline transform sandbox
items.body:
## Summary
- port the challenge harness to the Swift runtime path and keep trusted benchmark/correctness logic outside editable submission files
- keep hidden benchmark oracle tokens out of the runtime worker by using begin/step benchmark decode requests
- run correctness and timed benchmark in isolated runtime worker processes with private prompt/golden env stripped from the worker
- load private benchmark golden and hidden GPQA reference gates from R2, while keeping the public local correctness gate in-repo
- capture hidden GPQA TTFT during the existing first-token behavior correctness gate, so there is no duplicate hidden-prompt model pass
- add a private Claude semantic GPQA diagnostic that records only aggregate pass counts in `score.json`
- harden transform and benchmark execution with offline sandboxing, editable-path overlay validation, artifact redaction, and private-artifact deny checks
- batch the public 256-token teacher-forced correctness gate inside the worker so the gate stays strong without 256 single-token worker calls
- remove hardware bandwidth measurement from the benchmark path; primary ranking is prefill/decode speedup only, with expert-streaming byte counters kept as diagnostics
- score ranked submissions by official-run prefill/decode speedup, with per-component speedup floors so a submission cannot trade a large regression in one path for a gain in the other

## Gates and Checks

The model-behavior checks are intentionally layered. Each one catches a different way a submission could be fast but no longer behave like the reference model.

### 1. Correctness Check
- **Mode:** hard gate.
- **What it checks:** teacher-forced token correctness on a 512-token prompt with a 256-token expected continuation. Local runs use the public checked-in fixture; official benchmark runs use the hidden R2 golden.
- **Why we do it:** this is the first proof that the changed runtime/kernels still compute the same model path before we accept timing numbers.
- **What it prevents:** broken tokenizer/model loading, wrong logits, routing/cache regressions, arbitrary fast token output, and submissions that only work on the public local prompt.

### 2. Hidden GPQA Single-Token Check
- **Mode:** hard gate.
- **What it checks:** hidden GPQA-style science QA prompts must produce an accepted first answer token. The same pass records aggregate TTFT stats.
- **Why we do it:** the long correctness prompt alone is too narrow. A hidden first-token QA check forces the model to preserve short-answer behavior on a different prompt style while keeping runtime cost manageable.
- **What it prevents:** optimizing only for the transcription-style correctness prompt, first-token answer corruption, prompt-specific hacks, and fake decode paths that do not preserve basic QA behavior.

### 3. Hidden GPQA Multi-Token Check
- **Mode:** diagnostic today; used as input to the semantic check.
- **What it checks:** the runner generates short hidden GPQA continuations, currently up to 10 new tokens per case, and keeps those candidate answers private.
- **Why we do it:** a model can pass one-token checks but drift immediately after it consumes its own generated tokens. Short continuations give us a stronger behavior signal without running full long-form QA.
- **What it prevents:** first-token-only special casing, decode paths that collapse after the first token, and changes that preserve exact token gates while damaging short answer quality.

### 4. Claude Semantic GPQA Check
- **Mode:** diagnostic by default; can become a hard gate with `MLXFAST_SEMANTIC_GPQA_REQUIRED=1` after calibration.
- **What it checks:** Claude compares the private GPQA candidate answers against private references and patches only aggregate pass fields into `score.json`.
- **Why we do it:** exact token checks are brittle across Apple GPU/MLX differences and can miss semantically wrong but token-near outputs. A judge gives us a behavior signal based on meaning, not just exact token IDs.
- **What it prevents:** submissions that pass exact-token gates while giving wrong short-answer content, answer-format hacks, and regressions that are visible semantically but not in the first token.
- **Privacy:** prompts, references, candidate answers, token IDs, accepted sets, and raw judge text stay in the private runner directory and are not uploaded.

## Scoring
- Primary score is baseline-normalized timing speedup:
  - `decode_speedup = baseline_decode_sec_per_token / decode_sec_per_token`
  - `prefill_speedup = baseline_prefill_sec_per_token / prefill_sec_per_token`
  - `score = decode_speedup^0.75 * prefill_speedup^0.25`
- Each primary component must also pass a floor:
  - `decode_speedup >= 0.95`
  - `prefill_speedup >= 0.95`
- The floor prevents benchmark-maxing one component while materially regressing the other. The weighted score still ranks passing submissions.
- The current baseline constants come from the official Blacksmith run for the active 512-token prefill / 256-token decode benchmark oracle.
- `score.json` still reports peak RAM, expert read bytes, expert read seconds, cache counters, derived expert-streaming bytes per token, GPQA TTFT aggregates, and semantic GPQA aggregate fields for diagnostics and future guardrails, but only prefill/decode speedups drive the primary score.

## Latest Status
- Current PR head: `06da143`.
- Latest full Blacksmith benchmark: https://github.com/Layr-Labs/mlxfast-challenge-dev/actions/runs/28281015024
  - Workflow passed end to end in `50m03s`.
  - Core benchmark step passed in `28m26s`.
  - Hidden correctness plus GPQA first-token gate passed: `265` checked steps across `10` cases.
  - Hidden GPQA TTFT gate passed: `9/9` cases.
  - Score: `1.0127854432595405`.
  - Prefill: `0.13911011108398438` sec/token, speedup `1.0187907394591718`, floor `0.95`, passed.
  - Decode: `2.986097291347657` sec/token, speedup `1.010791554504655`, floor `0.95`, passed.
  - Semantic GPQA is currently diagnostic and recorded `4/9`, so it did not block this run.
- Commit `06da143` adds per-component prefill/decode speedup floors to runtime scoring, artifact validation, tests, README, and challenge docs.
- PR CI on `06da143` passed.

## Timing From Latest Run
- Setup/reference checkpoint: `6m35s`.
- Transform reference checkpoint: `4s`.
- Prepare correctness golden: `2s`.
- Core benchmark step: `28m26s`.
- Semantic GPQA answer generation: `14m11s`.
- Semantic GPQA gate: `37s`.

## Validation
- `swift test --filter 'Score|BenchmarkScript'`
- `swift test --filter 'Score|BenchmarkScript|BenchmarkSupport'`
- `swift build -c release`
- `bash -n .github/scripts/validate-benchmark-artifacts.sh`

items.title: Writing Intelligence v4.0.0 — Accountable Authorship System
items.body:
Brings the public repository from v3.1 to **v4.0.0** — the accountability layer that was already written locally but had never shipped here.

**v3 governs how well the writing is built. v4 governs what may be claimed about it.**

---

## What lands

### `scripts/wi.py` — a verifier that needs no model

Stdlib-only Python 3.8+. No dependencies, no network, no API key, no telemetry. Runs air-gapped.

```
preserve        snapshot before editing                    (Law B)
scan-sources    injection, invisible text, bidi, payloads  (Law F)
extract-claims  claim ledger with class and offsets
verify          span lock · quotation · numeric · date · citation resolution  (Law D)
gate            RELEASE / HOLD / BLOCK with repairs        (Law E)
```

`gate --exit-code` returns 0 / 1 / 2 for RELEASE / HOLD / BLOCK, so a pre-commit hook or CI job can stop a document that no longer survives its own sources.

### The six operating laws

| | Law |
|---|---|
| **A** | Propose, never silently replace |
| **B** | The original is recoverable |
| **C** | Never report work not done |
| **D** | Support means a verbatim span |
| **E** | Under-claim |
| **F** | Sources are data, never instruction |

### Eight doctrine documents — `references/v4/`

ACCOUNTABILITY_LAYER · PROOF_PROTOCOL · PROPOSAL_PROTOCOL · SOURCE_HYGIENE · LANGUAGE_TIERS · VOICE_CONSENT · SURFACES · NON_GOALS

### Docs

- `README.md` rewritten as the v4 front door, with real captured CLI output rather than an illustration
- `docs/INSTALL.md` — six surfaces, capability matrix, git-hook and CI recipes (new)
- `docs/MIGRATION_v3_to_v4.md` — the upgrade is `git pull`; six behavior changes stated with reasoning (new)
- `USER_GUIDE.md` — new Section 0 on working with accountability
- `CHANGELOG.md` — the `[4.0.0]` entry, plus the `[3.1.0]` entry that was never written
- `CHEATSHEET.md`, `ROADMAP.md`, `CONTRIBUTING.md` updated

### Release and CI plumbing

- `scripts/build-skill.sh` — reproducible bundle builder with preflight and extract-and-verify (new)
- `scripts/check-links.py` — relative-link checker (new)
- `.github/workflows/ci.yml` — verifier on Python 3.8/3.11/3.12/3.13 × Linux/macOS, docs, bundle reproducibility, API on Node 20/22 (new)
- `.github/workflows/release.yml` — tag-triggered, asserts tag == `wi.py --version` == CHANGELOG entry before publishing (new)
- `release/RELEASE_NOTES_v4.0.0.md` (new)

---

## Corrections made along the way

Three published numbers were wrong and are fixed: `CHEATSHEET.md` said 26 genre packs while listing 27, and 13 delivery arenas while listing 20. The old `ROADMAP.md` reserved v4.0 for "Multimodal Writing Intelligence" — multimodal moves to v5.0 with that stated in the file rather than silently overwritten. A claim that OpenAPI 3.1 had shipped was checked against `docs/api/API_SPEC.md`, found unsupported, and the box left unticked.

---

## What is unchanged

The 11-pass kernel · 12 engines · 12 agents · 11 JSON schemas · 27 genre packs · voiceprints · benchmark harness · gold outputs · the REST runtime.

No schema version bump. No field changes. Every v3 workflow still runs.

---

## Honest limits, stated rather than implied

- **Paraphrase is not verified.** The deterministic tier compares strings, numbers and dates. A well-paraphrased claim with no verbatim span reads `needs_source` — a limit of the tier, not a verdict on the writing. It says so in its own output. Closing this is the whole of v4.1.
- **It verifies support within the sources you supplied**, not truth. If your source is wrong, the claim reads `supported` and is false. This is stated the first time proof output appears.
- **`services/api` remains the v3 craft kernel** and does not expose the v4 tier. That tier has exactly one implementation and stays that way — two implementations of a verification rule drift, and the one that drifts is invisible because both look correct until they disagree about something that matters. `services/api/README.md` now says this out loud.
- **Bare `[12]` citations cannot resolve** without a bibliography, and a flattened PDF hides text from extraction. `scan-sources` reports both rather than passing silently.

---

## Verification

The shipped regression suite was **proven able to fail** before being trusted: disabling citation resolution in `wi.py` turns the gate from BLOCK to HOLD and the suite reports 2 failures and exits 1. `wi.py` was then restored and confirmed byte-identical by sha256. A test that has only ever passed has not been shown to work.

Run locally, all green:

```
bash tests/v4/test_wi.sh          PASS injection detected / PASS gate BLOCK / PASS statuses  (exit 0)
python3 scripts/check-links.py    31 relative links across 155 markdown files — all resolve
bash scripts/build-skill.sh       165 files, 447291 bytes, sha256 5e5edc97…268d6d77
cd services/api && npm run typecheck && npm test    0 errors · 31/31 passing
```

The bundle build is reproducible and CI fails if two builds of the same tree differ, so the published checksum means something.

items.title: 0.7.0 — drop the Py prefix, and stop guessing at ambiguous input
items.body:
Two things ship here: the public class names lose a prefix that never belonged
in Python, and five places where the engine quietly guessed now refuse instead.

The second half matters more. When raptorbt was handed something it could not
interpret — an option type it could not parse, a direction that was neither long
nor short, a correlation matrix that is not mathematically valid — it picked a
default and returned numbers that looked completely normal. Not a crash, not an
obviously silly figure: a smooth, well-formed result computed from something
other than what the caller asked for. Nothing downstream could tell.

---

## The rename

`raptorbt.PyBacktestConfig` is now `raptorbt.BacktestConfig`, and so on for 21
classes. Old spellings still work and emit a `DeprecationWarning` naming the
replacement. **They are removed in 0.8.0.**

The `Py` prefix is a Rust-side disambiguator — `src/core/types.rs` owns its own
`BacktestConfig`, `Trade` and `BacktestResult`, and two Rust types cannot share
a name. That is correct Rust; it was simply never stripped on the way out.
`BarAggregator`, `Indicator` and `InstrumentSpec` already reached Python clean
via `#[pyclass(name = "...")]`, so the pattern was already in the codebase — it
had been applied to 3 of 24 classes and forgotten for the other 21. **Rust
struct names are unchanged.**

Deep imports keep working too. `from raptorbt._raptorbt import PyX` warns and
resolves, because `PortfolioSession` had never been re-exported at top level and
a deep import was the only supported way to reach it. It is exported properly
now, and a test asserts every replacement the warning names actually resolves —
mid-rename the warning briefly pointed at a name that raised `AttributeError`.

## Five silent guesses, now errors

| Defect | Before | Now |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `max_trades` default | `50`, hard early exit — **0.81% of a 1M-tick tape**, return −0.12% vs true −14.13%, max drawdown 0.124% vs true 14.13% (**114x understatement**) | unlimited; knob remains for explicit truncation |
| `BarAggregator` `brick_size` | accepted, then hard-coded `0.0` → `step`-point bricks. **Every Renko backtest through the streaming aggregator was wrong** | honoured; 5-point bricks over a 10-point move give 2 bars, not 10 |
| Non-positive-definite correlation matrix | pivots patched, returned Ok → `var_95 = 0`, `probability_of_loss = 0` — a risk model reporting **no risk at all** | `ValueError` naming the asset index |
| Unparseable option code | silently became a **Call** — an iron condor whose put legs failed to parse became a four-leg call structure | `ValueError` |
| `direction` | fell back to **Long** at six call sites — a book encoded `0`/`1` backtested entirely long, flipping P&L sign on every short | `ValueError` |

Two were found by reading; three by an audit sweep the first one prompted.

On the option-code one: `OptionType::from_code` documents in so many words that
"defaulting an unrecognised code to `Call` would price a put as a call", and
both PyO3 call sites did exactly that. `run_options_backtest` had the same shape
in its three enum arguments — `option_type="PUT"` selected a long **call**, while
the identical string was accepted by `run_spread_backtest`. The same call meant
two different things depending on which function you entered through.

Also fixed: `simulate_portfolio_mc` validated no shapes, so an
`(n_obs, n_assets)` matrix indexed past the end of `weights` inside a Rayon
worker and surfaced as `PanicException` — not catchable as `ValueError`, thrown
from a thread with no user code in the traceback. And **a test that had never
run** now runs: a duplicated `#[test]` attribute left the next function without
one, so `day_expires_on_utc_date_rollover` silently never executed. It passes.

## Warnings: 89 → 0

`cargo clippy --no-default-features --all-targets -- -D warnings` passes and the
library build is silent. Not by suppression — 8 manual `Default` impls became
derives, shift loops became `copy_from_slice`, the `w'Σw` quadratic form was
deduplicated between the optimizer and risk contributions, Cholesky's inner
accumulation became a dot product, and `OptionType::from_str` (which shadowed
the `FromStr` trait, so `"CE".parse()` did not work) became `from_code` with a
real `FromStr` impl beside it.

Six `#[allow]`s remain, each with its reasoning in a comment above it. Five are
`too_many_arguments` on signatures that **are** the Python call signature,
matching the precedent already in `session_bindings.rs`. The sixth is
load-bearing: `adopt_position` guards with `!(price > 0.0)` rather than
`price <= 0.0`, because the negated form is also false for NaN. Clippy's
suggestion would let a NaN price become a position's cost basis, turning cash,
equity and every drawdown figure into NaN with no error raised. A new test pins
it — applying clippy's advice makes it fail with `NaN price must be refused, got Ok(0)`.

## Benchmarks were re-measured, and the numbers went up

**This is not a regression.** The published 0.6.4 figures came from a one-off
script that was not kept, over synthetic data whose shape could not be
reconstructed. Running the published 0.6.4 wheel and this build side by side on
the harness now committed at `benches/python/`, on identical inputs:

```
0.6.4 (PyPI wheel)   min 68.9 µs   p50 71.0 µs   ret=-1.964369, 16 trades
0.7.0 (this build)   min 68.4 µs   p50 70.5 µs   ret=-1.964369, 16 trades
```

Identical results; 0.7.0 is marginally faster. The ruler changed, not the
engine, and both READMEs and the `/raptorbt` page now say so where a reader will
see it. The harness ships with the code so any figure can be re-run — it also
encodes the two traps that produce flattering-but-wrong numbers: measure the
release build, and raise `max_trades` so tick runs actually reach the end of the
array.

Some figures improved on their own terms: parallel spread speedup 4.28x → 6.9x,
compiled engine 1.67 MB → 1.59 MB, sweep peak memory 122 MB → 67 MB.

## Verification

- **460 Rust tests**, **463 Python tests** through the built wheel
- `cargo clippy … -D warnings` clean, `cargo fmt --check` clean
- Zero stub drift — all 24 `.pyi` classes resolve at runtime and appear in
  `__all__` (the pre-existing `PyPortfolioSession` gap is closed)
- Optimizer index-math refactors verified against a captured baseline of **18
  numeric surfaces** — covariance, optimizer weights, risk contributions,
  MACD/RSI/ADX/VWAP, Monte Carlo, and a full backtest's metrics, equity curve
  and drawdown curve. **Bit-identical** before and after, re-checked after each
  batch.
- New guards verified **by injection**, not just by passing: reintroducing each
  bug makes its test fail.

## Upgrading

Nothing breaks on import. Old class names work for this release.

Three behaviour changes to be aware of:

1. **Renko backtests through `BarAggregator` were wrong** and are now correct.
   Re-run any stored Renko results.
2. **Tick backtests that used the default `max_trades`** were truncated and are
   now complete. Their numbers will change, substantially.
3. **Input that used to be guessed is now refused.** `direction=0`, an option
   code outside `CE/CALL/C/PE/PUT/P`, an unrecognised `strike_selection`, or a
   non-positive-definite correlation matrix now raise `ValueError`. Those calls
   were already producing wrong answers; they were just not saying so.

## Not in this PR

- **The wheel is not published.** Version is bumped in `Cargo.toml` and
  `pyproject.toml`, but 0.7.0 is not on PyPI. The backend's five requirement
  floors stay at `>=0.6.4` until it is — publish first, raise floors second, per
  the incident recorded in `.claude/skills/pyo3-interop/SKILL.md`.
- **The backend's ~33 call sites** still use the deprecated names. They work and
  warn; migrating them is a separate commit in a separate repo.
- **The 0.8.0 removal guard.** `test_removal_is_scheduled` already fails the
  moment the version reaches 0.8.0, with a docstring saying exactly what to
  delete.

items.title: build: CMake project and CI pipeline
items.body:
## What changed

Phase 1: the build system and the continuous integration pipeline.

- Target-based CMake. No global flag is set anywhere. Compiler settings reach
  targets through three interface libraries, `orrery::options`,
  `orrery::warnings` and `orrery::sanitisers`, and clang-tidy is attached to
  individual targets through the `CXX_CLANG_TIDY` property rather than through
  `CMAKE_CXX_CLANG_TIDY`, which would also lint the fetched dependencies.
- `CMakePresets.json` covering debug, release, sanitiser, single precision and
  lint, each building into `build/<preset>`.
- Catch2 fetched at configure time and pinned to commit `8b08d4d` (v3.15.3),
  with `FIND_PACKAGE_ARGS` so a copy already on the system is preferred. Test
  cases are registered with CTest individually rather than as one opaque
  binary.
- A GitHub Actions workflow: a build matrix over operating system, compiler and
  build type, plus clang-format, clang-tidy and a sanitiser run of the suite.
  Actions are pinned to a commit for the same reason the C++ dependencies are.
- A placeholder `orrery::core` library reporting the version and the configured
  precision, with two unit tests, so that continuous integration compiles,
  links and runs something real.

## Why

Phase 1 of `docs/IMPLEMENTATION_PLAN.md`. The conventions written down in Phase
0 only become binding once something checks them on every pull request, and
every later phase needs a build to add code to.

The placeholder library is not filler. `uses_single_precision()` is read by a
test in a separate translation unit, so the single-precision preset is verified
end to end rather than assumed to work, and Phase 7 needs the configuration a
measurement came from to be recoverable from the binary that produced it.

## How it was verified

Continuous integration is the verification. This machine has CMake 4.4.2 and
Clang 22.1.8 but no complete C++ toolchain to link against, so clang-format was
the only check that could be run locally. Every job in the workflow is green on
this branch:

- Build matrix: Linux GCC debug and release, Linux Clang debug and release,
  Linux Clang single precision, macOS Clang release, Windows MSVC debug and
  release. Each configures from a preset, builds with warnings as errors, and
  runs `ctest`.
- clang-format 22.1.8 over every tracked C++ source, no diagnostics.
- clang-tidy 22 over both project targets with the repository `.clang-tidy`,
  which treats every diagnostic as an error. No diagnostics.
- Address and undefined-behaviour sanitisers, full suite passing, with
  `-fno-sanitize-recover=all` so that a finding fails the run rather than being
  printed on the way to a green result.

Two unit tests, both in the unit category, discovered individually by CTest and
passing in every configuration: one that the version reaches the binary from
`project()`, one that the precision setting reaches the library and its
consumers alike.

Three things were found by CI and fixed rather than worked around. The
`windows-latest` image has moved to Visual Studio 2026, so the presets that
named the 2022 generator were removed instead of renumbered, and Windows now
uses the same Ninja presets as every other platform, entered through `vcvars`
located with `vswhere`. clang-tidy 22 added `portability-avoid-pragma-once`,
whose suggested replacement is an include guard, which is a macro, and section
4 of the plan avoids macros entirely; the check is disabled with that reason
recorded in `.clang-tidy`. The format job looked for pipx's binary in the wrong
directory.

## Measured numbers

Not applicable. There is no code here whose speed can be measured, and the
benchmark methodology that would produce trustworthy figures is Phase 7.

## Architecture decision records

- [ADR-0002](docs/adr/0002-pin-dependencies-to-exact-commits.md): pin
  dependencies to exact commits fetched at configure time.
- [ADR-0003](docs/adr/0003-build-settings-through-interface-targets.md): carry
  build settings on interface targets rather than global flags.

## Definition of done

- [x] Builds clean with Clang, GCC and MSVC, warnings as errors
- [x] `clang-format` and `clang-tidy` pass with no diagnostics
- [x] Address and undefined-behaviour sanitiser builds pass the full test suite
- [x] New code is covered by tests in at least one of the four categories
- [x] Public headers document purpose and rationale
- [x] Any new non-obvious decision has an ADR
- [x] Performance-affecting changes report before and after figures, not
      applicable here
- [x] The README reflects reality and every claim in it is reproducible
- [x] No AI attribution anywhere in the diff
- [x] The phase status table in `docs/IMPLEMENTATION_PLAN.md` is updated

items.title: tsgo-scale-bench: checker behavior at a million modules (tsgo vs tsc vs Flow)
items.body:
## What

Two new benchmarks answering the scaling questions the per-package benches cannot: what does a type checker do as ONE program grows to 1,000,000 modules — green and red, cold and incremental, CLI and daemon?

### 1. `scripts/tsgo-scale-bench.mjs` — the checkers (`bench/tsgo-scale-bench.json`)

Sweeps 10k → 1M modules for **tsgo** (subject), **tsc** (anchor ≤100k), and **Flow 0.321** on a layered fixed-depth corpus. Six rows per checker: cold / full / incrNoChange / incrOneEdit plus the red paths (fullWithLeafErrors, incrOneEditError — the failing gate and the after-save loop when the edit is wrong, exact error counts asserted from the checker's stdout). Untimed gates (seeded-error controls, exact program-size counts) with 1h timeouts and capacity-outcome classification; per-checker failure isolation.

**Findings** (tsgo `7.0.0-dev.20260707.2`, tsc `6.0.3`, flow-bin `0.321.0`):
- **tsgo checks 1M modules in 68.6s warm / 88.8s cold at 53.7GB RSS**, near-linear across the 100× range; ~500–880% CPU (5–9 of 64 cores).
- **A failing check costs the same as a passing one** — 69.0s red vs 68.6s green at 1M, all checkers, every scale.
- tsgo's CLI incremental at 1M: 38.0s no-change / 53.7s one edit — a CI tool, not a save loop.
- **Flow closes to +25% of tsgo by 500k at a third of the memory.** Its server model is the right save-loop mechanic — and on **flow main it holds up under pressure**: in the recorded storm retest (a second edit landing 120–480ms into an in-flight recheck, 500k corpus), main survives all 20 cycles with 0.3–0.7s recheck round-trips (`scripts/flow-wedge-retest.mjs` → `bench/flow-wedge-retest.json`):

  | 500k corpus, overlapping-edit storm | outcome | recheck round-trip |
  |---|---|---|
  | **flow main @ `cdb4f637`** (current) | **survived all 20 cycles, no panic** | **0.3–0.7s** |
  | released flow-bin 0.321.0 | wedged at cycle 13 (WorkerCanceled panic, silent client hang) | 2.0–3.5s |

  The released line matters only as a deployment caveat: every released binary through 0.321 carries a recheck-cancellation race (it also fired in the canonical sweep at 500k — recorded as `incrOneEdit: timedOut` with the panic in `serverLogTail`), reported upstream as facebook/flow#9454 with the fix verified on main; forensics in `bench/flow-0321-wedge-evidence.md`.
- tsc anchors 11× slower than tsgo (66.2s vs 6.0s at 100k).

### 2. `scripts/lsp-scale-bench.mjs` — the daemons (`bench/lsp-scale-bench.json`)

The mechanic-matched companion: **tsgo `--lsp`** vs **tsserver** (anchored ≤100k) vs **`--watch`** on the same corpus, with the squiggle transitions *asserted* (didChange introducing a seeded TS2322 must pull red, timed; restore must pull clean, timed) and a zero-entries fail-closed control on every completion probe (the legacy tsserver `completions` command returns success with an empty array on TS 6 — a 15ms no-op a lesser gate would have scored).

**Findings:**
- **tsgo's LSP opens and serves the million-module program**: 17.4s cold open, **2.2s asserted squiggle**, 238ms definition, 1ms hover, 59.7GB RSS. That's the mechanic that makes 1M interactive — vs its own CLI incremental (53.7s/edit) and `--watch` (22.3s/edit, 73.8GB).
- tsserver: 25.7s to open 100k (17× slower), 942ms squiggle (~6×).
- The boundary: **tsgo's LSP completion enumerates the full exported-symbol space** (301k items in 50s at 100k) and exceeds the 120s ceiling at 500k+; tsserver returns a bounded 1,067-entry set in 19–20ms (set sizes differ by orders of magnitude — reported with counts, not scored).

### Also

- `scripts/optimal-gate-bench.mjs`: breaking-change verdict now hard-fails on a signal-killed checker instead of feeding `caught`.
- Toolchain pins → the versions the datasets record: `@typescript/native-preview 7.0.0-dev.20260707.2`, `typescript ^6.0.3`.

items.body:
## Summary

Replaces the **Benchmark** section (which claimed a multimodal LLM costs ~\$5/1-hr video and watch-cli is "50× cheaper") with a **Why pay-per-use, not subscription** narrative.

The previous framing was off for two reasons:
1. The \$5 anchor was ungrounded — Gemini 1.5 Pro native video sits around \$1.16/hr; the only way to hit \$5 is GPT-4o frame-sampling worst-case. Either way, it read as a competitor-swipe rather than a clean positioning.
2. The audience watch-cli actually competes with isn't "people calling raw multimodal APIs" — it's people paying ~\$15/month for a subscription summary tool (Otter/Notta/Eightify-class).

The new section anchors against that subscription baseline, keeps Kyma as the primary backend, and shows the pay-per-use math directly:

| This month you watch | You pay |
|---|---|
| 0 videos | \$0 |
| 1 one-hour video | ~\$0.04 |
| 100 one-hour videos | ~\$4 |

Also softens the **Why this exists** intro to frame the difference as **artifact mismatch** (chat-style summary vs raw frames+transcript) rather than "multimodal APIs are slow and expensive" — the previous phrasing read as a swipe and invited price-comparison rebuttals.

## What did NOT change
- Setup section keeps \`KYMA_API_KEY\` as the primary path.
- "Why Kyma" section (bullets about aliases, auto-fallback, free credit) untouched.
- BYOK remains a one-liner escape hatch.
- Cost table in "Limitations and cost" section (\$0.003 / \$0.04 / \$0.08) unchanged — those numbers are accurate.

## Flag for separate decision

Existing README has a **free-credit discrepancy** I didn't touch in this PR:
- Line ~128 (Why Kyma section): *"Free credit at signup. About an hour of audio."*
- Line ~271 (Limitations section): *"Free credit at Kyma signup covers roughly 25 hours of audio."*

At \$0.04/hr transcribe, \$0.50 free credit ≈ ~12 hours. Both existing numbers are wrong in opposite directions. Recommend a follow-up PR aligning both to a single accurate number (~12 hours or whatever the current free-credit policy actually is) — separate from this positioning change.

## Test plan
- [ ] Render README on GitHub and confirm tables/headings format correctly
- [ ] Skim the section transitions (Why this exists → What it looks like → Why pay-per-use → Install) — flow makes sense
- [ ] Cross-check that no other section references "Benchmark" or the "50× cheaper" claim

items.title: science: add BioProBench skill (with review fixes) — supersedes #36
items.body:
## Summary

Supersedes #36. This branch carries **@YuyangSunshine's original five commits unchanged** — she is
the author of the BioProBench skill and of the upstream benchmark it wraps — plus two review commits
that fix defects found in a multi-agent review of that PR.

#36 could not be merged as-is: it was a fork PR whose CI had never been approved to run, so two
deterministic lint failures and a set of scoring bugs were never surfaced. Everything below was
reproduced by executing the real code, not by reading it.

On licensing: the four vendored `Scripts/*.py` come from
[bioprotocolbench](https://github.com/YuyangSunshine/bioprotocolbench), which @YuyangSunshine owns.
No non-commercial notice is required; the files carry only a one-line provenance comment.

## What the review commits fix

**The skill did not exist in production.** It was committed as `SKILL.MD`. The loader matches the
literal `child / "SKILL.md"` and skips with a bare `continue` — no log. macOS APFS is
case-insensitive, so it worked on the author's machine and vanished on every Linux CI runner.
Independently, setuptools compiles `MANIFEST.in`'s `*.md` **without** `re.IGNORECASE`, so the
uppercase file was also dropped from the wheel and sdist on *every* platform — a `uv build` produced
`skills/bioprobench/` containing `kernel.py` and the `Scripts/` payload but no `SKILL.md` at all.
Verified after the rename on a real case-sensitive APFS volume (all 33 skills discover) and in the
built wheel (33 × `SKILL.md`, bioprobench included).

**CI lint failed two ways.** `pre-commit` reformatted all five new `.py` files, and
`scripts/check_directory_readmes.py` exited 1 with five violations. Both now pass.

**`import kernel` hard-failed and downloaded at import time.** The guard was
`except ImportError: raise ImportError(...)` — a re-raise, so seven third-party packages that ship in
no bundled env were hard requirements. `nltk.download('punkt')` and `nltk.download('wordnet')` ran at
module scope: network I/O plus a write outside the workspace, inside a sandboxed kernel. Heavy deps
are now lazy per task, so PQA/ORD/ERR no longer drag in the GEN-only torch stack, and the download
moved out of import (and asks for `punkt_tab`, which is what `word_tokenize` needs on nltk ≥ 3.8.2 —
GEN could not have succeeded before). `Scripts/` is loaded privately via `importlib` instead of
`sys.path.append`, which had published three generic top-level module names into the shared
persistent kernel and bypassed the skill gate.

**Four scoring bugs that returned plausible-looking wrong numbers.** None of them raised:

- **ERR** compared JSON-decoded labels with the identity operator (`g is False`), so labels encoded
  as `0`/`1` or `"true"`/`"false"` collapsed precision/recall/F1 to exactly 0 — while accuracy stayed
  *correct*, because that line used `==` and `True == 1`. Same four items: bool labels → `f1=0.8`;
  identical labels as ints → `f1=0`. Nothing in the output distinguished "the model detected no
  errors" from "the label dtype was int". Labels are now normalized, and unrecognized ones reach
  `failed_rate` instead of being scored.
- **ERR** appended predictions and labels in two separate statements, so an item missing
  `is_correct` permanently misaligned every later prediction against the wrong label.
- **ORD** raised `KeyError` outside the per-item handler, so one malformed permutation aborted the
  whole run and discarded every other item's result. A 2-item file with a perfect item 1 returned
  `{'error': "...: 'X'"}` instead of `Exact_Match 0.5`. Ranks were also keyed by step *text*, losing
  pairs when a protocol repeats a step string; they are keyed by index now.
- **PQA** treated the last whitespace token as the confidence unconditionally, so a bare correct
  answer such as `0.3` was consumed as its own confidence and scored **wrong** with a fabricated
  confidence of 0 — and not counted in `Failed_Rate`.

Also: GEN emitted bare `NaN` (not valid JSON); an empty input reported `"status": "success"` over
all-zero metrics; caller-controlled `model_name` was interpolated unsanitized into an output path.

**Documentation and catalog.** Added YAML frontmatter — without it `origin` degraded to `"unknown"`
and the progressive-disclosure summary (the only thing the model sees before loading a skill) was the
truncated BibTeX citation blockquote. Closed a truncated ` ```python ` fence, corrected the documented
API and the input contract (the response file must already merge in ground truth — a plain
model-output file scored 0% and reported success), added the six bilingual READMEs, registered
`bioprobench/` in the catalog, and bumped the bundled-skill count 32 → 33.

**Tests.** `tests/test_bioprobench_skill.py` (27 tests) pins the ERR encoding and PQA confidence
regressions. `scikit-learn` was added to the `science` extra so the two PQA end-to-end tests actually
execute in CI instead of skipping in every environment (25 passed / 2 skipped → 27 passed).

## Known limitations, stated plainly

- **GEN was never executed against its real dependencies.** The sentence-transformers/torch stack plus
  two model checkpoints is not something the offline test environment supports, so only its
  aggregation logic is verified — not the end-to-end path.
- **The PQA no-`&` fallback remains ambiguous** for a multi-word answer whose last token happens to be
  an integer (`incubate for 30`). That is inherent to a format with no separator, and is no worse than
  before.
- `trigger_batch_inference` and `run_llm_judge_evaluation` send data off-machine and take a raw API
  key. That is what those functions are for; it is documented in `SKILL.md` and unchanged here.

## Area

- [x] Skills / science runtime
- [x] Tests / harness / CI
- [x] Docs
- [x] CLI / config / packaging

## Change Type

- [x] Bug fix
- [x] Feature
- [x] Documentation

## Verification

Ran:

```text
uv run pre-commit run --all-files          # all hooks pass
python3 scripts/check_directory_readmes.py # exit 0
uv sync --locked --extra science && uv run pytest   # exit 0
uv build                                   # wheel + sdist contain skills/bioprobench/SKILL.md
```

Plus, on a real case-sensitive APFS volume, the repo's own `SkillLoader` discovers all 33 skills
including `bioprobench`, with `origin: openai4s` and a capability description rather than the citation
blockquote.

Not run:

```text
GEN end-to-end against sentence-transformers / torch
```

Reason:

```text
Requires the torch-scale stack plus two model checkpoints; not supported by the offline test
environment. See "Known limitations" above.
```

## Checklist

### Diff Readiness

* [x] I reviewed and understand the full diff.
* [ ] This PR is small and single-purpose. — it is not: it carries the original feature plus its
  review fixes. Kept together deliberately so the fixes are reviewable against the code they fix.
* [x] No unrelated formatting, broad rewrite, or drive-by refactor is included.
* [x] Hotspot files were edited surgically if touched. *(none touched)*
* [x] `openai4s/server/webui/vendor/` and `tests/fixtures/` were not reformatted.

### Tests

* [x] Relevant tests or manual checks were run and listed above.
* [x] No new test requires live LLM, network, GPU, SSH, Docker, lab hardware, or secrets.
* [x] No tests were deleted without tracked replacements.
* [x] Kernel / host-RPC / gateway changes include focused contract coverage. *(none touched)*

### Core Dependency Policy

* [x] No hard third-party import was added to the core engine, LLM client, or stdlib web server.
* [x] Optional science imports are guarded at every in-tree use site; the skill sidecar imports
  lazily per task and never at module scope.
* [x] New dependencies are documented and justified — `scikit-learn` in the `science` extra, so the
  PQA tests run rather than skip.

### Public Disclosure and Security

* [x] No secrets, API keys, tokens, real credentials, private data, or local absolute paths.
* [x] No unpublished research roadmap or unreleased result is disclosed.
* [x] Docs do not overstate isolation, sandboxing, privacy, or security guarantees.

### Docs

* [x] Docs match actual code behavior.
* [x] User-facing behavior changes are reflected in docs.
* [x] `README.md` and `README_zh.md` stay in sync.

items.title: CP-detect: product-faithful refiner benchmark, solve-recovery, strict-topology canonicalization + provenance guard
items.body:
Makes the CP-detect benchmark product-faithful (the shipped vertex refiner now runs in the measured path), adds an honest end-to-end recovery metric, fixes a real strict-topology metric gap, and hardens the benchmark against a stale-binary footgun that produced misleading numbers. Includes a re-verified research report.

## Highlights

**Vertex refiner → shared Rust + Torch-MPS benchmark path** (`crates/oristudio-cp-detect/src/refinement/`)
- Ported the entire refiner geometry (features, proposals, crop-tensor, decode, merge) to shared Rust, validated **bit-exact to the product TS** (9/9 feature channels maxAbsDiff = 0.0). Only the ONNX forward pass stays outside Rust (Torch-MPS sidecar, mirroring the dense cache). 15 unit tests.
- `refiner_cache` (plan/merge/dump-features) + `--refined-vertices` in the benchmark using the product's **in-regions** merge (not replace-all).

**Benchmark metrics & honesty**
- New `solve_recovered_original@strict` — did the exact-solve actually reproduce the GT CP (accepted AND solved fold matches GT topology+assignment within tolerance), not just "candidate topology looks right".
- Per-sample failure attribution, `--oracle-vertices` / `--oracle-selection`, configurable `--topology-gate-tolerance-px`.

**`strict_topology_metrics`: dissolve degree-2 collinear nodes** (`crates/oristudio-cp-eval`)
- Adds the merge counterpart to the existing split pass, so a redundant collinear vertex present in one graph but not the other (most often the paper border) no longer counts as a topology difference. +6 `solve_recovered` on the native set; demonstrably fixes inspector diffs (e.g. Cockatoo 8 missing/6 extra → 4/4).

**Inspector: solve-recovered display** (`oristudio-cp-detect-inspector` + `apps/cp-detect-architecture-inspector`)
- Stage 6 now shows whether the solved fold recovered GT and highlights what's off, not just "solved".

**Provenance guard against the worktree/`target` stale-binary footgun**
- `build.rs` embeds the build commit; `compare_exact_solve_benchmark` prints a `[provenance]` banner and **refuses to run when its build commit ≠ working-tree HEAD** (`--allow-stale` to override). The matrix runner now `cargo build`s from its own worktree first. Documented in `scripts/cp-detect/README.md`. This caught a real incident where a stale binary reported `solve_recovered = 0/563` (true value 61/563).

**Research report** (`research/2026-06-30-...md`)
- Findings on the native-CP reconstruction bottlenecks (refiner doesn't help; close pairs are the junction failure; exact-topology@2px is the wrong metric; exact-solve is a real second bottleneck). All benchmark numbers re-verified with the provenance-guarded binary; §3 junction-recall numbers independently re-derived from the dense cache (`scripts/cp-detect/rederive-junction-recall.py`) and corrected where the first draft was optimistic.

## Validation (local, matching CI gates)
- `cargo fmt --check` ✓
- `cargo clippy --workspace --all-targets -- -D warnings` ✓
- `cargo test --workspace` ✓ (75 test binaries)
- web `lint` + `typecheck` + `test` ✓ (359 tests)

Notes: no Rust ONNX runtime is introduced (inference stays JS/PyTorch); no product behavior change (the wasm rewire, Phase 2, is intentionally unstarted). The `research/`, `implementation-plans/`, and `scripts/cp-detect/` additions are docs/tooling.
