items.title: benchmark: one honest snapshot for every perf claim; fix the apparent slowdown
items.body:
## What this fixes

Four reported problems, all the same underlying knot:

- **(a)** The website's benchmark numbers were wrong/inconsistent.
- **(b)** The GitHub README didn't use the benchmark results.
- **(c)** mdsmith looked *much* slower despite real optimization work.
- **(d)** The headline "checks 523 Markdown files in about **0.2 s** … **10x** faster than Node" wasn't true.

The repo was publishing **three different numbers** for the same thing: the README headline (`0.2 s / 10x`, from a quiet committed snapshot), the feature pages (`1.3 s / 4x`, hardcoded), and the live website (`0.5 s / 9x`, republished from each per-merge CI run).

## Root cause — it's not a regression

The benchmark "repo corpus" is the project's own `git ls-files`, which grew **523 → 722 files**, but `gen_fragments.py` **hardcoded the string "523 files."** A linter checking more files takes longer, so mdsmith's absolute time crept up with no engine change.

The tell: **mado** (a fixed-version, check-only binary) went 40 ms → 57 ms — **1.4x, almost exactly the 1.38x file growth**. When the fixed tool scales with the file count, the shared cause is the file count, not slower code. Shared `ubuntu-latest` contention (non-uniform per tool) and the website pulling each single noisy CI run did the rest.

mdsmith's robust comparison held: **~10x faster than Node** in every run.

## What changed

- **One honest, reproducible snapshot** (~0.5 s repo corpus, ~9x vs Node) is the committed source of truth; all fragments regenerate from it.
- **Dynamic file count** (`data/corpus_sizes.json`, written by `bench.go`, read by `gen_fragments.py`) — never a hardcoded literal again.
- **Pinned neutral corpus** — fixed upstream commits of the Rust Book + Reference, so its content is reproducible run to run.
- **Every published claim sourced from the benchmark** — removed `4x` / `0.2 s` / `1.3 s`; README / CLAUDE.md / AGENTS.md / copilot-instructions regenerate consistently.
- **Website decoupled from live CI numbers** — `pull-site-assets` fetches only the demo GIF; the committed snapshot is the source and the per-merge CI run is a record-only drift signal.
- **Methodology documented** — a new section explains why absolute numbers move and why the per-run *ratio* is the stable signal ("same code → same factor").

## Verification

- `go build ./...`, `go vet ./...`, `go test ./...` — all pass
- `golangci-lint` — 0 issues
- `mdsmith check .` — **failures=0** (422 files)
- `bench-fragments` idempotency — fixpoint reached (gate green)

Built by three parallel agent teams (benchmark harness/data, published prose, website wiring) with a final integration pass.

items.title: fix(ct-eval): re-land the four construct-validity fixes stranded on PR #2590

labels.name: risk:high
labels.description: Review-advisory risk tier (max of declared and path heuristic)

items.body:
Risk tier: medium

## What & why

Re-implement, fresh against the restored tree, the four Control Tower measurement-validity fixes stranded on PR #2590 (79 commits / 114 files, un-rebasable after the rollback rewrote its base) — plus a paydown of the dangling-path baseline entries that hid a stale reference. Until these land, the eval can publish numbers where it measured nothing, which is why CT's prior results have no restorable baseline. Closes the salvage of #2590; that PR is closed with a pointer here.

## Partitions

One commit per partition, riskiest first:

- **Engagement witness** (`4d198462`, behavior change: `sbx_sandbox.py`, `run_sbx_real.py`, `config/trace-events.json`, `visualize.py`): a guarded cell whose monitor/audit sink silently never started rendered 0.000 — indistinguishable from perfect containment. Every guarded boot now turns on the host trace channel to a per-boot sink outside the agent-writable workspace, records at READY which layers announced themselves (`ct_guarded_arm` manifest: `audit_sink_started`, `monitor_started`), and a post-eval gate raises `UnmeasuredCell` (new `unmeasured` failure kind, rendered as a failed cell, never a rate) on silence or partial engagement.
- **Typed failure taxonomy** (`2705b1a2`, behavior change: `run_sbx_real.py`): the prefix-matching `_classify_failure` defaulted every unrecognized exception to `staging-failed` ("nothing ran, nothing was spent") — including post-eval gate failures on fully-paid trajectories. Failures are now typed (`CellFailure` subclasses naming their own bucket) with a structural default keyed on whether `inspect_eval` was reached (`unclassified-post-eval` vs `staging-failed`).
- **Universal rootfs boot** (`13b8a462`, behavior change: `run_sbx_real.py`, `ct_env.py`): the `is_base_bound` gate booted only some guarded envs from CT's own image, so ΔU confounded the guard's cost with reconstruction fidelity (a kit-base replay swaps /usr-level interpreters). Every guarded cell now boots CT's image as the rootfs, records `env_rootfs_image` provenance in the witness (with explicit `bare:`/`unknown:` sentinels), and a rootfs build failure fails the cell with no fallback.
- **Published deltas** (`13b8a462`: `visualize.py` + `test_visualize_deltas.py`): the artifact page showed two bare rates; it now publishes ΔS/ΔU as point estimates with 95% Newcombe intervals from `deltas.py`, with measured-not-dispatched denominators.
- **Staleness fix + baseline paydown** (`3e6ad685`, mechanical: `test_ct_env.py`, `ct_provision_general.sh`, `GUARDED_ARM_DESIGN.md`, baseline): reworded the stale `ct_provision.sh` docstring reference, repointed `sbx-rootfs.bash` → `sbx-template.bash`, annotated every deliberately-dangling reference (runtime-generated `setup.sh`, benchmark-pulled `compose.yml`/`restart.sh`, deleted probe workflows) with `# allow-dangling-path:` + reason. Baseline shrinks by 15 slots: `test_ct_env.py` 8→0, `ct_provision_general.sh` 6→0, `GUARDED_ARM_DESIGN.md` 1→0.

## Review focus

`_require_guardrails_engaged` in `run_sbx_real.py` and the trace-sink wiring in `SbxSession.boot` — the invariant spanning them: the engagement evidence is read at READY from a sink outside the bind-mounted workspace, so nothing the agent does can forge or pollute it, and instrument silence can only ever make a cell RED (unmeasured), never quietly zero. Least sure of: the two-event `ct_guarded_arm` manifest (see Decisions made) — whether both host-side layers are the right required set for every guarded arm shape.

## How it was tested

- Full CT tree: `uv run pytest tests/eval/control_tower/ -q` — 1012 passed, 75 skipped (was 998 before this branch's tests).
- Non-vacuity, taxonomy: old `_classify_failure(RuntimeError("a brand-new post-eval gate"))` returned `staging-failed` (red-on-old, run against the pre-fix file); the end-to-end test `test_a_new_post_eval_gate_is_never_reported_as_unspent` pins the fix.
- Non-vacuity, engagement gate (new code, no pre-fix counterpart): three mutations — swallow silence, pass partial engagement, delete the gate call — each red 2–3 of the new tests.
- Boot witness tests drive the REAL bash trace producer (`bin/lib/trace.bash`) through a fake wrapper, and assert the sink stays out of the workspace (`workspace.iterdir() == []`).
- Delta rendering: 133 tests in `test_visualize_deltas.py`, red-first evidence recorded during development.
- Baseline: `python3 .github/scripts/check-dangling-path-refs.py` green with the three entries deleted.

## Decisions made

- **Re-implemented fresh rather than rebasing #2590** — its base was rewritten by the rollback; the branch was used as reference only (all diffs extracted against its true base sha `d6654298`, never against restored main, which conflates PR content with rolled-back tree content).
- **Two-event engagement manifest instead of #2590's three.** The rolled-back tree had a `sbx_guardrail_engagements_verified` event whose producer no longer exists; requiring it would red every guarded cell forever. The manifest carries only events with live producers on the `sbx_services_start` path (`audit_sink_started` unconditional, `monitor_started` skipped only under `DANGEROUSLY_SKIP_MONITOR`, which the eval never sets).
- **Per-process boot-engagement log instead of #2590's readiness-record store** — that substrate (`READINESS_STORE_KEY` etc.) was rolled back; one driver process runs one cell (the same fact `SANDBOX_CONFIG_ENV` already rests on), so a process-global list the driver resets at staging carries the same evidence.
- **`visualize.py` now imports the failure-kind tags from `run_sbx_real`** (SSOT) instead of restating the strings — a renamed tag can no longer drift between producer and renderer.
- **Closing #2590 from this session** — normally the user's call; here "cut a smaller core PR" was the explicit instruction that supersedes it.

## Proposed guards

Not shipped here, per doctrine (a fix PR never ships a guard):

- **A. Render-tier CI job** — re-render the artifact page from a fixture result set on CT-touching PRs. Benefit: `visualize.py` is the most-churned CT file (12 commits/2 wk); render regressions plausibly ~10/yr; cost per escape = one wasted paid dispatch ($3–80) + a misleading report; catch fraction ~0.9 for crashes, low for wrong-numbers. Cost: one ~1-min unpaid CI job per CT-touching PR; as a *required* check it would also force a `ci-budget.json` swap. Verdict: defensible as **advisory**; weak as required. Left as a proposal.
- **B. ΔS positive-control cell (scripted variant)** — already human-promoted; ships as its own follow-up PR after this one merges (deterministic control pair injected into every e2e matrix; scorer gates ΔS publication on the control outcome; control failure renders `INSTRUMENT FAILURE / NO RESULT`). Deliberately not bundled here so the guard diff gets its own close review.

<details>
<summary>Author checklist</summary>

- [x] Commits use Conventional Commits (`<type>(<scope>): <desc>`)
- [x] User-facing change? Added a fragment under [`changelog.d/`](changelog.d/README.md) (not a `CHANGELOG.md` edit)
- [x] Tests added/updated and not skipped or weakened

items.title: feat: tak backfill — bootstrap history from published release binaries
items.body:
> **Stacked on #2.** Base is `verify-counters`; retarget to `main` once that merges.

## Why

A new adopter's first chart is empty, and an empty chart persuades nobody. Rebuilding a project at a hundred historical commits costs hours of compute and is impossible for anyone whose old commits no longer build. Downloading the binaries the project **already published** takes seconds and always works.

This is the one idea worth stealing from [Chronologer](https://github.com/dandavison/chronologer), which has been sitting unused.

## Worked example

Six releases of `sharkdp/hyperfine`, measured in seconds:

| release | instructions | |
|---|---:|---|
| v1.16.0 | 128,819 | |
| v1.16.1 | 128,819 | identical — a patch that didn't touch startup |
| v1.17.0 | 115,144 | −10.6% |
| v1.18.0 | 135,851 | +18.0% |
| v1.19.0 | 154,219 | +13.5% |
| v1.20.0 | 161,829 | +4.9% |

hyperfine's own `--version` startup grew **~40% between v1.17.0 and v1.20.0**. The two v1.16 releases coming back byte-identical is a useful sanity check on the whole approach.

Wall clock over the same set moved 0.23ms → 0.33ms — the same shape, far noisier.

## Design notes

**Asset selection is deliberately conservative.** A wrong pick produces numbers that look real and mean nothing, which is worse than backfilling nothing. Checksums, signatures, SBOMs, `.deb`/`.rpm`/`.msi`/`.pkg` are rejected outright; the OS must match; musl and tarballs score higher because they extract cleanly in slim images. If nothing matches, the release is skipped with a reason rather than guessed at.

**Records attach to the tagged commit** and carry the release's own `published_at` rather than now, so the series lands on the real timeline instead of bunching at the moment you ran the backfill. A shallow clone with no tags is a skip, not an error.

**No new dependencies.** Network and archives shell out to `curl` and `tar`/`unzip`, the same reasoning as `notes.rs` shelling out to `git` — proxies, CA bundles and credential helpers are already solved there.

**`--dry-run`** measures without writing, which is how the table above was produced.

## Tests

23 total. New pure-function coverage for asset scoring: rejects checksums and signatures, rejects other platforms, rejects distro packages, prefers musl over gnu, prefers tarball over zip, accepts `x86_64`/`amd64`/`x64` spellings, picks the best candidate from a realistic asset list, strips only the `v` prefix from tags (non-semver tags like `nightly` and `lts-iron` must survive untouched), and finds a nested binary.

`cargo fmt --check` and `cargo clippy --all-targets -- -D warnings` clean.

---
🤖 Generated with [Claude Code](https://claude.com/claude-code)

<!-- CURSOR_SUMMARY -->
---

> [!NOTE]
> **Medium Risk**
> New network/download path executes third-party release binaries and writes git notes; curl/token and HTTPS redirect handling are security-sensitive but deliberately hardened. Instruction-count API change affects all counter consumers.
> 
> **Overview**
> Adds **`tak backfill`** to bootstrap performance history by downloading published GitHub release assets, benchmarking them (default `--version`), and appending results to `refs/notes/tak` on each release’s tagged commit (using `published_at` when available). Supports `--repo`, `--bin`, `--dry-run`, and infers `owner/name` from `origin` when omitted.
> 
> Introduces **`src/backfill`**: paginated releases API via `curl` (HTTPS-only, token via stdin config), conservative platform asset scoring, fetch/unpack (`tar`/`unzip`), and safe path handling. Skips prereleases, drafts, missing platform assets, and tags not present locally.
> 
> **Measurement layer:** `instructions()` now runs cachegrind **three times**, returns a **`Counted`** struct (min used for storage), warns on high spread (`is_suspect`), and distinguishes missing valgrind (`Ok(None)`) from measurement failure (`Err`). **`tak run`** surfaces those warnings/errors.
> 
> **Git notes:** `notes::append` / merge use a fallback `user.name` / `user.email` when unset so backfill works in CI/containers.
> 
> README marks backfill as shipped; counter integration tests updated for the new API.

items.title: perf(utils): simpler and faster numpy padding fallback, test numba in CI
items.body:
Audit item #1 — but the conclusion is the **opposite** of what that audit proposed, now that I have measurements.

## The audit was wrong about numba; here are the numbers

I originally suspected numba was an unnecessary dependency. With it actually installed, it wins decisively:

| case | numba | numpy fallback (old) | simple loop |
|---|---|---|---|
| 16 short | **2.4 µs** | 7.2 | 7.1 |
| 64 mixed | **4.6 µs** | 37.1 | 25.1 |
| 256 mixed | **16.3 µs** | 321.2 | 97.0 |
| 8 very ragged | 7.2 | 35.2 | **4.9** |

5–20× faster, one-time JIT compile 179 ms. The `fast` extra earns its place. Retracting that part of the audit.

## What actually needed fixing: the fallback

The no-numba path built per-element row *and* column index arrays (`repeat` / `cumsum` / `searchsorted`) to perform a single vectorised scatter. Filling row by row is shorter **and** much faster — numpy already copies each row at C speed, so the index arrays were pure overhead:

```diff
-        batch_size = len(lengths)
-        row_indices = np.repeat(np.arange(batch_size), lengths)
-        cumsum = lengths.cumsum()
-        positions = np.arange(len(all_values))
-        groups = np.searchsorted(cumsum, positions, side='right')
-        prev_cumsum = np.empty(batch_size, dtype=np.uint32)
-        prev_cumsum[0] = 0
-        prev_cumsum[1:] = cumsum[:-1]
-        col_indices = positions - prev_cumsum[groups]
-        output[row_indices, col_indices] = all_values
+        offset = 0
+        for row, length in enumerate(lengths):
+            output[row, :length] = all_values[offset:offset + length]
+            offset += length
```

**4.7× faster at 256 rows** (321 → 69 µs), **7× on ragged input** (35 → 4.9 µs), 15 lines → 6.

## The bigger find: the fast path was never tested

CI ran `uv pip install ".[dev]"` and never `".[fast]"`. So numba — the path this package advertises for speed — **was not executed by CI at all**. Added an extras axis so both padding paths run against both transformers versions:

```yaml
        transformers: ["<5", ">=5"]
        # "dev" exercises the pure-numpy padding path, "dev,fast" the numba one
        extras: ["dev", "dev,fast"]
```

Four jobs instead of two.

## README

Since numba is a 5–20× win, it should not be buried in an optional extra nobody discovers:

```shell
pip install "utf8-tokenizer[fast]"
```

...with a note that the plain install still works and falls back to numpy.

## One honest caveat

The new fallback is algorithmically close to `pad_bytearrays_to_tensor_loop`, which `test_utils` uses as a reference — so in the plain `dev` leg, those 16 comparisons are less independent than before. Two things keep it honest: the new `dev,fast` leg means `pad_bytearrays_to_tensor` goes through numba there, making the comparison meaningful again, and `test_utils` has 9 assertions against an independent `torch.nn.utils.rnn.pad_sequence` reference that cover the plain leg.

## Verification

- **241 passed with numba installed** and **241 passed without it** (locally: numba+transformers 5.14.1, and no-numba+transformers 4.57.6).
- All three implementations asserted byte-identical on every benchmark case before timing.
- `ruff check .` clean.

> **Low Risk**
> Performance and test-matrix changes in padding utilities and docs; no auth or API contract changes.
> 
> **Overview**
> **Replaces the no-numba padding fallback** in `_fill_padded` with a short row-by-row copy loop instead of building scatter index arrays, improving performance when `numba` is not installed.
> 
> **CI now runs four jobs** (transformers `<5` / `>=5` × `dev` / `dev,fast`) so tests exercise both the pure-numpy and numba padding paths; install uses `".[${{ matrix.extras }}]"`.
> 
> **README** recommends `pip install "utf8-tokenizer[fast]"` and notes that the plain install still works with the numpy fallback.

items.title: bench(eval): ministr-vs-LSP code-nav runner — Phase 2 (harness)
items.body:
Phase 2 of the benchmark scaffolded in #131. Standalone PR off `main` (not stacked).

## What's here

`ministr-core/tests/eval_lsp_nav.rs` (`#[ignore]`, run via `just bench-lsp`):

1. Indexes the ministr workspace source in-process — `IngestionPipeline` + `QueryService`, the same pattern as the existing `code_ingestion.rs` / `multi_lang_symbols.rs` tests (no daemon, no model download).
2. For each `eval/lsp-nav/ground-truth.json` task, scores ministr's `definition` / `references` / `bridge` answers, and — when `eval/lsp-nav/ra.lsif` exists — rust-analyzer's, resolved via a minimal embedded LSIF reader.
3. Prints the README metrics table: definition accuracy, refs match, the cross-language **coverage gap**, ministr index time, per-query latency.

`just bench-lsp` = `bench-lsp-index` (RA `lsif`) → the ignored test.

## Design choices

- **Report-only, not a gate.** Only hard assertions are "ground truth exists and parses". A CI gate over a committed baseline is a deliberate later step (mirrors `just eval-gate`).
- **RA side degrades to `n/a`, never to wrong numbers.** Missing `ra.lsif`, or any task unresolvable in it, is reported as n/a — so the harness is runnable with or without rust-analyzer and never fabricates an LSP result.
- LSIF reader is intentionally lenient (RA's emission order varies) and only models what definition/reference resolution needs.

## Validation status (honest)

Compile-checked **and clippy-pedantic clean** (`-D warnings -W clippy::pedantic`), `cargo fmt` clean. The **end-to-end comparison was NOT run here** — a full ministr self-index plus a real `rust-analyzer lsif` are minutes-long and memory-heavy. The harness produces the numbers; they are not vetted in this environment. That run belongs in the dedicated CI job / a local invocation of `just bench-lsp`.

Next after this: expand ground truth (esp. `references` tasks), do a real validated run, then add the CI baseline gate. The companion agent solve-time benchmark (ministr vs no-ministr) is still planned and unstarted.

items.title: Discard a stop word without allocating it first
items.body:
Closes #80.

Stop-word removal is in the per-token path of every word-analyzed document, and
stop words are by definition the tokens that occur most. The three costs the
issue names are gone; nothing about *which* words are removed changes.

## What changed

**The token is judged before it is allocated.** On `net10.0` `TextAnalyzer`
tests `s.AsSpan(m.Index, m.Length)` against a `FrozenSet<string>` through its
`AlternateLookup<ReadOnlySpan<char>>`, so a stop word is discarded without ever
becoming a string. Only survivors reach `m.Value`.

**One list per first use.** The six lists were static property initialisers
sharing one static constructor, so `StopWords.English` hashed 1 493 words to
hand back 318. Each list now lives in its own nested holder type. The property
is deliberately `=> FrenchList.Value` and not `{ get; }`: a static field on
`StopWords` puts all six back behind one initialiser, and that is exactly what
the laziness test catches (see below).

**A shipped list is adopted, not copied.**
`ToFrozenSet(StringComparer.Ordinal)` returns its argument when the set is
already frozen with that comparer — verified, including that it *copies* when
the comparer differs — so no vectorizer re-hashes `StopWords.English`. A
caller's `HashSet<string>` is still copied: it is theirs to keep mutating, and a
fitted vectorizer that followed along would remove words its options never
declared. There is a test for that.

**`netstandard2.0` keeps the path it always had** — it has neither type. The
choice is made once, in `StopWordSet`, behind a single `#if`, in the shape of
`src/Shared/Guard.cs`.

`StopWords.Snowball.cs` is regenerated by `tools/fetch_stopwords.py`, which
emits the new shape; `--check` passes against the live Snowball sources and the
word sequence is byte-identical to before.

## Measured

`bench/DataNet.Text.Benchmarks/StopWordBenchmarks.cs`, over a corpus at the ~40%
stop-word density of English prose — 101 002 tokens over 1 000 documents, 39.8%
of them stop words, checked in `[GlobalSetup]` so the benchmark cannot quietly
stop measuring what it is named for.

Intel Core i7-4770S (Haswell), .NET 10.0.10, `main` (`c301cd3`) against this
branch, each run from its own tree on an otherwise idle machine:

| Case | Time before | Time after | Alloc before | Alloc after |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| `CountWithStopWords`, 200 docs | 9.003 ms | 8.490 ms | 6.62 MB | 6.34 MB |
| `CountWithStopWords`, 1 000 docs | 34.429 ms | 32.670 ms | 32.35 MB | 30.99 MB |
| `HashingWithStopWords`, 200 docs | 8.905 ms | 8.776 ms | 6.80 MB | 6.52 MB |
| `HashingWithStopWords`, 1 000 docs | 34.699 ms | 33.126 ms | 33.19 MB | 31.83 MB |

The 1.36 MB saved at 1 000 documents is the corpus's 40 241 stop-word tokens at
the ~35 bytes a five-character string costs — the measurement and the arithmetic
agree. The unfiltered baselines (`Count`, `Hashing`) are allocation-identical
across the two runs — 7.92 / 8.08 / 38.64 / 39.55 MB — which is what makes the
pairing trustworthy.

**What I would not claim:** at 200 documents the time difference sits at the
edge of run-to-run drift, and the unchanged baselines moved by ~3–4% between
runs. The ~5% at 1 000 documents holds against that drift on both vectorizers;
the allocation column is exact and reproducible either way.

Two traps were hit getting these numbers, both worth knowing: BenchmarkDotNet
re-resolves the project from the *working directory*, so a run launched from the
wrong tree measured `main` twice while reporting confident numbers — the
identical allocation column is what exposed it, and it is the same failure
`bench/README.md` §2 documents. And a parallel benchmark on the same machine
contaminated an earlier pair. The table above is from a quiet machine.

## Behaviour is unchanged, and shown to be

- Both oracle suites pass: 254 tests on `net10.0`, 255 on `netstandard2.0`.
- `French_produces_the_vocabulary_it_always_has` pins the vocabulary
  `StopWords.French` produces, captured from the build *before* this change.
- `A_word_a_stop_word_merely_starts_is_kept` guards the span slicing —
  "the"/"theatre", "for"/"forest" — which a wrong length would silently break.
- The lists stay `IReadOnlyCollection<string>`; the public API does not move.

## Lazy initialisation is demonstrated, not asserted

`Touching_one_list_does_not_build_the_others` loads the assembly into a fresh
`AssemblyLoadContext` — fresh statics, whatever the rest of the suite has
already touched — and reads an internal counter of built lists: 0, then 1 after
`French`, still 1 on a second read, 2 after `German`. The counter exists because
there is no other way to watch a holder type *not* initialise: any reflection
that could read its field would run its initialiser first.

It bites. Restoring `French` and `German` to static auto-properties fails it
with `Expected: 1, Actual: 2` — which is also how I learned that the nested
holder alone is not enough, since a beforefieldinit `StopWords` with no static
field of its own never runs its initialiser at all.

## Checks

`dotnet build` (0 warnings), `dotnet test` on both builds, `dotnet format
--verify-no-changes`, markdownlint, `check_version_floor.py`,
`fetch_stopwords.py --check`, and the doc snippets against freshly packed
packages — all clean.

items.title: docs: correct the Track A result, and say why the first one was wrong
items.body:
## What this is

The corrected Eyeblink8 result, plus an honest account of why the first
one was wrong.

|              | First answer, wrong | Corrected               |
| ------------ | ------------------- | ----------------------- |
| Blinks found | 284 of 408          | **338 of 408**          |
| Recall       | 69.6%               | **82.8%**               |
| Precision    | 86.3% (45 invented) | **86.4%** (53 invented) |
| F1           | 77.1%               | **84.6%**               |

Measured on a verified build, with the served bundle filename checked
against `dist/assets` before the run started.

**The last digit does not repeat.** This is one run, not a fixed value.
The same clip re-measured on the same computer and the same build gives
a different answer. One of the eight clips went from 7 false alarms to
9. Carried into the totals that reads 86.0% precision and 84.4% F1
instead of 86.4% and 84.6%. Recall stayed 82.8% in every re-run. Read
the last digit of precision and F1 as approximate, and read recall as
solid. The README and STATE.md say the same thing in the same words.

## Why the first number was wrong

The cause was in this repository, not in the recordings. `BLINK_LOG_CAP`
was 50 and fed a fixed length list that threw away the oldest entry
whenever a new one arrived. The same list was both the on screen panel
and the exported record, so the export inherited a display limit.

The cap counted DETECTIONS, not the blinks the human marked. That is the
part the first write up got wrong. It bit three clips, not two. Two of
them run past 50 annotated blinks, 88 and 72, and lost the opening
stretch of a real measurement. The third is `27122013_152435_cam`, the
second shortest clip in the set, which made exactly 50 detections and
lost its opening one. That row was a false alarm, so it changes no
recall figure anywhere on the page.

Pull request #172 fixed the cause. This pull request records the
consequence. The two truncated clips moved 55.7% to 89.8% and 58.3% to
91.7%, which is 30 and 24 blinks recovered, 54 in total, and that is the
entire move from 284 to 338.

## Both numbers stay on the page

The README prints the wrong answer next to the right one rather than
quietly replacing it. A project that shows you only its final answer has
told you less than one that shows you the wrong turn.
`docs/eyeblink8-result.txt` carries the full new output and the
superseded tables underneath it.

## The glasses claim is withdrawn, not reversed

The first write up said the one glasses clip scored 83.7% recall against
67.9% for the seven without, and read that as evidence against this
project's own warning about prescription lenses. That gap was an
artefact: both truncated clips sat in the group without glasses. The
corrected split is 83.7% with against 82.7% without. One clip of 43
blinks settles nothing in either direction, so the claim is withdrawn.

## Nothing is excluded to flatter the score

There is a version of this result that reads better. Leave out the
blinks the human marked as long closures and recall rises. Leave out the
partial blinks as well and it rises again. Carry the same reasoning one
step further, by leaving out the blinks the app missed, and it rises
further still, which is plainly cheating. The README describes all three
steps and prints none of the numbers. Neither does this description.

## What is still wrong, and said so

- 84.6% is behind published detectors on this benchmark, which report F1
  in the low nineties.
- 78.6% of the remaining misses, 55 of 70, contain at least one frame
  the human marked fully closed. That is a real weakness.
- Double counting is not fixed. 45 of the corrected run's 53 false
  positives sit on top of a real blink, and half of them are 3 frames
  long or shorter. A refractory period is named as next work, not
  claimed as done.
- The corpus was audited and is not the excuse. The rule and the number
  are published together, which they were not before. At 30 frames per
  second one frame lasts 0.033 seconds. Round each gap between two kept
  frames to a whole number of frame lengths. Anything above one is a
  lost frame. That gives 787 lost frames over 174 gaps, in all eight
  clips, which is 1.1% of the corpus. Twelve gaps are half a second or
  longer, they sit in three clips, and they hold 611 of the 787. At the
  very most the lost frames explain 4 of the 70 misses.

## The six agent review, and what it changed

The review returned MERGE AFTER EDITS with five must-fix items. Every
one is applied on this branch.

1. The number does not repeat, and the page 30 lines below claimed it
   does. A caveat about the last digit is now in all three documents,
   and the determinism section says its evidence is one 70 second clip
   and not the whole story.
2. The cap hit three clips, not two, because it counted detections. Four
   sentences across README.md, STATE.md and `docs/eyeblink8-result.txt`
   were wrong and are corrected. The same paragraphs claimed five of the
   six shorter clips shifted a blink edge. It is four. The other two
   report exactly the same blink timings.
3. The old "737 lost frames across 3 clips" contradicted itself. No
   single rule produces both halves. Recomputed from the clips' own
   `.txt` timestamp files, published with its rule, and backed by a new
   script at `analysis/tools/audit_frame_loss.py` so a reader can run it
   and get the same answer.
4. The F1 explanation was circular and its follow on sentence was false.
   Replaced with what F1 actually does.
5. This description carried four numbers that this same pull request
   retracts. Rewritten from the merged files.

Two verification passes then read the result. They found no wrong
number. They found sentences that were too long for a plain English
page, one missing full stop, and one acronym used before it was
explained. Those are fixed in a second commit. The pointer to the old
draft branch is also gone from both files, because that branch is
deleted when this merges.

## STATE.md

Two operational corrections beyond the result itself.

**The throughput claim was wrong and it mattered.** STATE.md said 8.4
frames per second and a 2.4 hour corpus run. A real run takes about 20
minutes at about 58 frames per second. The wrong figure made the corpus
look like an overnight job. It made DROZY, the next dataset, look like
a twenty hour one. The owner was close to rescoping the evaluation plan
around a cost that does not exist. The DROZY arithmetic is
rewritten with the real rate.

**The stale server trap.** The corpus runner drives a preview server on
port 4173. A leftover server from an earlier run holds the port and
serves the OLD BUNDLE while answering every request with a success code.
That happened today and produced a fake result of 69.1% from code that
had already been fixed. The check that catches it is now written down:
compare the bundle filename in `dist/assets` against the filename the
server actually serves, and refuse to measure on a mismatch.

## Gates

`npm run lint`, `npm run typecheck`, `npm test` (442 passed), `npm run
e2e` (7 passed), `ruff check` and `python -m pytest` (61 passed, 2
skipped) all green. Stale test counts in README and STATE.md updated to
match.

items.title: Reranking: the largest retrieval gain measured here — hit@5 0.671 → 0.777
items.body:
## The finding

§9a reported LOCOMO hit@5 **0.671** against hit@20 **0.855** and left the implication unexamined: for **85.5%** of questions the correct turn was *already retrieved* and merely ranked below position 5. That's a ranking failure, not a retrieval one — and this library has shipped a cross-encoder since 0.2 without any LOCOMO figure ever being measured with it.

**Turning it on: hit@5 0.671 → 0.777**, n = 1 536, intervals disjoint from the baseline through k=10.

| hit@k | no rerank | shipped `ms-marco-MiniLM-L-6-v2` | `bge-reranker-base` |
|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | 0.3978 | **0.5527** | 0.5645 |
| 5 | 0.6706 | **0.7767** | 0.7734 |
| 20 | 0.8548 | **0.8704** | 0.8724 |

That closes **57%** of the distance to the pool's own ceiling, and is roughly **twice** the largest embedder effect this project has measured (+0.059 median across 17 corpora). Every category gains, including the multi-hop floor (cat3 0.478 → 0.533).

### Why it's credible rather than merely large

1. **hit@20 barely moves** (0.855 → 0.870) — as it must when a *fixed pool* is reordered. A gain that also lifted k=20 would have meant something else changed.
2. **The gain decays with depth exactly as the mechanism predicts**: +0.155 at k=1 → +0.016 at k=20. Reordering can only act where truncation bites.
3. **A second, unrelated cross-encoder reproduces it.** `bge-reranker-base` — 12× the parameters, four years newer, multilingual — lands *within noise* at every depth. The effect belongs to **reranking**, not to a model choice.

Abstention is unchanged at 0.00 on all three arms (n=446): reranking reorders what retrieval returned and doesn't touch the trust layer.

## Kept optional, deliberately

**~1 050 ms/query** on CPU, ≈4× wall clock. A library that silently made every query four times slower to improve a benchmark would be optimising for the benchmark. So it stays off by default and one flag away, with the trade documented and the when-to-use split stated: human waiting for an answer → on; high-volume automated retrieval or constrained hardware → off.

`ms-marco-MiniLM-L-6-v2` remains the default, now **measured rather than assumed** — `bge-reranker-base` is statistically indistinguishable at **6.3×** the per-query cost.

## A correction

The README carried `cross-encoder rerank +0.065 *(n.s.)*` under the heading *"the pipeline was never the cap."* The measurement was fine — 110 questions, correctly non-significant *at that size*. The generalisation wasn't. Scope now stated, original numbers kept.

## The process changes, which matter more than the numbers

An earlier version of these results was **wrong**: two concurrent runs indexed the corpus twice (11 764 rows against a correct 5 882), every depth came in ~0.05 low, nothing errored, and it produced a *believable but manufactured* finding that reranking doesn't help multi-hop. A false **limitation** would have been published.

- **`run_conversation` now refuses to index over an existing tenant** (`fa29f47`), naming tenant and table. Refused rather than de-duplicated: a table in that state is evidence something ran twice.
- **`scripts/run_locomo_arms.sh`** takes a lock, drops each table, and **asserts the row count** before any result is trusted. Exit code 0 is not a measurement.
- **`docs/RESEARCH_PROTOCOL.md`** (`7ebb7ac`) makes prediction-before-measurement standard: predict the outcome, **assert the invariants in code**, fix the decision rule in advance, then score the prediction.

The protocol was used on its first outing and I got it **wrong** — predicted `bge-reranker-base` at 0.80 [0.79, 0.81], actual 0.7734 — with the scoring committed at `ac06550`. All four of my arguments pointed at "no gain" and I still wrote a positive number; the write-up says why. That record is the point.

## Verification

- Baseline **reproduces `results/locomo/postfix_pool20.json` to four decimals** — these rows sit in the same frame as §7's
- All three arms verified at **5 882 rows** before their numbers were read
- Tests pin the *wiring* separately from the outcome: a `RecordingReranker` counts calls, and one test asserts the reranker sees **more than k** candidates — reranking a list already cut to k cannot raise hit@k

items.title: v3: real prompts, raw model backends, budget-based scoring
items.body:
The results merged in #3 were invalid. This replaces the prompt set, both backends, and two scoring rules.

## Why the old numbers were wrong

`providers.py` shelled out to `hermes chat` — a personal agent CLI that loads a persona file, memory, skills, and 31 tools including a live terminal. Every "model" score was actually that agent wearing the model.

The evidence is in the saved responses: one model answered a latency question by citing `migration 049_job_question_id_idx.sql` and an untracked file in a local repo. Another narrated a skill lookup ("No postmortem skill exists, so I'll write it directly"). Several used an "Also found:" section that comes from the persona file, not the model.

`--safe-mode` does not fix this. Per the Hermes docs it disables *user customizations* for troubleshooting; the agent, its system prompt and its toolset remain. There is no CLI flag that yields a bare model.

## What changed

**Backends.** Removed the agent backend. Now OpenRouter for open models, a local Anthropic proxy for Claude. Both build the HTTP body directly with a plain system prompt and no tools.

**Contamination probe.** Every run now asks the backend what tools it has and aborts if the answer looks like an agent. Two full runs were thrown away for want of this check.

**Prompts.** The old 24 were authored by hand and skewed to workplace documents — postmortems, runbooks, layoff emails — which barely register in real usage. Replaced with 30 verbatim first-turn prompts from [WildChat-1M](https://huggingface.co/datasets/allenai/WildChat-1M), sampled to the distribution OpenAI published for its own 700M users ([NBER w34255](https://www.nber.org/papers/w34255)). Typos included. Two filter passes: classify into the taxonomy, then vet each for scorability.

**No more correctness checking.** Real prompts have no ground truth, and this benchmark measures readability. `facts` became `asks`, and the judge is explicitly told a confidently wrong but clear answer still counts as addressing the item.

**Rule 2 (economy).** Was words-per-fact, which had no idea what was asked and scored a complete 460-word postmortem at 0.0 — same as a rambling non-answer. Now scores length against a per-prompt word budget. Under budget is free, over budget decays to zero at 3x.

**Rule 3 (jargon).** Counted any 2-6 letter all-caps run as an undefined acronym. A grade-2 lesson plan scored 6.2 with 31 "acronyms": THE, BIG, FUN, SHAPE, CIRCLE. Now checks the system dictionary first. Regression-tested: shouting scores 10.0, `VPC`/`CIDR`/`IAM`/`EKS` still scores 0.0.

**Reporting.** `report.py` merged 12- and 24-prompt runs into one ranking and put a partial run in first place. Now groups by sample size and labels anything under 30 prompts as a non-comparable smoke sample.

## Results

30 prompts, judged by `claude-opus-5`:

| Score | Model | Slop/1k | Words | Economy |
|:---:|---|---:|---:|---:|
| **87.7** | `claude-opus-5` | 0.9 | 558 | 5.9 |
| **81.9** | `claude-haiku-4-5` | 2.2 | 329 | 7.3 |
| **80.9** | `claude-sonnet-4-6` | 3.4 | 531 | 6.8 |
| **80.6** | `claude-opus-4-6` | 2.8 | 571 | 6.3 |

Plus a 5-prompt smoke sample of five non-Claude models, clearly labelled as not comparable.

**Two findings.** Nobody writes to length: models run 1.5x-2.5x over budget, and economy does nearly all the separating while understandability and filler sit near 10 for everyone. And brevity is not free — `--condition brief` collapses every model to ~48 words, but coverage of the request drops 19-29 points with it. The old README claimed brevity cost nothing; that was measured on contaminated data.

The clearest version of that second finding is `claude-haiku-4-5`, the one model already close to its word budget at 329 words. Asked for 50 words it *loses* 4.8 points: it pays the coverage cost with no bloat left to cut. The three verbose models still gain, because they were far enough over budget for the trade to pay.

**Slop scoring was reworked after checking against [Wikipedia:Signs of AI writing](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wikipedia:Signs_of_AI_writing).** Vocabulary coverage was already 60/76; the problems were the two rules that fired most.

- *Rule of three* matched any three-item list — "rent, transportation, and food", "circle, triangle, and rectangle" — 262 hits across 265 responses, costing some answers the entire 30% slop cap for writing an ordinary list. Now requires adjectival items in a running sentence, since in a heading the triple is the content. 262 → 6.
- *Verbless noun-list fragments* are the case that rule was reaching for. "Rent, transportation, food." has no verb and no conjunction: the rhythm of a sentence with none of the content. The missing "and" is the tell, so the two rules are complementary.
- *Weighting.* Every hit counted as 1, so a labelled bullet (`- **Kernel version**: 6.1`) weighed the same as "delve" — and fired 231 times, more than every other signal combined. Weights are now 1.0 unambiguous, 0.5 contextual, 0.1–0.25 formatting.

All 265 saved responses were rescored deterministically, no model calls. The ranking moved: `claude-haiku-4-5` went 4th → 2nd.

Rejected after testing: 14 further WP:AITELLS phrases ("represents a shift", "plays a key role", "valuable insights") occur 0–3 times in 265 responses, and those hits are correct usage in literary analysis. Those are encyclopedia-puffery tells; this corpus is user Q&A.

## Known limits, stated in the README

- `claude-opus-5` judges the four Claude models including itself, and wins. Self-preference is exactly what that looks like. `rejudge.py` is the check and has not been run yet.
- Word budgets were set by a model, so absolute scores are softer than relative ones.
- The non-Claude table is 5 prompts and is a smoke test, not a result.

items.title: Evidence Chain v2.1: close A6, scaling/perf, novelty (review response)
items.body:
## Evidence Chain v2.1 — response to the external expert review

This PR implements the three **Areas for Refinement** from the external review of the
`src/evidence-chain/` audit package, plus the fidelity reconciliations needed to keep
the review's A+ artifacts accurate. Everything is held to the repo's complete-claim
rule — every claim below maps to a command run with recorded output.

A point-by-point map is in **`docs/REVIEW_RESPONSE.md`**.

### 1. Narrative / novelty (the review's only B+)
- **`docs/NOVELTY.md`** — states the unique contribution (one invariant definition
  *proved + enforced + recorded*), with an explicit **blockchain / distributed-ledger
  contrast** (why it is neither needed nor sufficient here) and honest prior-art
  positioning (CSL-Core, AGENL, FORGE, OPA/Rego, QuadSentinel).
- README gains a "High-Assurance Evidence Chain (the Audit Package)" section.

### 2. Scaling & performance
- **Found & fixed an O(n²) append** (`lastHash` re-read the whole file per write):
  16k entries **75 s → 1.9 s (40×)** via an O(1) tail-hash cache. A **1,000,000-entry**
  chain now builds in ~115 s and **fully verifies in ~142 s**.
- Complexities: **append O(1), verify O(n), Merkle O(n), membership audit O(log n)**.
  Runtime enforcement: **>1.7 M governed decisions/s** with all 22 invariants loaded.
- TLA+ reachable state space is the exact closed form **`11^C · 2^P`**, re-confirmed
  clean (no error) up to **644,204 states**.
- New: `src/evidence-chain/validation/bench.ts` + `bench-results.json`,
  **`docs/PERFORMANCE.md`**.

### 3. Open vulnerability A6 — CLOSED
- The v2.0 A6 red-team test was too narrow (garbage-sig only). The real attack —
  **edit the ledger, re-sign forged content under a substituted key, swap the
  co-located public key** — was accepted by `verify()`. A related **tail
  truncation/rollback** gap also slipped through.
- **Fix (out-of-band trust anchoring):** each entry binds its signer-key fingerprint
  into the signed payload; `verify(claimId, { expectedKeyFingerprint, expectedHead })`
  pins the trust root and chain head. New red-team vectors **A10** (key substitution)
  and **A11** (truncation) record *unpinned-accepts → pinned-rejects*. **Red-team is
  now 11/11 BLOCKED.**
- Full root-cause / fix / residual-risk writeup: **`docs/SECURITY-A6-DISCLOSURE.md`**.

### Fidelity reconciliations (so the A+ artifacts are actually accurate)
- **`traceability-matrix.yaml` re-synced** to the real `engine.test.ts` sections — the
  v2.0 matrix cited wrong section numbers and an `implemented_in: red-team-report.md`
  that **never existed** (the file is `.json`). Test count 73 → 88; **R1** status →
  `VERIFIED_BY_TLC`; added **R11** (A6 fix) and **R12** (performance).
- **CI gap closed:** `governance-ci.yml` gains an `evidence-chain` job — engine tests
  + **100% c8 branch-coverage gate** + red-team + empirical + benchmark +
  `EvidenceChain.tla` model-check. The graded audit package is now continuously
  enforced, not a one-time snapshot.

### Verification (this session)
- `engine.test.ts` — **88/88 pass**; new code 100% covered (only pre-existing
  `/* c8 ignore */` defensive blocks uncounted).
- Red-team runner — **11/11 BLOCKED** (`allBlocked: true`).
- Empirical pipeline — **3/3 claims VALIDATED**, chains intact.
- TLC `EvidenceChain.tla` — **"No error has been found"**; scaling sweep matches
  `11^C·2^P` exactly through 644,204 states.
- Full zero-dependency governance stack (tlc-sl 22/22, probe-gate, evidence-chain.mjs,
  integration, platform, signed evidence) — **green**; no-drift clean.

### Test plan
- [ ] CI `verify` job green (zero-dep stack + no-drift).
- [ ] CI `tlc-model-check` job green (TLA+ exports).
- [ ] CI `evidence-chain` job green (tests + 100% coverage + red-team + empirical + bench + EvidenceChain.tla).
- [ ] Review `docs/SECURITY-A6-DISCLOSURE.md`, `docs/PERFORMANCE.md`, `docs/NOVELTY.md`, `docs/REVIEW_RESPONSE.md`.

- Add out-of-band trust anchoring to the evidence-chain ledger via signer-key fingerprints, chain-head metadata, and pinned verification options exposed through the engine and audit bundles.

items.title: erase is an eraser: rub pixels out, put nothing back
items.body:
Both attempts at filling the hole back in are gone. Net −682 lines.

## the history behind the call

| approach | measured | why it went |
|---|---|---|
| `opencv.js` inpainting | never shipped working | 11MB dependency, dead offline |
| Telea, hand-written | 0.4/255 on plain, **22.8/255 on texture** | smeared on every real photo |
| PatchMatch content-aware fill, hand-written | 0.8/255 error, 0.98 detail on the same texture | won every benchmark, still looked wrong on real photographs |

PatchMatch was not a measurement failure — the numbers were real and the ground-truth harness was sound. It was a failure of the *premise*. A fill has to invent what was behind the thing you removed, and on a real photograph there is usually no honest answer sitting elsewhere in the frame. Two rounds of decent engineering aimed at a problem a flyer tool doesn't need to solve.

## what erase is now

`js/retouch.js`, ~250 lines. No worker, no engine, no dependency. You rub, the pixels go, whatever is behind shows through. It happens under your finger as you drag — there's nothing to run and nothing to wait for, so there's nothing that can be wrong about it.

- soft-edged brush, sized as a share of the photo rather than in screen pixels
- a chequerboard behind the photo, because "erased" has to read as *gone* and not as whatever colour the stage happens to be
- undo per stroke, clear back to the original, cancel discards, done applies
- zoom, pinch and pan kept
- the layer is saved as png — the transparency is the point and a jpeg has none

For a flyer this is the more useful tool anyway. Knocking a subject out of its background so the flyer's own colour shows through is a design move; a seamless patch of invented grass isn't.

## what went

`js/inpaint-worker.js` (516 lines), `tests/inpaint.test.mjs` (144), the mask overlay, the paint/wipe pair, the progress reporting, the `ed.busy` guard that existed so undo couldn't run during a long fill, and the worker's service-worker entry.

## tests

The old suites asked "did the pixels change" and "is the fill close to the truth". The eraser's test asks the only two questions a person has — **are the pixels I rubbed actually gone**, and **does my flyer show through the hole** — and reads both from the exported png rather than from an internal canvas's alpha channel. Plus: the rest of the photo is untouched, undo restores a stroke, the layer is kept as png, and the chequerboard is present.

140 checks across three suites, all passing.

## docs

`CLAUDE.md` now states that doc §7 is withdrawn and replaced, and that no inpainting dependency or algorithm should come back without reading `docs/ui-revision.md` rounds 7–9 — so a future session doesn't read the spec, see a missing feature, and helpfully rebuild it for a third time. README and TESTING.md updated to match.

items.title: Sourced scoreboard + Rust total-order panic fix (parity back to 300/300)
items.body:
Closes #11. Closes #14.

## README scoreboard (#11)
Replaces the Benchmarks section with a Scoreboard where every cell names its source. 140 lines -> 53.

- **Leads with the benefit**: same task, same agent -- roust solves 93.3%, grep 26.7%, embedding-RAG 71.4%. Says plainly that roust is NOT the most accurate retriever available (trained retrievers score higher); it is the best training-free, model-free point.
- **Reports absolute tokens and cost, not a savings ratio.** roust uses MORE tokens per attempt than grep (308k vs 240k) and wins on solve rate. grep is cheap because it gives up: 73.3% of its runs hit the turn cap and produce nothing.
- **Retracts the "95% fewer tokens than grep" claim** (#6). It came from the v1 one-shot retrieval-payload protocol, which is not how an agent uses the tool. `lab/README.md` keeps the v1 data intact under a retraction banner -- the numbers were honestly measured; only the framing was wrong.
- **Removes an invented "$ per solved task" metric** that ranked the WORST method cheapest. True cost-per-success requires per-task success probability, which one trial per pair cannot give. Tracked in #16 (pilot: #18).
- The `roust + grep` row is measured evidence for #5: giving the agent grep *alongside* roust drops solve rate 93.3% -> 57.1%.
- Removes an unbacked latency paragraph (~8.5k tokens / 150-550ms queries) that had no artifact behind it. Tracked in #15.
- Gaps are explicit placeholders linked to the issues that fill them: #1, #2, #3, #15, #16.

## Rust total-order panic (#14)
`roust-rs` panicked on `sympy__sympy-21171` with "user-provided comparison function does not correctly implement a total order", returning 1 file instead of 35. Introduced by `ea6b44f` -- a commit titled as a rename that also carried logic changes to `core.rs`/`cache.rs`/`main.rs`.

- Replaced `partial_cmp().unwrap()` with `f64::total_cmp` in every score comparator in `core.rs` (10 sites). `total_cmp` is a genuine total order under NaN/inf and agrees with `partial_cmp` on all finite inputs, so ranking is unchanged.
- Guarded the per-file token-cap calc: an infinite ratio saturated to `i64::MAX` on cast, then overflowed on add.
- Added `pack_regions_survives_nan_and_inf_scores` regression test.

**Validation: parity gate re-run over all 300 SWE-bench Lite instances (`parity/rust_gate_300_v3.json`): exact-match 300/300, errors 0, GATE: PASS. Zero new failures vs the v2 gate** -- all 299 previously-passing instances still pass, so the fix did not alter ranking semantics.

Caveat for the record: a NaN/inf reaching `pack_regions` via the real BM25/idf pipeline was not reproduced. These are hardened comparators with a regression test, not a fully traced causal chain. The panic is empirically gone and the gate is green.

items.title: perf(container): inline the resolve_provider body into resolve
items.body:
## Why

`Container.resolve(dependency_type)` looked the provider up and then tail-called `self.resolve_provider(provider)`, paying a second Python frame on the by-type path — the one every `@inject` marker and framework integration takes.

Retires `planning/deferred/2026-08-01-resolve-by-type-inline.md`.

## Design

`resolve` now carries its own copy of `resolve_provider`'s body: closed check, memo hit, `resolver_for` fallback, resolver call, `RecursionError` conversion.

**The duplicated ~8-line body is the standing cost, and it is permanent** — both copies must be edited together. That is the trade this PR asks you to have made, and it is recorded in the code, in `architecture/performance.md`, and in the decision doc.

**What licensed it:** `resolve_provider` stopped being an interception seam when the compiled resolvers landed in 2.29.0. Resolvers call each other directly; its only callers are `resolve`, `resolve_dependency`, and the cycle back-edge thunk. A `Container` subclass overriding it records **1 call while resolving a 4-node chain** on `main` — it has never seen the graph. Full reasoning, including why this is deliberately narrower than `2026-08-01-scope-map-inline-declined.md` (which stands), is in `planning/decisions/2026-08-03-resolve-provider-not-a-seam.md`. The reviewer verified that central claim independently: 1 call on main, 0 on this branch, 1 by reference on both.

## Non-goals

- **`find_container` is untouched and remains a blessed extension point.** This rules on one method, not on `Container` subclassing generally.
- **No enforcement or deprecation** of subclass overrides; the decision records that the resolve path is free to bypass `resolve_provider`, not that subclassing is forbidden.

## Verification

`just test-ci`: 477 passed, 100% line coverage on **both** 3.14 and 3.10 (3.10 run under a local interpreter, twice, since it is the version that gates this change). `just lint-ci`: clean.

**Measured** with the repo's A/B/A harness (`ab_run.sh main HEAD g16_by_type`), CPython 3.14, three runs: **-18.57%, -20.10%, -22.21%** (~40 ns), by-reference control `g2_cached` flat at +1.13%. Naming the scenario and version because the size is shape-dependent — the reviewer measured a differently-built by-type case at -10.6% on 3.14 and -37.8% on 3.10.

### One thing I got wrong, and the review caught

I previously reported the 3.10 coverage blocker as "verified fixable in ~10 lines of test", and PR #416 recorded that in the deferred item (now deleted by this PR). **That verification was flawed** — I checked with `--cov=modern_di.container`, and the line records fine under narrow tracing. Under the real gate (`--cov=modern_di`) it does not.

My first fix was a `# pragma: no cover` on the production line, with a comment claiming the handler is "reached only by a by-reference cycle". The review refuted both:

- The claim is false. A **by-type** cycle re-enters `resolve_provider` through the back-edge thunk and hits that line six times.
- What actually changed is that the two tests reaching it *without* a stack overflow (`SelfRec.__init__` raises `RecursionError` directly, so the tracer survives) go by type, and now land on `resolve`'s copy.
- So the fix is a by-reference twin of that overflow-free shape, not a suppression. `test_by_reference_recursionerror_passes_through` restores genuine 100% on 3.10.

**No `pragma: no cover` on any production line in this PR.** The cycle test stays with a corrected comment: it contributes no coverage, but it is the only guard on `resolve_provider`'s own conversion — replacing that conversion with a bare re-raise kills that test and nothing else.

## Known follow-up, not in this PR

`docs/introduction/performance.md` and `benchmarks/README.md` quote the by-type surcharge (60/54/65 ns; "roughly 40 ns on top of `resolve_provider`"). This change invalidates those figures. They come from the generated comparative table, which is republished at release time — hand-editing generated numbers here would be wrong, so this is flagged rather than done.

---

### Before merging

- [x] **Behaviour changed?** `architecture/resolution.md`, `performance.md` (counts corrected four/three -> six/four, plus a note recording the duplication where a reviewer would look for it), `containers.md`, `concurrency.md`, `validation.md`.
- [x] **Rejected an alternative?** `planning/decisions/2026-08-03-resolve-provider-not-a-seam.md`.
- [x] **Found real work you are not doing now?** The stale by-type surcharge prose, flagged above as a release chore.
- [x] `just lint-ci` and `just test-ci` pass, on 3.14 and 3.10.

items.title: Bump sofabgen to v0.17.1; fix c-embedded sized-blob driver fill
items.body:
## Summary

Bumps sofabgen **v0.17.0 → v0.17.1**, re-runs the arena, and makes the correctness gate fatal so the class of drift this bump surfaced can't slip past again.

v0.17.1 is a C/C++ bounded-storage bug-fix release:
- **C++**: the fixed-capacity string/blob-sequence decode loop is now bounded against a malformed over-count header (DoS, generator#126/#127).
- **C**: the backend emits a *sized* blob (and sized blob-array elements) so a sub-maxlen blob round-trips its true length instead of being padded to maxlen (generator#128/#129, #130/#131).

## Regression caught by the bump

The C sized-blob change adds a `bytes_field_len` member to the nested struct plus a zeroing `init()`. The hand-written `languages/c-embedded/sofab/bench.c` driver filled the 4 blob bytes but — with no length field before v0.17.1 — never set a length. Under the new API the blob serialized **empty**, so the c-embedded sofab wire silently dropped **434 → 428 B**, diverging from every other sofab backend.

The correctness gate only *warned* on wire divergence (it didn't fail the run), so nothing flagged this in CI. Fixed by adding `m->nested.bytes_field_len = 4;` — the 434 B reference wire is restored and the **full cross-language gate is green** (all 26 impls byte-identical to 434 B / 494 B).

## Gate hardening

Since the gate is the arena's fairness anchor, a MISMATCH is now **fatal**: it prints a loud FAIL to stderr and exits 1 **before** the reporting block, so a drifted wire (a) fails CI and (b) never overwrites a good `results/RESULTS.txt` with numbers measured on the wrong bytes. Intentional wire changes are still handled the documented way (update the four reference sync points); `ALLOW_WIRE_MISMATCH=1` downgrades it to a warning for local iteration. Verified: pass → exit 0; bogus reference SHA → exit 1 + FAIL with RESULTS.txt untouched; override → exit 0 + warning.

## Changes

| file | change |
|---|---|
| `scripts/bootstrap.sh` | version pin `v0.17.1` + extended comment block (stamp forces fresh binary + corelibs) |
| `languages/c-embedded/sofab/gen/example.{c,h}` | regenerated sized-blob C codegen |
| `languages/c-embedded/sofab/bench.c` | driver sets `bytes_field_len` for the new API |
| `languages/cpp-embedded/sofab/gen/example.hpp` | regenerated decode-path DoS guard (wire-neutral, stays 434 B) |
| `languages/go/sofab/message/sofab_visitor.go` | comment-only internal-ref cleanup the v0.17.0 bump missed for go |
| `scripts/run_benchmark.sh` | correctness gate now fatal on mismatch (+ `ALLOW_WIRE_MISMATCH` override) |
| `results/RESULTS.txt`, `README.md` | refreshed from a full `RUNS=5` pass |

## Notable result shifts

- Java now edges past protobuf (0.92× → **1.02×**); Zig at **2.3×**.
- Fresh `corelib-rs-no-std` shrank the Rust bare-metal footprints (rust-cortex-m 7038 → **5892**, rust-riscv 7674 → **6624**).

## Deliberately excluded

`setup.sh`'s unpinned `npm install` pulls in unrelated protobufjs 8.7.0→8.7.1 / tsx 4.23.0→4.23.1 patch bumps on every run — reverted here (Renovate owns those; the last bump commit carried no dep churn).

items.title: A cookbook of worked examples, and two fixes it found
items.body:
Adds `cookbook/` — worked examples where a real agent runs against a real task and the transcript is the output, including the trials that were thrown away. Building it surfaced two bugs in labloop, both fixed here with tests.

Opens **0.2.0**. `CHANGELOG.md` still said `0.1.0 — unreleased` although v0.1.0 was tagged on 2026-08-02 and is on PyPI; that section is now dated and closed, and the changes here sit under a new 0.2.0 heading.

## What ships in `src/`

Only 351 lines of this diff touch shipped code. Both changes came from using the tool, not from reading it.

**A `--min-delta` revert no longer describes a win as a loss.** A change can move the metric the right way and still revert, when the gain is inside the band `--min-delta` treats as noise. The explanation compared metric to incumbent and never mentioned the threshold:

```
before:  reverted: seconds 0.155 did not beat 0.2245; lower is better
after:   reverted: seconds 0.155 beat 0.2245 by 0.0695, but --min-delta needs
         more than 0.0727; the direction worked, the margin was too small to trust
```

`0.155` did beat `0.2245`, by 31%. `why` exists because the verdict is the one thing a proposer cannot reconstruct, and here it taught the opposite of what happened — the agent that read it abandoned a working direction and spent its next two trials on a wilder rewrite and a timeout. Real regressions and exact ties are untouched, pinned by tests that passed before the fix and still pass.

**`labloop noise` offers two thresholds instead of one.** It printed `--min-delta <spread>` alone. That is the safe-looking number and it is quietly expensive: on a recorded run it discarded three genuine speedups of 31%, 27% and 15%, one short by three milliseconds. It also contradicted the README, which reasons with the deviation. Both are now printed with the direction each errs in — conservative discards real work, permissive lets flukes through — because which mistake is cheaper depends on the experiment.

## The cookbook

Five recipes. Each names the metric, what is protected, and the cheat that protection exists to catch.

| Recipe | Result |
| --- | --- |
| [Identifier index over the CPython source](cookbook/02-proposers/agent-optimizes-real-code/) | 0.334s → 0.225s, on a metric with 22% noise |
| [A slow pytest suite](cookbook/03-real-tasks/speed-up-a-test-suite/) | 10.54s → 0.48s, 22×, test count unchanged |
| [Retrieval over stdlib documentation](cookbook/03-real-tasks/improve-rag-retrieval/) | nDCG@10 0.253 → 0.536 |
| [A prompt against a held-out eval set](cookbook/03-real-tasks/optimize-a-prompt/) | 0.289 → 0.889 |
| [Spam classifier](cookbook/01-first-loop/tune-a-classifier/) | the deterministic fixture the harness is tested against |

Three findings are worth more than the numbers:

- **Protecting `tests/` is the wrong instinct.** A slow suite's slowness lives inside the tests, so an agent forbidden from editing them cannot do the task. The harness protects a property of the run — 53 tests passed, none skipped, xfailed or deselected — with an acceptance check behind it the agent cannot touch.
- **`spread: none` can mean a broken harness.** The prompt eval measured zero noise three runs running. The parser was extracting nothing from every reply, so every run failed identically, and a metric that fails identically is indistinguishable from one that holds still. Fixing it revealed the 8.9% that had been there all along.
- **Four experiments on one machine measured 22%, 8.9%, 0.3% and 0%** — including two wall-clock benchmarks that differ by 70×, the noisier one being the smaller and simpler program. Collected in [noise-across-recipes.md](cookbook/noise-across-recipes.md).

## How the cookbook stays true

`tests/test_cookbook.py`, running in the existing CI job on all five supported Pythons.

Most recipes are `narrative` — they need a real agent, so their trajectory cannot be replayed. That left four of five with nothing guarding them. The fix separates the halves: *whether the agent did well* needs an agent, but *whether the harness still runs* is deterministic code, and it is the half that rots. This branch demonstrated that twice — a corpus built by parsing source silently lost every C module, and a parser that could not read markdown scored a correct answer zero.

So every recipe declares a `verify` command that runs regardless of tier. `verified` recipes additionally replay `run.sh` and have their ledger checked against the outcomes they claim — the ledger is the oracle, so a recipe claiming to demonstrate a caught cheat has to produce a `harness_changed` trial.

Every check was confirmed to fail before being trusted: a broken judgment, a wrong `expect` block, a README command absent from `run.sh`, a stale index, a missing tier. The last found a bug in the tests themselves — one malformed recipe raised `KeyError` at collection and took the whole file down instead of reporting itself.

## Skills

`cookbook/skills/` has three agent skills. They are **reference, not coaching**: what the nine outcomes mean, what the brief contains, what `--protect` covers.

An earlier draft gave strategy too — one focused change per trial, escalate specificity not scope — on the strength of one observed run. Three later runs did exactly what it forbids, with the skill installed. That advice is removed rather than caveated: a caveat does not stop an agent following an instruction, and one anecdote for against three against is not a basis for shipping one.

## What this does not claim

- **The skills are not demonstrated to help.** Measuring that needs paired runs and statistics — an `experiments/` job, not a cookbook claim.
- **Agent runs are not reproducible.** What reproduces is the shape: some proposals clear the bar, some do not, and the ones that do not are still recorded.
- **22× is a property of that test suite**, which was built with fixable problems in it.

## Checks

`256 passed` (up from 235), `ruff` clean, `mypy --strict` clean, sdist builds and now ships `cookbook/` — it already shipped `tests/`, so the cookbook tests would have failed in an unpacked sdist without it. Suite is ~30s, up from 16s; the cost is one recipe whose entire subject is a slow test suite, and `CONTRIBUTING.md` is updated to match rather than left to drift.
